It does not say what the findings rest on: a selection of 80 rows chosen by the author, rated with LLM help against statutes and a single housing benchmark of about 6 000 completions a year. It also does not say what would change a rating, for example a new state law on short-term rentals or the tourist fee, or a project that is further along than the programme shows. The most useful practical sentence is buried at the end of line 124: 'The steps most clearly in the city's own hands are its building regulations, its parking and fares, the rules for allocating city flats and its own budget rules.'
findings.evidence: Lines 91-96; line 124, last sentence.
findings.fix: Add two bullets: 'What is clearly in the city's hands: building regulations, parking and fares, allocation of city flats, budget rules.' and 'Ratings are one reader's judgement on 80 selected promises against the statutes cited; a change in state law or a project already further along would change them.'
findings.note: It is true that the tldr (lines 91–96) does not say what the findings rest on or what would change a rating. Line 95 does give the scope caveat. This is an editorial preference rather than a verifiable error.

findings.location: texts/prague-programmes-2026.html:116 'builds the motorway ring' / :124 'the city ring road'
findings.problem: The note relies on the difference between the 'motorway ring' (Pražský okruh, state, rated 'other') and the 'city ring road' (Městský okruh, city, rated 'partly' or 'yes'), but never explains it. English readers will take the two as the same road. The STAN row (lines 396-399) adds to the confusion: the city ring road appears in the 'Why not' text but not in the row title.
findings.fix: At line 116 add: 'the motorway ring (Pražský okruh, an outer motorway built by the state) is not the city ring road (Městský okruh, an inner road built by the city)'.
findings.note: The note never explains the difference between the 'motorway ring' (lines 116, 220) and the 'city ring road' (lines 192, 315, 593, 702). Line 399 discusses the city ring road although the row title (line 396) does not name it.

findings.location: texts/prague-programmes-2026.html:173, 287, 315, 324, 526, 663, 192
findings.problem: Several technical terms are used without explanation at first use: 'planning contract' (173), 'acceleration-zone act' (287), 'radial' (315, 467), 'general measure' (324), 'Housing First' (526), 'pre-emption right' (663), 'Blanka II' and 'Industrial half-ring' (192, 199), 'local coefficient' (116, explained only partly). Also 'zoning plan' vs 'building regulations' (543, 574).
findings.evidence: First-use lines as listed.
findings.fix: Add a short gloss in parentheses at first use, e.g. 'radial (a road from the centre to the city ring road)', 'general measure (a decision of the city council that binds everyone, below the level of an ordinance)', 'planning contract (an agreement in which a developer pays or gives something to the city in exchange for a zoning change)'.
findings.note: 'General measure' (line 324), 'planning contract' (line 173), 'radial' (line 315), 'pre-emption right' (line 663) and 'acceleration-zone act' (line 287) appear without a gloss anywhere on the page. Low severity.

findings.location: texts/prague-programmes-2026.html:124 'even 8 000 city flats would be more than the whole market completes in a year'
findings.problem: The comparison is framed against one year, but Praha Sobě's promise is to 'start preparing' 8 000 flats with no timeframe, and the note itself uses a four-year term as its yardstick (about 24 000 completions). Comparing it to one year's output makes the promise look more infeasible than the rating ('partly') says it is.
findings.evidence: Line 164 (rated partly, 'Start preparing'); line 117 (6 000 a year).
findings.fix: Use 'Praha Sobě's 8 000 city flats, with no timeframe, would be a third of what the whole market completes in four years'.
findings.note: Line 124 is literally accurate: 8 000 is more than the roughly 6 000 completed a year. The Overall at line 236 already flags '8 000 flats' as a number without a timeframe. Whether comparing it to one year is misleading is a judgement call, not a factual error.

findings.location: texts/prague-programmes-2026.html:787-789 changelog
findings.problem: The change log is out of order: version 3 is listed between version 1 and version 2.
findings.fix: Order the entries version 1, 2, 3, or newest first (3, 2, 1).
findings.note: This duplicates [10]. Lines 787–789 order the versions 1, 3, 2.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html, meta 'data' row and Data section: "kworb.net Spotify chart totals for the global chart and 76 national charts" / "for the global chart and 76 national charts"
findings.problem: The collection has 76 totals pages in all, one of which is the global chart, so there are 75 national charts and not 76.
findings.evidence: tools/data/pop/raw/totals/ holds 76 files including global.html; tools/data/pop/raw/daily has 75 non-global files; collected.json 'countries' list includes 'global' and 'missing': ['ad']. 72 countries in assets/pop/harry-styles/countries.csv, i.e. cy, mt and ru are the 3 national charts where As It Was did not appear.
findings.fix: "for the global chart and 75 national charts" (both places), or "76 charts, the global one and 75 national".
findings.note: tools/data/pop/raw/totals has 76 files, one of them global.html; raw/daily has 75 non-global files. So it is 75 national charts, not 76.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html, 'One song or a catalogue': "The list counts every song on his page, including the few where he is a featured artist"
findings.problem: The data contain no featured songs. All 49 rows have feature=False, so the sentence describes something that is not in the data.
findings.evidence: assets/pop/harry-styles/songs.csv: count of feature=='True' is 0 of 49. The raw page tools/data/pop/raw/songs/harry-styles.html has no trailing '*' on any track title (the parser at tools/pop/parse.py:217-223 uses that mark for features).
findings.fix: "The list counts every song on his kworb page; none of the 49 is marked as a feature, and it counts only Spotify." Alternatively, check whether kworb leaves features off this page and say so.
findings.note: songs.csv has 0 of 49 rows with feature=True (the same holds for every artist's songs.csv). The sentence 'including the few where he is a featured artist' describes nothing in this data. Design §4 only requires the article to state the rule.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html, 'How long As It Was lasted': "the share still in falls to 25 % at two years"
findings.problem: The Kaplan–Meier survival at 730 days is 26 %, not 25 %. The generator reads the first curve step at or after t (750 days) and not the last step at or before t.
findings.evidence: results.json q1.curve: (717, 0.2624), (750, 0.2544). tools/pop/article.py:48 surv = next(v for d,v in curve if d >= t), which returns S(750)=0.254 for t=730. The correct S(730)=S(717)=0.262. The 1000-day value (14 %) is correct because a step falls exactly at 1000.
findings.fix: "falls to 26 % at two years". In article.py, use the last step with d <= t: max((d,v) for d,v in curve if d <= t).
findings.note: In results.json the curve has steps (717, 0.2624) and (750, 0.2544). article.py's surv lambda uses the first step with d >= t, so S(730) is reported as 25 % when it should be 26 %.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html, 'Where it lasted': "the middle country kept it about 2.1 times as long"
findings.problem: The median of the 72 ratios is 2.0497, which rounds to 2.0. The 2.1 comes from taking the upper of the two middle values (sorted[len//2]), and it makes Czechia (2.06 rounds to 2.1) look identical to the median.
findings.evidence: q2.countries ratios: rank 36 Singapore 2.0505, rank 37 Italy 2.0488, so the median is 2.0497. tools/pop/article.py: q2_median_ratio = sorted(...)[len(cs)//2].
findings.fix: Use the true median (statistics.median) and write "about 2.0 times as long" (or "about twice").
findings.note: statistics.median of the 72 ratios is 2.0497, which rounds to 2.0. article.py takes sorted[len//2] = 2.0519, which rounds to 2.1.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html, references r1–r9 and the order of first citation
findings.problem: The references are not numbered in order of first citation. In the body, r4 (Aguiar & Waldfogel) is cited before r3 (Courty & Pagliero). The 'About this study' meta box cites r6–r9 before any of r1–r5. r5 (Kaplan–Meier) is first cited only after r6–r9.
findings.evidence: Sequence of <sup class=cite> in the page: meta 6,7,8,9; introduction 1,2,4,3; Data 6,7,8,9; Methods 5.
findings.fix: Renumber by first citation. If the meta box is excluded, swap so Aguiar & Waldfogel becomes [3] and Courty & Pagliero [4]. If it is included, renumber all nine.
findings.note: Citations appear in the order 6 7 8 9 1 2 4 3 6 7 8 9 5. In the body r4 comes before r3, and r5 is first cited after r6–r9.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html, introduction: "Concert prices, meanwhile, are set by a few promoters in one currency for very different audiences, and Courty and Pagliero describe how much of the pricing happens in ways a fan never sees[3]"
findings.problem: The claims next to the citation (a few promoters set prices, in one currency for different audiences, pricing a fan never sees) are not what Courty and Pagliero's chapter is about. The chapter covers pricing styles: price discrimination across seat categories, underpricing and resale. The sentence over-reaches what the source supports.
findings.evidence: Crossref 10.1016/B978-0-444-53776-8.00013-1: 'The Pricing of Art and the Art of Pricing: Pricing Styles in the Concert Industry', Handbook of the Economics of Art and Culture vol. 2, 299–356. The metadata matches the reference.
findings.fix: "…and Courty and Pagliero describe how concert tickets are priced: how many seat categories, how far below what fans would pay, and what resale does to that[3]." Drop the promoter and currency clause or give it its own source.
findings.note: The sentence on line 75 says prices are 'set by a few promoters in one currency'. Tickets are sold in local currencies (line 160 itself mentions the exchange rate), and the chapter title is about pricing styles. At least the promoter/currency clause has no support in [3]. I did not read the full chapter.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html, deck, og:description and 'What this means': "the same tour cost 10.4 days of income per ticket in the Philippines … 0.29 in Norway"
findings.problem: The Q5 country averages pool two tours, Harry Styles: Live on Tour (2017–18) and Love On Tour (2022–23), so 'the same tour' is not accurate.
findings.evidence: assets/pop/harry-styles/tour.csv: the Philippines has entries from 2018 (Mall of Asia Arena, Live on Tour) and 2023 (Philippine Arena, Love On Tour). Norway has 2018 (Oslo Spektrum) and 2022 (Telenor Arena). pop-measured-design.md §4 computes the per-country price over all of a country's entries.
findings.fix: "his tours cost 10.4 days of income per ticket in the Philippines and 0.29 in Norway" (or "the same tours").
findings.note: tour.csv: PHL has Pasay 2018 (Live on Tour) and Bocaue 2023 (Love On Tour); NOR has Oslo 2018 and Oslo 2022. 'The same tour' is inaccurate. This duplicates [13].

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html, TL;DR: "Czech listeners were exactly as loyal as the world's middle" and "two other songs come close to it"
findings.problem: Both are stronger than the numbers in the body. Czechia ranks 35th of 72 at 2.06×, against a median of 2.05×, so it is near the middle but not exactly at it. Watermelon Sugar (11 %) and Sign of the Times (8 %) have 73 % and 53 % of As It Was's streams, which the body itself describes as 'more than half its streams', not 'close'.
findings.evidence: q2.czechia rank 35, ratio 2.0557. songs.csv shares 0.153, 0.112 and 0.081.
findings.fix: "Czech listeners sat near the world's middle" and "two other songs each have more than half its streams".
findings.note: Czechia is 2.056×, rank 35 of 72, against a true median of 2.050, so it is near the middle, not 'exactly' there. Shares are 15.3 %, 11.2 % and 8.1 %. The body says 'more than half its streams', not 'close'.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html, 'Where it lasted': "By days alone, … Czechia is 21th."
findings.problem: Wrong ordinal suffix.
findings.evidence: q2.czechia.rank_by_days_post_hoc = 21. The template appends 'th'.
findings.fix: "Czechia is 21st." Ordinals should be generated with the correct suffix in tools/pop/article.py or the template.
findings.note: Line 104 reads 'Czechia is 21th.' and rank_by_days_post_hoc is 21.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html, 'Where it lasted': "Japan (0.35×, 236 days against a median of 678)" and "Turkey (0.51×, 184 days against a median of 360)"; also "a median of 678 days"
findings.problem: The medians are half-days that the formatter rounds inconsistently: 678.5 is shown as 678 (banker's rounding) and 359.5 as 360.
findings.evidence: q2.countries: jp median_ones_days 678.5, tr 359.5. Python's f'{x:,.0f}' rounds half to even.
findings.fix: Show one decimal for half-day medians (678.5, 359.5), or round half up consistently (679, 360).
findings.note: In results.json jp median_ones_days is 678.5 and tr is 359.5. The page shows 678 and 360, because round-half-to-even rounds the two in opposite directions.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:41, 92, 155 (headline '5.5 % ... 165 songs'); docs/research/harry-styles-ones.csv row 'The Chainsmokers - Closer'
findings.problem: The headline reference set includes The Chainsmokers' 'Closer', a 2016 song whose start in the chart is not seen. The registered rule (design §3 Q1) excludes such songs. It got through only because the parser gave it a first_listed date of 2026-03-05. The song is censored at 1 952 days, above As It Was's 1 594, so it sits in the at-risk set and raises the headline figure.
findings.evidence: harry-styles-ones.csv: 'The Chainsmokers - Closer', days 1952, first_listed 2026-03-05, still_charting True, kept True. Starboy (2016) is correctly excluded with first_listed 2016-09-22. Recomputing the Kaplan–Meier S(1594) with the same estimator as analyse.py gives 0.0552 with Closer and 0.0456 without it, with n = 164 and 30 exclusions instead of 29.
findings.fix: Treat an impossible first_listed date (later than a song's own peak or chart run, or a song known to be pre-2017) as unseen, and exclude Closer. Re-run Q1, update 5.5 %, the 165/29 counts and the interval everywhere, and log the correction under 'What changed after registration'.
findings.note: Closer has first_listed 2026-03-05 but 1952 days, which is impossible, and kept=True; Starboy is correctly excluded. My own KM recompute gives S(1594) = 0.0552 with Closer and 0.0456 without, n = 165 against 164.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:92 'Because it has not left, that share can only fall.' and :155 'the figure can only fall while it stays in the chart'
findings.problem: The page says the 5.5 % estimate can only fall. That is true only of the true quantity, and only if every other song's run were complete. 28 of the 32 censored number ones have fewer days than As It Was so far, mostly 2024–2026 hits. Kaplan–Meier assumes they will leave at the usual rate. If some of them pass 1 594 days, the estimated share above As It Was's mark goes up. So the estimate can move either way.
findings.evidence: Censored songs in harry-styles-ones.csv with fewer than 1594 days include Beautiful Things (986), Djo – End of Beginning (957), Espresso (902), BIRDS OF A FEATHER (867), Die With A Smile (776) and APT. (712). analyse.py surv_at() treats them as at risk under independent censoring.
findings.fix: Change it to: 'Because As It Was is still charting, its true place is at or above this one, but the estimate can still move as the 31 other songs still in the chart finish their runs.'
findings.note: Of the 32 censored kept songs, 27 (not 28) have fewer than 1594 days. If they later run past 1594, the KM estimate at 1594 can rise, so 'can only fall' does not hold for the estimate.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:41 facts box '5.5 % <small>... still charting, so at least</small>'
findings.problem: The label 'at least' points the wrong way. The censored quantity is As It Was's days, which are at least 1 594. That makes the share of number ones that lasted longer at most 5.5 %, as the body text says ('can only fall'). A reader of the facts box will read 'at least 5.5 %'.
findings.evidence: Design §4 applies 'still charting, at least' to days, not to the share. Line 92 of the body says the share can only fall.
findings.fix: Use '1 594 days, still charting, so at least' as the label, or reword it to '5.5 % or fewer (still charting)'.
findings.note: Line 41 puts 'still charting, so at least' under the 5.5 % share. Censoring makes the days a lower bound, so the share is an upper bound, and line 92 says it can only fall.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:39 deck 'the same tour cost 10.4 days of income per ticket in the Philippines ... 0.29 in Norway'; :53 'the same ticket weighed very differently'; :135 'the same tour cost'; :155 'the same tour cost a ticket-buyer'
findings.problem: Q5 pools two tours and several years (2017–2018 Live on Tour and 2021–2023 Love On Tour) into one figure per country. The Philippines and Norway figures each mix a 2018 show with a 2022 or 2023 show. 'The same tour' and 'the same ticket' are therefore inaccurate. The ticket prices also differ: 104 against 83 dollars.
findings.evidence: harry-styles-tour.csv: PHL has Pasay 2018 (Live on Tour) and Bocaue 2023 (Love On Tour); NOR has Oslo 2018 (Live on Tour) and Oslo 2022 (Love On Tour). analyse.py q5() sums revenue and tickets per iso3 across both tours.
findings.fix: Say 'his two tours (2017–2023), pooled' in the deck, the tldr, line 135 and line 155. Replace 'the same ticket' with 'a ticket'.
findings.note: Same check as [6]: PHL and NOR each mix a 2018 Live on Tour show with a 2022 or 2023 Love On Tour show. 'Same tour' and 'same ticket' (lines 39, 53, 135, 155) are inaccurate.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:137 'It does show who the price was set for: one tour, priced in dollars, landed on very different wallets.' and :75 'Concert prices ... are set by a few promoters in one currency for very different audiences'
findings.problem: Tickets were sold in local currencies. Boxscore converts the gross to US dollars at the exchange rate of the time of reporting, which the page itself says at line 160. 'Priced in dollars' and 'set ... in one currency' therefore misdescribe the data. 'Who the price was set for' is a claim about the pricers' intent, and no data here measure it.
findings.evidence: Series design §4 Q5: 'exchange rates are those used when the gross was reported'. Nothing in tools/pop measures how prices were set.
findings.fix: Rewrite line 137 as: 'Converted to dollars, the average tickets were close in price, but they weighed very differently against local incomes.' Remove 'in one currency' from line 75, or add a source for it.
findings.note: Line 137 says 'one tour, priced in dollars', and line 75 says 'in one currency'. Line 160 itself says grosses are converted at the reporting exchange rate, and the two tours are pooled. Nothing in the data measures who the price was set for.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:87 'the same song's days in each national chart are divided by the median days of that country's own number ones'
findings.problem: The country median is a plain median of raw Days, and the page does not say so. It counts still-charting number ones at their current days, unlike Q1, which uses Kaplan–Meier. It counts songs whose start predates the country chart, it counts the focal song itself, and it ignores when each country's chart began. These choices drive the central Q2 ratio and the Czech rank. Only the late-start problem appears, and only at the end (line 160).
findings.evidence: analyse.py q2(): med = np.median(ones) over every value in ones_days. harry-styles-countries.csv, ae row: ones_days contains 1533, As It Was itself. Line 160 is the only mention of chart start dates.
findings.fix: Add one sentence at line 87: 'Unlike the global curve, the country median uses each number one's days as they stood on 1 October, including songs still in the chart and this song itself, so for countries with many recent number ones it is a low estimate.' Repeat the caveat next to the Czech result.
findings.note: analyse.py q2 uses np.median over the raw ones_days with no censoring adjustment. The ae row's ones_days includes 1533, the focal song itself. Line 87 does not mention either point.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:51 tldr 'Czech listeners were exactly as loyal as the world's middle' and :155 'Czech listeners sat at the world's middle'
findings.problem: 'Loyal' turns a ratio of chart days to a country's median number one into a statement about how listeners behave. 'Exactly' overstates rank 35 of 72 with a 95 % interval of 1.7–2.4. On the post-hoc measure of days alone, Czechia ranks 21st. Line 103 itself warns that the ratio 'says more about [a] chart than about its listeners'.
findings.evidence: results.json q2.czechia: ratio 2.056, CI 1.73–2.39, rank 35, rank_by_days_post_hoc 21. The median ratio across countries is 2.05.
findings.fix: Use: 'In Czechia it lasted about 2.1 times as long as the typical Czech number one, close to the middle of 72 countries.'
findings.note: q2.czechia: ratio 2.056, CI 1.73–2.39, rank 35, rank by days 21. 'Exactly as loyal' and 'loyal' both overstate the result. This overlaps [7].

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:102 'two markets where domestic music fills the top of the chart'
findings.problem: This explains the Japanese and Turkish results by the domestic share of their charts. That is a causal explanation, and the study does not measure the domestic share. Line 87 says 'Nothing here is causal'.
findings.evidence: No variable for the domestic share exists in harry-styles-countries.csv or in parse.py and analyse.py.
findings.fix: Remove the clause, or mark it as untested: '(the study does not measure how much of these charts is domestic music)'.
findings.note: No variable for the domestic share exists in countries.csv or in analyse.py. The clause on line 102 is an unmeasured explanation, while line 87 says nothing here is causal.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:93 'the chart cannot tell, on the day a song reaches the top, which kind it will be'
findings.problem: This claims that durability cannot be predicted at the time of the peak. No analysis tested that: no model was fitted on peak-day features.
findings.evidence: analyse.py q1() computes only a Kaplan–Meier curve and placements. No predictive step exists.
findings.fix: Remove the clause, or reword it as: 'this study does not test whether durability can be told on the day a song reaches number one.'
findings.note: analyse.py q1 fits only KM and placements, with no predictive step. 'The chart cannot tell, on the day a song reaches the top' is an untested claim.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:48-55 details.tldr
findings.problem: The short version has no numbers and no clear basis for each result. It says nothing about what would overturn the results, for example the censoring of As It Was and of 31 other songs, the use of plain median ratios by country, or the pooling of tours. 'Two other songs come close to it' (line 52) also overstates 11 % and about 8 % against 15 %.
findings.evidence: tldr lines 50–54. results.json q4: top share 0.153, top three 0.346, so the third song is about 8.3 %.
findings.fix: Add figures (5.5 %, 2.1×, 93 % sold out, 10.4 against 0.29 days). Add one line on what could change them: 'The rank rests on songs still charting; if recent hits outlast As It Was, it falls.' Change 'come close to it' to 'each have more than half its streams'.
findings.note: The facts box next to the TL;DR already carries the figures, so asking for numbers in the TL;DR is a style call. The 'come close' overstatement is real but duplicates [7].

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:86 'Kaplan–Meier estimator ... censored ... 2 000 bootstrap resamples'; :87 'Spearman's correlation'
findings.problem: The central technical terms appear without a plain explanation. 'Kaplan–Meier' has only a gloss on censoring. 'Bootstrap resamples' and 'Spearman's correlation' are not explained. 'Censored' is explained in passing only.
findings.evidence: Line 86 introduces the Kaplan–Meier estimator, censoring and the bootstrap. Line 87 introduces Spearman's correlation. Neither line says what the terms mean in practice.
findings.fix: Add a short explanation for each. Kaplan–Meier: 'a way to estimate how many songs remain in the chart after t days when some have not left yet'. Bootstrap: 'repeating the calculation on 2 000 random redraws of the songs to see how much it moves'. Spearman: 'whether longer runs tend to sell a smaller share, using ranks rather than values'.
findings.note: Line 86 glosses censoring but not bootstrap. 'Spearman's correlation' on line 87 has no plain explanation. This is a low-severity clarity point.

findings.location: texts/pop-harry-styles.html:93 'a few become part of what people play every week for years'
findings.problem: The measure is total days, not consecutive days, as line 160 says. 'Every week for years' implies a continuous run, which the measure cannot show.

findings.problem: The United States figure is wrong: Cruel Summer spent 902 days in the US chart, not 0.7. The 0.7 looks like a template slot filled with the wrong value; it matches the US ticket cost in days of income (0.746) or the Japan ratio.

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:51 and :115 and :163 "Her listening is the most spread of the series" / "57 songs, the most of any artist in the series" / "Her listening is the most spread in the series"
findings.problem: Only the raw count of songs that make up half the streams supports "most spread", and that count grows with catalogue size (500 songs listed for her, against 271 for Bad Bunny and 319 for BTS). The registered Q4 measures point the other way. Her Gini (0.642) is the highest in the series, which makes her the most concentrated by that measure. Bad Bunny has a lower top-song share (2.1 % vs 2.7 %) and a lower top-three share (5.9 % vs 6.3 %). As a share of catalogue, 57/500 = 11 % is the lowest of the five: BTS 13 %, Harry Styles 12 %, Bad Bunny 17 %, Billie Eilish 18 %.
findings.evidence: q4 in the *-results.json files: gini HS 0.561, TS 0.642, BTS 0.640, BB 0.541, BE 0.518; top_share TS 0.027, BB 0.021; top3 TS 0.063, BB 0.059. Half-of-streams counts recomputed from *-songs.csv: HS 6/49, TS 57/500, BTS 41/319, BB 46/271, BE 14/79.
findings.fix: Drop "most spread of the series" in the TL;DR, body and conclusion, or say "half her streams come from 57 songs, the largest number in the series, partly because her page lists the most songs (500); by the Gini coefficient (0.64) her listening is as concentrated as any in the series."
findings.note: q4: TS Gini 0.642 is the highest of the five (BTS 0.640, HS 0.561, BB 0.541, BE 0.518). BB top_share 0.021 and top3 0.059 are below TS (0.027, 0.063). Songs listed are 500 vs 271/319, so 'most spread' rests only on the raw count of songs to half.

findings.note: pop-measured-design.md lines 95-97 date the peak-2 reference-set change '2 October 2026, same note', i.e. after the part 2-5 results were first computed. The article line 154 says '1 October 2026, before any data of this part were parsed'.

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:39 deck "the Eras Tour moved no measurable price for residents of the countries it played"; also :148 "It says that residents, at the level of their country's prices, did not pay for the tour."
findings.problem: This overstates the registered result. Accommodation, the primary question (Q1), is labelled inconclusive with a 95 % CI of −3.02 to 4.59 pp, which does not rule out a sizeable effect. Only restaurants and all items are "not supported".
findings.evidence: assets/pop/taylor-swift/eras-results.json: accommodation label "inconclusive" (att 0.79, lo −3.02, hi 4.59, p 0.5625); restaurants and all_items "not supported". The design (§3) names Q1, accommodation, as the primary estimate.

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:80 "its reference set is the 128 songs since 2017 that also peaked at two and whose start can be seen"
findings.problem: The 'kept' rule does not use a song's first chart date. It uses the earliest date on its kworb track page, and for Cruel Summer that date is 2023-08-31 (a summary or peak row), not its 2019 entry. So the reference set is not defined by "whose start can be seen". The claim that most of its 1 026 days come from the post-2023 revival also has no source in the repo, which has no split of days by period.
findings.evidence: tools/pop/parse.py first_date(): min of YYYY/MM/DD on the track page; tools/data/pop/raw/tracks/1BxfuPKGuaTgP7aM0Bbdwr.html: first date row 2023/08/31, then only 2026 dates; ones.csv: Cruel Summer first_listed=2023-08-31, and The Weeknd 'One Of The Girls' also 2023-08-31.
findings.fix: Describe the set as "songs whose kworb track page dates from 8 January 2017 or later". Either note that for Cruel Summer this date is its 2023 peak, or recompute first_listed from the first daily chart date. Remove or source "most of its days come from that second life".
findings.note: parse.py first_date() takes the min date on the track page. On Cruel Summer's page that is a 2023/08/31 summary row, then only 2026 rows (62 dates). ones.csv first_listed is 2023-08-31. So 'whose start can be seen' is not what the filter checks. The 'second life' claim has no computation behind it.

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:39 (deck) "the Eras Tour moved no measurable price for residents of the countries it played"; also :9 og:description "left no measurable mark", :44 facts box (restaurant −0.12 pp), :163
findings.problem: The headline, the og description and the facts box all lead with the restaurant result (Q2, secondary). The registered primary estimate, accommodation in month 0 (Q1), is inconclusive, and its pre-trend fails. 'Moved no measurable price' is a blanket null that the primary outcome does not support. The design also records the author's prior that accommodation would rise, and the page never says that this prior was neither confirmed nor refuted. Putting the secondary outcome forward because it yields a clean null is outcome emphasis-switching.
findings.evidence: docs/research/eras-inflation-design.md §3: 'Primary estimate. The effect in the show month (event month 0) for Q1' (accommodation); §0: 'The author expects accommodation prices to rise in a show month'. eras-inflation-results.json accommodation month0 att 0.79, band −3.02 to 4.59, label 'inconclusive', why 'a pre-trend band excludes zero; permutation p ≥ 0.05; interval wider than ±1 point'.
findings.fix: Deck and og: 'the Eras Tour's effect on hotel prices, the registered main question, is inconclusive at the national level (−3.0 to +4.6 pp); restaurant and overall inflation did not move by more than about half a point.' In the facts box, show the accommodation estimate as the primary row or next to the restaurant row, and say in the Eras section that accommodation was the primary, pre-expected outcome.
findings.note: The deck makes a blanket null claim, while the primary Q1 (design §3 line 51, accommodation month 0) is inconclusive with the month -4 pre-trend band excluding zero. The author's prior (accommodation would rise, line 17) is not mentioned. The og:description is accurate in itself but leads with the secondary outcome, and so does the facts box.

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:143 "for the prices residents pay most often, any effect large enough to notice at the national level is ruled out"; :53 tldr "overall inflation did not move"; :163 "did not move ... by anything near a percentage point"
findings.problem: The registered ±1 pp margin for 'not supported' is very wide for the all-items index. The all-items interval reaches +0.67 pp of headline year-on-year inflation, which is a large effect. A Beyoncé-sized effect of roughly 0.2 pp on Swedish headline CPI, the very episode the section opens with, would fall well inside this interval and could not be detected. The label is applied faithfully, but the prose turns 'not supported' into 'ruled out' and 'did not move'.
findings.evidence: eras-inflation-results.json all_items month0 att 0.23, lo −0.21, hi 0.67, permutation p 0.171. Restaurants hi 0.31. Text line 142 cites the Beyoncé/Stockholm hotel-price episode as the motivation.
findings.fix: Replace the claim with: 'effects larger than about +0.7 pp on overall inflation and +0.3 pp on restaurant inflation are ruled out; smaller effects, including one the size reported for Beyoncé in Stockholm, cannot be excluded.' In the tldr, change 'did not move' to 'did not move by more than about half a percentage point'.
findings.note: all_items is 0.23 (-0.21 to 0.67), restaurants hi 0.31. Line 143's 'any effect large enough to notice ... is ruled out' and the TL;DR's 'did not move' are stronger than the registered 'not supported' (within ±1 pp).

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:148 "It says that residents, at the level of their country's prices, did not pay for the tour."; :39 "for residents"; :143 "the prices residents pay"; :75 "did the people who live there pay more"
findings.problem: The HICP covers household consumption on the national territory, which includes tourists' spending. It is not a residents' price index, and the design says so. The text repeatedly frames the result as what residents paid. The closing sentence 'residents did not pay for the tour' also asserts a null that the inconclusive accommodation estimate cannot support.
findings.evidence: eras-inflation-design.md §6: 'Prices actually paid by visitors versus residents; the index mixes both.' The article's own limits section (line 168) admits that it cannot separate tourists' prices, which contradicts the 'residents' framing used in the deck and at line 148.
findings.fix: Replace 'residents' with 'national consumer prices' throughout. Delete the closing sentence at line 148 or rewrite it as: 'At the level of national monthly prices, restaurant and overall inflation show no effect above about half a point; whether hotel prices rose cannot be told from these data.'
findings.note: Design §6 line 79: 'the index mixes both' visitors and residents. Line 168 admits it cannot separate them, yet lines 39, 143 and 148 frame the result as what residents paid. Line 148's 'did not pay for the tour' also ignores the inconclusive accommodation estimate.

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:51 tldr "Her listening is the most spread of the series"; :115 "Half of all the streams come from 57 songs, the most of any artist in the series"; :163 "Her listening is the most spread in the series"
findings.problem: 'Most spread' rests only on how many songs it takes to reach half of the streams. That count grows mechanically with catalogue size, and her listed catalogue is 500 songs against 49 for Harry Styles and 79 for Billie Eilish. Re-recordings also split one song into two. On the registered concentration measure, the Gini coefficient, she is the most concentrated artist of the five, not the least. Bad Bunny's top song also holds a smaller share than hers. The headline claim is therefore contradicted by the study's own registered statistic.
findings.evidence: Computed from docs/research/*-results.json q4 and *-songs.csv: Gini HS 0.561, TS 0.642, BTS 0.640, Bad Bunny 0.541, Billie Eilish 0.518. Top-song share: TS 0.027, Bad Bunny 0.021. Songs listed: 49 / 500 / 319 / 271 / 79. Songs needed for half: 6 / 57 / 41 / 46 / 14. The series design §4 registers top share, top-3 share and Gini, not 'songs to half'.
findings.fix: Remove 'most spread of the series' from the tldr and 'What this means'. Report the Gini as the registered measure, with its rank in the series: 'the highest Gini of the five, because a 500-song catalogue includes many rarely played tracks'. If 'songs to half' is kept, label it post hoc and say that it scales with catalogue size and counts re-recordings twice.
findings.note: This duplicates [1]. Reproduced: the registered q4 Gini puts TS highest (most concentrated). Songs-to-half is not a registered q4 field (q4 holds songs, top_share, top3_share, gini).

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:47-55 details.tldr
findings.problem: The short version does not say what the results rest on: Spotify only via kworb, Boxscore figures as cited on Wikipedia, and a national monthly price index for 10 host countries. It does not give the labels (registered, not supported or inconclusive) or say what would overturn the results, for example city-level or weekly hotel prices, or Eras Tour gross figures. The most useful practical limitation of the price study, 'a city's hotels can be full and dear for three nights without moving a national monthly index' (line 148), appears only in the body.
findings.evidence: Lines 50-54 contain only results. Line 148 holds the key caveat.
findings.fix: Add a bullet: 'Rests on Spotify chart totals, Billboard Boxscore figures and Eurostat national monthly price indices; a city-level or weekly hotel price series could overturn the price finding, which cannot see a city's prices over a show weekend.'
findings.note: TL;DR bullet 4 (line 53) already says hotel prices are 'too noisy at the national level to tell', so part of the caveat is there. The missing data-source and label information is an editorial judgement, not a verifiable error.

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:7, 63, 146 'difference-in-differences'; :143 'permutation p'; :146 '95 % uniform bands'; :143 'month −4'
findings.problem: These are the central terms of the price study, and none is explained. 'Difference-in-differences' appears in the meta description, the status line and fig. 7 but is never named or defined in the body. 'Permutation p' is given without saying what was permuted. 'Uniform bands' is not explained. Event-month notation such as 'month −4' is used before event time is introduced.
findings.evidence: Line 142 describes the comparison but never links it to the term. Line 143 has 'permutation p = 0.54' and 'month −4'. Line 146 has '95 % uniform bands'.
findings.fix: Line 142: '...a difference-in-differences: the change in host countries minus the change in the others over the same months.' Line 143: 'permutation p (the share of 2 000 random reassignments of show months to countries that gave an effect at least this large)'. Fig. 7: 'bands that hold for all 13 months at once'. Introduce 'month 0 is the month of the first show, month −4 four months before'.
findings.note: 'difference-in-differences' appears only at line 7 (meta), line 63 (status), line 146 (caption) and line 186 (reference), never in the body text at line 142. Line 143 says 'permutation p' without saying what was permuted, and 'month −4' without defining event time. Line 146's 'uniform bands' is not defined.

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:39/41 'Boxscore'; :86 'Kaplan–Meier', '95 % bootstrap interval'; :115 'Gini coefficient is 0.64'
findings.problem: Several terms are used without explanation at first use. 'Boxscore' first appears in the deck and facts box (lines 39 and 41); it is only half-explained at line 81 as 'Billboard's Boxscore figures', which does not say what they are. Kaplan–Meier is glossed only as 'treated as unfinished'. The bootstrap interval is not explained. The Gini coefficient is given with no scale or meaning.
findings.fix: Line 81: 'Billboard's Boxscore, the trade reports of tickets sold, tickets available and gross for each run of shows'. Line 115: 'The Gini coefficient, 0 if every song had the same streams and 1 if one song had them all, is 0.64.' Line 86: 'the bootstrap interval comes from re-drawing the reference set 2 000 times'.
findings.note: Line 115 gives 'The Gini coefficient is 0.64' with no scale. Boxscore is never defined (lines 39, 41, 81). The bootstrap interval is not explained at line 86.

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:64 "the price study's design at f5d702c on 2 October 2026, before any price index was downloaded"; :142 "committed before any index was downloaded"
findings.problem: The design itself records that one Eurostat request returning four index values was made before registration, for a format check, so 'before any index was downloaded' is not literally true. The design, code, data and results commits also fall within two minutes of each other (10:06:30 to 10:08:32). Their order therefore gives the reader little evidence that the design preceded the data.
findings.evidence: eras-inflation-design.md §0: 'One request to the HICP monthly index ... for Sweden and Austria, January–February 2023, was made to check the format; it returned four values, which were not printed or read.' git log: f5d702c 10:06:30, d1d25cd 10:07:22, dc9dba3 10:07:32, 4401fda 10:08:32.
findings.fix: 'before any price index was read (one format-check request returned four values, not printed); design, code, data and results were committed within two minutes of each other, so the order rests on the self-reported sequence.'
findings.note: Commits f5d702c 10:06:30, d1d25cd 10:07:22, dc9dba3 10:07:32, 4401fda 10:08:32, all within about 2 minutes. Design §0 records the four-value format check, so 'before any price index was downloaded' (line 64) is not literal.

findings.location: texts/pop-taylor-swift.html:124 "Every entry sold 99.5 % of its tickets or more; most report exactly as many sold as available. The longest run was 6 nights at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood ."
findings.problem: The minimum sell-through is exactly 1.0, so every entry, not most, reports as many tickets sold as available. There is also a stray space before the full stop.
findings.evidence: taylor-swift-results.json q3 sell_through_min 1.0, share_sold_out 1.0.
findings.fix: 'Every entry reports exactly as many tickets sold as available. The longest run was 6 nights at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood.'
findings.note: Duplicate of [5]: sell_through_min 1.0, share_sold_out 1.0, and the stray space comes from city 'Inglewood '. It misses the 6-night tie with Singapore.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:126 "an average of 66 dollars a ticket on the Love Yourself World Tour in 2018 and 198 dollars on the Arirang World Tour in 2026, about three times as much" (also :81 "Two entries of 2018 give one total for several venues", :125 "60 shows in 27 Boxscore entries")
findings.problem: The Taoyuan (Taiwan) 2018 entry is a leg total spanning several venues, but the parser did not flag it multi_venue, so it stays in the run question and in the per-tour price. Its 250,000 tickets cover nine Asian shows. Its $7,111,720 gross covers only the two Taoyuan nights (NT$220 million). That gives a spurious $28 a ticket, which drags the 2018 average down to $66. With Taiwan left out, the 2018 average is about $123, so the rise is about 1.6x rather than three times. The run question should also have 26 entries and 58 shows, not 27 and 60, and the count of 2018 leg entries is three, not two.
findings.evidence: assets/pop/bts/tour.csv row 'Taoyuan ... 2,250000,250000,7111720,False,False'. The Wikipedia revision 1375294102 raw text for that row reads '250,000 / 250,000{{efn|name=Asia|The score data is combined from the shows held in Asia from December 8, 9, January 19, March 20, 21, 23, 24, April 6, & 7}}' with the comment '<!--NT$220 million was converted to USD-->'. Recomputing the 2018 non-hybrid, non-multi entries gives 66.01 with Taiwan and 123.44 without. tools/pop/article.py:102-107 computes tp_<tour> over all entries of the tour that have revenue. docs/research/pop-measured-design.md 'Changes after registration' says 'Only BTS has such entries (Los Angeles and Tokyo, 2018)'.
findings.fix: Flag Taoyuan 2018 as multi_venue and drop it from Q3 and the per-tour price. Re-run analyse/article. Restate the price rise as roughly $123 to $198 (about 1.6x). Change the text to 'Three entries of 2018' and update the design note. Also recompute and restate the entries, shows, share sold out, rho and CI.
findings.note: Wikipedia oldid 1375294102 line 212: 250,000 sold is an efn-combined Asian leg total (Dec 8-Apr 7), and revenue is NT$220M for Taiwan only. tour.csv has Taoyuan multi_venue=False. Recomputed Love Yourself price: 66.01 with Taoyuan, 123.44 without. The design note names only LA and Tokyo. Q3 shrinks to 26 entries and 58 shows, and the sold-out share stays above 0.9 (24/26).

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:51 (TL;DR) "The hit lasted longest against local songs in South Korea, Vietnam and Japan" and :154 "Against local hits it lasted longest in South Korea, Vietnam and Japan"
findings.problem: The registered Q2 measure (ratio to the local median number one) ranks Japan 5th, behind the Dominican Republic (3rd) and the UAE (4th). The body at :102 correctly names South Korea, Vietnam and the Dominican Republic as the top three. Japan is first only by days alone, which is the post-hoc ranking. So the summary and the conclusion contradict the body and the registered measure.
findings.evidence: bts-results.json q2.countries: kr ratio 2.83 rank 1, vn 2.67 rank 2, do 2.65 rank 3, ae 2.49 rank 4, jp 2.41 rank 5 (rank_by_days_post_hoc 1).
findings.fix: Use 'South Korea, Vietnam and the Dominican Republic' in both places, or say 'by days alone, Japan and South Korea'.
findings.note: results.json q2: kr rank 1, vn 2, do 3, ae 4, jp 5 (rank_by_days_post_hoc 1). TL;DR :51 and conclusion :154 say Japan. Body :102 gives the registered top three.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:102 "Across most of Europe it lasted less than the local median number one: 0.5× in the United Kingdom, 0.6× in Poland, 1.1× in Germany."
findings.problem: Germany is given as an example of a European country where Dynamite lasted less than the local median, but its ratio is above 1. The example contradicts the sentence it supports.
findings.evidence: bts-results.json q2: de ratio 1.148, CI 1.03–1.33, rank 25.
findings.fix: Replace Germany with a country below 1 (e.g. 'and 0.6× in France'), or write '..., though Germany, at 1.1×, is an exception'.
findings.note: de ratio 1.148 > 1, yet it is given as an example of 'less than the local median'.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:65 and :80 "for the global chart and 76 national charts"
findings.problem: The collection hashes 76 totals files, but one of them is the global chart, so there are 75 national charts. Dynamite's 72 plus the 3 missing countries (cy, mt, ng) also gives 75.
findings.evidence: docs/research/pop-measured-files.sha256 lists 76 'totals/*.html' entries including totals/global.html. assets/pop/bts/countries.csv has 72 rows, and cy, mt and ng are absent.
findings.fix: Say 'the global chart and 75 national charts' (the same wording recurs in the other pop-* articles).
findings.note: sha256 file has 76 totals/ entries, including totals/global.html. countries.csv has 72 rows. So 75 national charts, not 76.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:81 "Three entries of Permission to Dance count online viewers together with the hall, so that one reports more tickets sold than seats and another three percent of its "capacity" sold"
findings.problem: Two of the three hybrid entries report more tickets sold than available, not one.
findings.evidence: tour.csv: Inglewood 2021 213751/18000, Paradise 2022 199697/22000 (both sold > available), Seoul 2022 45000/1400000 (3.2 %).
findings.fix: 'so that two report more tickets sold than seats and the third three percent of its "capacity" sold'.
findings.note: tour.csv: Inglewood 2021 213751/18000 and Paradise 2022 199697/22000 both sold more than available; Seoul 2022 45000/1400000 is 3.2%.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:92 "25 % were still in after two years"
findings.problem: The Kaplan–Meier survival at 730 days is 26 %, not 25 %. The helper surv(t) in tools/pop/article.py:48 takes the first curve step at or after t, which is 750 days (0.254), so it returns survival just after the 750-day drop. The 1000-day figure is unaffected because there is a step exactly at 1000.
findings.evidence: q1.curve: (717, 0.2624) is the last step at or before 730, and (750, 0.2544) is the next one. article.py: surv = next(v for d, v in curve if d >= t).
findings.fix: Use the last step with d <= t (survival is right-continuous) and say 26 %. The same template sentence appears in the other parts.
findings.note: Curve steps (717, 0.262) and (750, 0.254). article.py surv uses the first d>=t, so it returns 0.254 at 730 days and the text shows 25%. The right-continuous value is 26%.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:125 "The longest runs were four nights, in stadiums; the longest listed is 4 nights at Allegiant Stadium."
findings.problem: Two entries tie at 4 nights: Allegiant Stadium and SoFi Stadium (2026). Calling Allegiant 'the longest listed' implies it is the only one, and the sentence repeats itself.
findings.evidence: tour.csv: Paradise/Allegiant Stadium 2026 nights 4; Inglewood/SoFi Stadium 2026 nights 4 (both non-hybrid, non-multi).
findings.fix: 'The longest runs were four nights, at Allegiant Stadium and SoFi Stadium.'
findings.note: tour.csv: Allegiant 2026 and SoFi 2026 both have 4 nights, non-hybrid and non-multi. The sentence names only Allegiant and repeats itself.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:136 "Its stadium shows were priced like American ones, in dollars"
findings.problem: The Mexico average ($279) is well above the US average ($208). The article itself says this is the dearest ticket in dollars, so 'priced like American ones' understates it.
findings.evidence: bts-results.json q5: MEX price_usd 279.4, USA 208.5.
findings.fix: 'Its stadium shows were priced above American ones, in dollars, ...'
findings.note: q5: MEX 279.4 vs USA 208.5 USD. 'Priced like American ones' understates a 34% higher price. This is minor wording.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:86 "Kaplan–Meier estimator<sup>5</sup>"
findings.problem: References are not numbered by order of first citation. In the body, r6 (:80), r7 and r8 (:81) are cited before r5 (:86). The meta box at :65 also cites r6–r8 before r1. The DOI metadata of r1–r5 all match Crossref.
findings.evidence: First citations in the body in order: r1–r4 (:75), r6 (:80), r7, r8 (:81), r5 (:86).
findings.fix: Renumber so that Kaplan–Meier comes after kworb, Wikipedia and World Bank, or cite r5 earlier.
findings.note: r6 is first cited in the meta box (:65) and at :80, r7 and r8 at :65 and :81, and r5 only at :86. The numbering does not follow first-citation order. Low importance if the house style does not require it.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:64 "Two data definitions were added after the results" vs :148
findings.problem: The 'What changed after registration' list has three post-registration items. The third is the post-hoc ranking of countries by days alone. The meta box mentions only two.
findings.evidence: Lines 146–148 list three items, and rank_by_days_post_hoc is used at :102–103.
findings.fix: 'Two data definitions and one post-hoc ranking were added after the results.'
findings.note: The changes list (:146-148) has three items. The third, the days-alone ranking, is a post-hoc analysis, not a data definition. The meta box says only two.

findings.problem: Wrong ordinal suffix.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:116 "This is the clearest result of this part. BTS's fans ... stream deliberately, so the listening is spread across a large catalogue in a way no other artist in the series is likely to match." (also :154 "BTS's listening is the more spread across songs. The next parts will show whether either pattern is unusual.")
findings.problem: The catalogue claim is contradicted by the series' own published results, and the explanation is causal when nothing was measured. All five parts are already published (texts/pop-taylor-swift.html, pop-bad-bunny.html, pop-billie-eilish.html exist), and two artists are more spread than BTS by the registered top-song share. 'The next parts will show' is stale. The claim that deliberate fan streaming caused the spread is not tested; the page itself says 'Nothing here says why'.
findings.evidence: assets/pop/*/results.json q4.top_share: BTS 0.042, Taylor Swift 0.027, Bad Bunny 0.021, Billie Eilish 0.068, Harry Styles 0.153. Gini: BTS 0.64, Taylor Swift 0.64, Bad Bunny 0.54. The design's §0 says 'Prior expectations. None stated for parts 2–5'.
findings.fix: Drop 'in a way no other artist in the series is likely to match' and 'The next parts will show'. Compare against all four other parts, e.g. 'Dynamite's 4 % is less concentrated than Harry Styles's (15 %) and Billie Eilish's (7 %), but more than Taylor Swift's (2.7 %) and Bad Bunny's (2.1 %)'. Recast the fan-streaming sentence as a possible explanation that is not tested here.
findings.note: q4 top_share: BTS 0.042, TS 0.027, BB 0.021, BE 0.068, HS 0.153. Gini: TS 0.642 > BTS 0.640. All parts are published (texts/pop-*.html exist), so 'no other artist ... likely to match' is false and 'The next parts will show' is stale. The fan-streaming cause is untested.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:126 "an average of 66 dollars a ticket on the Love Yourself World Tour in 2018 and 198 dollars on the Arirang World Tour in 2026, about three times as much ... consistent with prices that were ... set below what fans would pay"
findings.problem: The 'three times' comparison across tours is not a registered measure (Q5 in the design is per country, not per tour), and the page does not label it exploratory. It also rests on a misparsed entry. The Taoyuan row (250,000 sold, $7.1M) is a combined total for an Asian leg, but it was kept as a 2-night run. Its implied price is about $28 a ticket, which pulls the Love Yourself average down to $66. Without it, the tour average is about $124 and the rise is about 1.6x. The same row also counts as a sold-out 2-night entry in Q3, so it affects the 27 entries, the 60 shows and the sold-out share.
findings.evidence: docs/research/bts-tour.csv:10 'Taoyuan ... 2,250000,250000,7111720,False,False'. Wikipedia oldid 1375294102, line 212: '250,000 / 250,000{{efn|... combined from the shows held in Asia from December 8, 9, January 19, March 20, 21, 23, 24, April 6, & 7}}'; revenue note: 'NT$220 million', Taiwan only. tools/pop/article.py:102-107 computes tp_<tour> from the Q3 entries. Love Yourself sum: 27.36M / 413,517 = $66; without Taoyuan: 20.25M / 163,517 = $124.
findings.fix: Flag Taoyuan as multi_venue, which is the same rule as the existing 2 October deviation, and rerun Q3 and Q5. Label the per-tour price comparison as exploratory and not registered, or cut it. Remove 'set below what fans would pay', because design §4 says the sold-out data 'cannot say how far above' capacity demand is.
findings.note: Same Taoyuan defect as [0], reproduced: $66 becomes $123, about 1.6x not 3x. The per-tour price comparison is not part of the registered Q5, which is per country. 'Set below what fans would pay' goes beyond the registered sold-out rule ('cannot say how far above').

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:92-93 "Dynamite sits past the middle of that curve, which is where a song reached by a wide public as well as by fans would be expected to sit"; "That is what a release carried mainly by an organised fan base looks like in these data ... staying there needs more than the fans"
findings.problem: These paragraphs say why songs lasted (fan-driven pushes versus broad radio audiences) as if the data showed it. Nothing measures fan share, radio play or audience breadth. The 'expected' position was never registered (design §0: no prior expectations). Generalising from Take Two (one song) to 'staying there needs more than the fans' is a causal claim. It also contradicts the limitations section (:159 'Nothing here says why a song lasted'). Line 103 does the same: 'a large, loyal fan base in Asia, and a broad but shorter-lived public elsewhere' explains the country pattern with audiences that were not measured.
findings.evidence: Design §1: all questions descriptive; results.json q1 holds only days, share_longer and CI. No variable for fans, radio or audience type exists in tools/pop/analyse.py.
findings.fix: Cut or hedge to: 'One possible reading, not tested here, is that ...'. Keep the measured facts: 780 versus 46 days, 24 % versus 91 % of number ones lasting longer.
findings.note: Paragraphs :92-93 and :103 attribute durations to fan-driven vs broad/radio audiences. No such variable exists in results.json. This conflicts with :159 'Nothing here says why a song lasted', and the design has no prior expectations.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:51 tldr "lasted longest against local songs in South Korea, Vietnam and Japan"; :154 "it lasted longest in South Korea, Vietnam and Japan"
findings.problem: The headline mixes the registered ranking with the post-hoc one, and neither the summary nor the conclusion says so. By the registered ratio, the top three are South Korea (2.83), Vietnam (2.67) and the Dominican Republic (2.65), with the UAE 4th and Japan 5th (2.41). Japan reaches the top three only through the post-hoc ranking by days alone, where it is 1st.
findings.evidence: results.json q2.countries: jp rank 5, rank_by_days_post_hoc 1; do rank 3. tools/pop/analyse.py:86-89 names the field rank_by_days_post_hoc.
findings.fix: Use the registered top three in both places ('South Korea, Vietnam and the Dominican Republic'), or write 'South Korea and Vietnam by the registered ratio; Japan by days alone, a ranking added after part 1's results were seen'.
findings.note: Duplicate of [1]: the registered ranking puts Japan 5th, and it is 1st only by days, post hoc. The TL;DR and conclusion do not say so.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:148 "Countries are also ranked by days alone, as in part 1, because small markets ... inflate the ratio."; :103 "by days alone Czechia is 52th"
findings.problem: The 'What changed after registration' list includes this ranking without a date and without saying it was added after results were seen. The body cites the days-alone Czech rank without marking it as post hoc.
findings.evidence: docs/research/harry-styles-design.md:107 '1 October 2026, after the results were seen. Q2 also reports the countries ranked by ... days'. The results field is named rank_by_days_post_hoc.
findings.fix: Date the entry and add 'added after part 1's results were seen (post hoc)'. In line 103, write 'by days alone, a post-hoc ranking, Czechia is 52nd'.
findings.note: The third bullet in #changes has no date and no post-hoc label. :103 cites the days-alone rank (52) without marking it post hoc. The field is named rank_by_days_post_hoc.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:91 "The band's other number ones: SWIM, 195 days (71 % of number ones lasted longer)"
findings.problem: SWIM is still charting, so its 195 days is a lower bound and the 71 % figure will fall. The text presents both as final and gives no interval. In contrast, the same paragraph says plainly that Dynamite 'is no longer in the chart'.
findings.evidence: results.json q1.own[1]: still_charting true, share_longer 0.707, ci95 [0.637, 0.774].
findings.fix: 'SWIM, still charting at 195 days so far (so far, 71 % of number ones lasted longer; 95 % CI 64 % to 77 %)'.
findings.note: q1.own SWIM still_charting true, share_longer 0.707, CI 0.637-0.774. The text presents 195 days and 71% without flagging them as provisional.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:75 "their fans are known for streaming whole albums on purpose, which should show in how their listening is spread"
findings.problem: This states a directional expectation as if it were set before the data. The series design registers no prior expectations for parts 2–5, so the Q4 result is later presented as confirming a prediction that was never registered.
findings.evidence: docs/research/pop-measured-design.md §0: 'Prior expectations. None stated for parts 2–5.'
findings.fix: Remove 'which should show in how their listening is spread', or add 'an expectation not written into the registered plan'.
findings.note: :75 'which should show in how their listening is spread' states an expectation. The design line 21 says 'Prior expectations. None stated for parts 2-5.' :116 then frames the result as 'the clearest result'.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:102 "Across most of Europe it lasted less than the local median number one: 0.5× in the United Kingdom, 0.6× in Poland, 1.1× in Germany."
findings.problem: Germany is given as an example of 'less than the local median', but its ratio is above 1. Several other European charts are also above 1 (Switzerland 1.54, Lithuania 1.50, Romania 1.27, Austria 1.10).
findings.evidence: results.json q2.countries: de ratio 1.15, ch 1.54, lt 1.50, ro 1.27, at 1.10.
findings.fix: Use a European chart below 1 instead (for example France 0.6× or Sweden 0.5×), and add 'though it beat the local median in Germany (1.1×) and Switzerland (1.5×)'.
findings.note: Overlaps [2]. Ratios: de 1.15, ch 1.54, lt 1.50, ro 1.27, at 1.10 are above 1; fr 0.58 and se 0.46 are below 1.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:48-54 details.tldr
findings.problem: The short version states results but not what they rest on (one chart provider, 165 reference songs, 27 Boxscore entries) or what would overturn them, such as Melon or YouTube data, or a different focal-song rule. The ticket bullet says 'the same show in the United States', but these are different shows, averaged per country. It also says 'average income' where the measure is GDP per capita.
findings.evidence: Lines 50-54. results.json q5 averages per country over 24 entries.
findings.fix: Add a bullet such as: 'Rests on kworb Spotify totals for 72 charts and 27 Boxscore entries; YouTube or Korean-service data, or a correction to the Boxscore entries, could change it.' Rewrite the ticket bullet: 'An average ticket in Mexico cost 7.3 days of GDP per capita; in the United States, under one day.'
findings.note: The TL;DR ticket bullet says 'the same show in the United States', but q5 averages different shows per country (24 entries). 'Average income' stands for GDP per capita. The missing-basis bullet is a softer editorial point.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:42-43, 86, 116 (key figures and methods)
findings.problem: Several central terms are used without explanation at first use. 'administrative count' (:42, :44) is never defined. 'Gini 0.64' (:42) is only glossed as 'high' at :116. '95 % CI' (:43) appears in the key figures before any explanation. 'Kaplan–Meier estimator' and 'bootstrap resamples' (:86) get no plain-language gloss. 'Spearman's correlation' (:86) is not explained. 'Boxscore' (:81) is not explained. '0.6×' against 'the Czech median number one' (:44) appears before the ratio is explained at :86 and :103.
findings.evidence: Text extract of texts/pop-bts.html at the cited lines.
findings.fix: Add short glosses at first use, e.g. 'Gini (0 = every song equal, 1 = one song has everything)', 'administrative count (a full count, so no sampling interval)', 'Spearman's correlation (whether more nights go with lower sell-through, by rank)', 'Boxscore (Billboard's reported attendance and gross)'.
findings.note: The terms are indeed unglossed at first use (administrative count, Gini, CI, Spearman, Boxscore). Whether glosses are needed depends on the series' house style, since other parts use the same template. This is editorial, not a verifiable error.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:103 "by days alone Czechia is 52th"; :135 "in United States the average ticket"
findings.problem: There are typos: '52th' should be '52nd', and 'in United States' is missing 'the'.
findings.evidence: Lines 103 and 135.
findings.fix: '52nd'; 'in the United States'.
findings.note: :103 '52th' and :135 'in United States the average ticket' (article missing). The fig. 6 alt text also says 'in United States'.

findings.location: texts/pop-bts.html:103 "Korea's own figure is a Spotify figure, in a market where most listening happens on Melon and Genie; it is the more striking for that."
findings.problem: The text calls Korea's low Spotify coverage a reason the result is more striking. A small, self-selected Spotify user base in Korea makes the ratio less representative, not more striking. This framing goes against the limitation stated at :159.
findings.evidence: Lines 103 and 159.
findings.fix: 'Korea's figure describes Spotify's Korean listeners only, a minority in a market led by Melon and Genie.'
findings.note: :103 'it is the more striking for that' presents low Spotify coverage as strengthening the result. :159 says Korea's figures describe Spotify's Korean listeners only. The framing is unsupported.

findings.location: texts/pop-bad-bunny.html:91 "He has more global number ones than any other artist in the series"; also :51 (tl;dr) and :151 "Bad Bunny has the most number ones in the series"
findings.problem: False. Taylor Swift (part 2) has more global number ones than Bad Bunny in the same dataset.
findings.evidence: docs/research/bad-bunny-ones.csv, the shared list of 194 global peak-1 songs: Taylor Swift appears 15 times (14 kept since 2017: Anti-Hero, cardigan, Fortnight, The Fate of Ophelia, willow, Patient Zero and others). Bad Bunny appears 7 times, 6 distinct songs if Dakiti/DÁKITI is one song. Billie Eilish 6, Harry Styles 3, BTS 3.

findings.location: texts/pop-bad-bunny.html:102 "The pattern is linguistic and regional more than it is about reach: a Spanish-language album held the charts of the Spanish-speaking world..."; :151 "held in place by the Spanish-speaking world"; :151 "a language region holding one album in place"

The registered ratio does not show a language pattern: Spanish-speaking countries sit mid-table (es 18th, mx 32nd, co 27th, pe 35th with ratio 0.99), while German-speaking and Baltic countries rank above them. The language pattern appears only in the ranking by days alone, which was added after the results were seen, and the text never reports or labels that ranking.
findings.evidence: results.json q2 rank vs rank_by_days_post_hoc: bo 23 vs 1, co 27 vs 2, cr 34 vs 3, ec 33 vs 5, es 18 vs 6. tools/pop/analyse.py:85 comments that rank_by_days is 'added after the results were seen (labelled so in the article)', but no sentence in the article reports it or labels it.

Replace 'held in place by' and 'holding in place' with descriptive wording, e.g. 'stayed every day in the charts of the Spanish-speaking world'. Add a sentence noting that German-speaking and Baltic charts also kept it longer than their local hits.
findings.note: On the registered ratio, Spanish-speaking countries sit mid-table (bo 23, co 27, cr 34, ec 33, es 18), and German-speaking and Baltic charts rank above them. Only rank_by_days_post_hoc puts bo, co, cr, do and ec at the top, and the text never reports or labels that ranking. 'Held in place' is causal wording.

findings.location: texts/pop-bad-bunny.html:53 (tldr) "in Central America and the Andes a ticket cost six to eight days of the average income, at home in Puerto Rico less than one"; :133

Costa Rica (2.0) and Panama (1.7) are Central American but far below six days, and Ecuador and El Salvador are 5.8. findings.location: texts/pop-bad-bunny.html:39, :42, :9, :115 "Half of all his streams come from 46 songs, and 20 songs each hold one percent or more"; :134 "Prices also rose across his tours: ... 85 ... 168 ... 152"
findings.problem: Two headline numbers are not registered measures and are not labelled as added: the half-of-streams count and the per-tour average price. The half-of-streams count is in the deck, the facts box and og:description. Registered Q4 measures are the top-song share, the top-three share and the Gini; registered Q5 is per country. The tour comparison also uses nominal dollars with no inflation adjustment, and it suggests an explanation ('which played more of Latin America and Europe').
findings.evidence: docs/research/pop-measured-design.md §4 lists only top share, top-3 share and Gini (Q4), and per-country price (Q5). The extra figures are computed in tools/pop/article.py:94-108 (q4_half, q4_over1, tp_<tour>), not in analyse.py.
findings.fix: Label both as 'added after registration' in 'What changed after registration', or move the per-tour prices into a clearly exploratory sentence. Add 'in current dollars, not adjusted for inflation' and drop the causal clause about where the tour played.
findings.note: q4_half, q4_over1 and tp_<tour> are computed in article.py:100-107, not in analyse.py, and design §4 does not list them. Line 134 has no inflation note and does add the clause about where the tour played.

findings.location: texts/pop-bad-bunny.html:133-134, :156
findings.problem: The article leaves out two Q5 limits that the design says must be stated: Boxscore gross mixes all seat prices and fees, and exchange rates are those used when the gross was reported. It also does not say that the 18 entries from 2026 use an earlier year's GDP per capita.
findings.evidence: pop-measured-design.md §4 Q5: 'Limits stated in the article: ... findings.location: texts/pop-bad-bunny.html:115 "The Gini coefficient over songs is 0.54."
findings.problem: A central Q4 measure appears without explanation or a reference point, so the reader cannot interpret 0.54.

findings.location: texts/pop-bad-bunny.html:86 "Kaplan–Meier estimator", "95 % bootstrap interval", "Spearman's correlation"; :41-44 "administrative count"; :81 "Boxscore"
findings.problem: Technical terms are used without a plain-language explanation at first use. 'Administrative count' in the facts box (:42, :44) is never explained. 'Boxscore' (:81) is not described as Billboard's reported gross and attendance per engagement.
findings.evidence: The methods paragraph at :86 gives no example. A concrete case would help, e.g. 'a song still charting at 634 days counts as at least 634'.
findings.fix: Add short glosses, e.g. 'Kaplan–Meier, which counts songs still in the chart as lasting at least as long as they have so far'; 'bootstrap interval, from re-drawing the set of songs 2 000 times'; 'Spearman's correlation, which compares ranks (from −1 to 1)'; 'administrative count: a full count from the source, so no sampling interval'.
findings.note: 'Administrative count' appears at lines 42, 44 and in figure captions without a definition anywhere in the article. KM, bootstrap and Spearman get no gloss at line 86. This is a clarity point.

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:125 "Across her entries, longer runs sold a slightly larger share: the correlation ... is 0.21 (95 % CI 0.14 to 0.27), an interval that excludes zero ... If anything, it points away from the idea that a city tires of a long run." (also TL;DR line 53 "where a few did not, longer runs sold a little better")
findings.problem: The registered rule says that when 90 % or more of entries are at 99.5 % or more, rho is reported but not interpreted. Here 91.5 % meet that bar, so the rule applies, yet the article interprets rho: it gives a direction, stresses that the interval excludes zero and draws a substantive conclusion. That contradicts the article's own methods sentence (line 86, "the correlation is not read") and its next sentence ("reported and not read further").
findings.evidence: docs/research/harry-styles-design.md:74-75: "If 90 % or more of entries are at 99.5 % or more ... ρ is then reported but not interpreted"; pop-measured-design.md:81-83 applies the same rule to parts 2-5. billie-eilish-results.json q3.share_sold_out = 0.915 and demand_at_capacity = true. Template tools/pop/templates/billie-eilish.html:125 hard-codes the interpretive sentences.
findings.fix: Keep only: "The correlation between nights and the share sold is 0.21 (95 % CI 0.14 to 0.27); under the registered rule it is reported and not read, because nine entries in ten were at capacity." Delete "Across her entries, longer runs sold a slightly larger share", "an interval that excludes zero" and "If anything, it points away...". In the TL;DR, replace "longer runs sold a little better" with "the data cannot say how far above capacity demand was".
findings.note: q3.share_sold_out=0.915, demand_at_capacity=true; harry-styles-design.md:74-75 says rho 'reported but not interpreted'. Line 125 still gives a direction ('longer runs sold a slightly larger share'), notes the interval 'excludes zero' and adds 'If anything, it points away...'. TL;DR line 53 repeats it as a finding. Duplicate of [11].

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:92 "25 % were still in after two years"
findings.problem: At 730 days the Kaplan–Meier survival is 26.2 %, not 25 %. The published 25 % is S(750), the next step after two years. The cause is article.py: its surv() takes the first curve point at or after t, where it should take the last point at or before t.
findings.evidence: results.json q1.curve: [717, 0.2624], [750, 0.2544]; there is no step between 717 and 750, so S(730) = 0.262. tools/pop/article.py:48: `surv = lambda t: next((v_ for d_, v_ in q1["curve"] if d_ >= t), ...)` returns 0.2544. (s1000 happens to be correct because a step falls exactly on day 1000.) The same helper fills s730 in the other four parts.
findings.fix: Change surv to the last step with d_ <= t (e.g. `max((p for p in curve if p[0] <= t), default=(0,1.0))[1]`), regenerate, and the text becomes "26 % were still in after two years".
findings.note: q1.curve has [717,0.2624] then [750,0.2544]. article.py:48 surv() takes the first d>=t, so it returns 0.254 (prints 25 %). The correct S(730) is 0.262 (26 %). s1000 is right only because a step falls exactly on day 1000.

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:102 "It lasted less than the local median number one in Mexico (0.9×) and in Japan (0.31×) ... and barely entered the charts of Turkey and India."
findings.problem: The sentence reads as a complete list of the countries where the song fell short, but 15 of 71 countries are below 1×. Nigeria (0.26×) is lower than Japan, and Colombia (0.65×), Ecuador (0.68×), Guatemala and Uruguay (0.86×) are among those left out. Mexico's interval (0.85–1.02) also includes 1, so "less than" is not established for Mexico.
findings.evidence: results.json q2.countries: 71 countries, 56 with ratio > 1, so 15 are below 1. Lowest ratios: in 0.03, tr 0.05, ng 0.26, jp 0.31, co 0.65, ec 0.68, gt 0.86, uy 0.86. mx ratio 0.920, ci95 [0.854, 1.016].
findings.fix: "It lasted less than the local median number one in 15 countries, among them Japan (0.31×), where number ones last a median of 678 days, and Nigeria (0.26×); it barely entered the charts of Turkey and India." Drop Mexico, or add "(0.9×, interval reaching 1)".
findings.note: 15 of 71 countries are below 1x: in .03, tr .05, ng .26, jp .31, co .65, ec .68, gt/uy .86, py .87, es .89, mx .92, eg .92, cr/ve .97, ar .99. The sentence names only mx and jp and leaves out Nigeria, which is lower than Japan. Mexico's CI is 0.85-1.02, which includes 1. Japan's median of 678.5 days checks out.

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:135 "The cheapest ticket in dollars was in Portugal, 30 dollars, on her first tour, and the dearest 160: a ratio of 5.4"
findings.problem: "Cheapest/dearest ticket" switches units without saying so. 160 is Thailand's country average, not the dearest ticket or entry: several US entries average 181–185 dollars a ticket. The 5.4 ratio is a ratio of country averages, so it should be labelled as one.
findings.evidence: q5.countries max price_usd = 159.99 (Thailand). Per-entry gross/sold from billie-eilish-tour.csv: Philadelphia 185.2, Omaha 184.4, Inglewood 183.4, Boston 181.1 (2024). The minimum, Lisbon 29.5, is both an entry and a country, so only the maximum is mislabelled.
findings.fix: "By country, the average ticket ranged from 30 dollars in Portugal, on her first tour, to 160 in Thailand: a ratio of 5.4, against about 41-fold in days of income."
findings.note: q5 country maximum is Thailand at 160.0 (a country average from one entry). Per-entry gross/sold reaches 185.2 (Philadelphia 2024), 184.4 (Omaha) and 183.4 (Inglewood). 'The dearest 160' is mislabelled as a ticket; the minimum, Lisbon at 29.5, is both an entry and a country.

findings.problem: Three English-language and two non-English focal songs, all descriptive, are generalised into a claim about the language of Czech listening. The series design rules out cross-artist inference ("No test across artists is made"). With n = 2 non-English artists (one Korean group, one Spanish-language artist), language cannot be separated from artist, genre or fan base.
findings.evidence: Czech ranks in the results files: harry-styles 35/72 (2.06), taylor-swift 35/68 (1.03), billie-eilish 38/71 (1.69), bts 60/72 (0.60), bad-bunny 49/65 (0.24). pop-measured-design.md §3: "No test across artists is made."

findings.note: pop-measured-design.md §3/§4 allow only listing the five Czech places side by side, with 'No test across artists'. Line 103 goes further and generalises to 'Czech listening... lets hits in other languages pass quickly' from 2 non-English songs. Ranks quoted match the results files (35/72, 35/68, 60/72, 49/65, 38/71). Duplicate of [13].
