findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:125 "the correlation between nights and the share sold is 0.21 (95 % CI 0.14 to 0.27), an interval that excludes zero ... If anything, it points away from the idea that a city tires of a long run." (also TL;DR line 53 "where a few did not, longer runs sold a little better")
findings.problem: The registered rule says that when 90 % or more of entries are at 99.5 % or more, rho is reported and NOT interpreted. The text does interpret it, twice: it stresses that the interval excludes zero, then says what the result 'points away' from. The TL;DR states it as a finding. The positive rho also rests on 10 entries that did not sell out. Seven of them are single-night shows from the 2019 When We All Fall Asleep Tour, a tour with no multi-night runs. So the correlation largely reflects which tour (career stage) an entry belongs to, not run length.
findings.evidence: harry-styles-design.md §3 Q3: 'If 90 % or more ... rho is then reported but not interpreted'; pop-measured-design.md §4 'Reading Q3'. results.json q3: share_sold_out 0.915, rho 0.205. Recomputed from tour.csv: 10 entries below 99.5 %, 7 of them from When We All Fall Asleep Tour (17 entries, all 1 night, 10 sold out). Hit Me Hard and Soft: 46/46 sold out, 25 multi-night. Dropping the 2019 tour gives rho 0.13 (n=101).
findings.fix: Remove 'an interval that excludes zero' and the 'If anything, it points away...' sentence. In the TL;DR, replace the bullet with 'Her shows sold out (92 % of entries); by the rule set in advance, the data cannot say whether longer runs sold differently.' If the tour mix is mentioned at all, say: 'Seven of the ten entries that did not sell out are one-night shows on her smaller 2019 tour.'
findings.note: Same rule violation as [0]. Recomputed from tour.csv: 10 entries are below 99.5 %. Seven are 1-night 2019 WWAFA entries (that tour has 17 entries, 0 multi-night, 10 sold out); HMHAS has 46/46 sold out with 25 multi-night. Spearman over all 118 = 0.205 (matches); without 2019, n=101, rho = 0.132. Tour confounding is reproduced.

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:153 "Across the series, she is the artist whose staying power is least tied to one release: a durable hit is a pattern in her work rather than a single event."
findings.problem: This ranks artists, but no measure in the study ranks staying power across artists, and the series design rules out cross-artist tests. The claim rests on two songs in Q1. It also contradicts the article's own Q4: half of BTS's and Bad Bunny's streams come from 41 and 46 songs against her 14, so on the catalogue measure she is less spread out than two other artists. Taylor Swift also has several long-lived songs, but her reference set (peak 2) is a different one.
findings.evidence: pop-measured-design.md §3: 'No test across artists is made.' Line 116 of the article: 'Harry Styles's half came from six songs, BTS's from 41 and Bad Bunny's from 46.' The other parts' results.json files show no measure that ranks 'staying power' across artists.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'She is the only artist in the series with two global number ones that each outlasted about five in six of the others; that is two songs, not a measured pattern.'
findings.note: Line 153 'the artist whose staying power is least tied to one release' ranks artists, which design §3 rules out ('No test across artists'). It rests on 2 songs, and the article's own Q4 (14 songs to half, against BTS 41 and Bad Bunny 46) does not back 'least tied to one release'.

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:103 "That is the plainest result the series has about Czech listening: it is English-language and close to the world's average in how long it keeps a global hit, and it lets hits in other languages pass quickly."
findings.problem: This draws a general conclusion about Czech listening, and about language as the reason, from five songs, one per artist, with no interval or test across them. Language is fully confounded with the artist and the song, and the design sets no cross-artist comparison beyond listing the five places side by side. 'Lets hits in other languages pass quickly' is a causal-sounding generalisation from two songs (BTS, Bad Bunny).
findings.evidence: pop-measured-design.md §3 and §4 'Czechia across the series': list the five places side by side, no test across artists. n = 5 focal songs; language is not a registered variable.
findings.fix: Rewrite as: 'Side by side, the five places put Czechia near the middle for the three English-language songs and lower for the Korean and Spanish-language ones. Five songs cannot separate language from the artist or the song.' Drop 'the plainest result the series has'.
findings.note: Duplicate of [4]. 'The plainest result the series has about Czech listening' plus a language explanation draws on n=5 focal songs, with language not a registered variable and fully confounded with artist and song. The design asks only for a side-by-side listing.

findings.fix: Line 147: '1 October 2026, after the part 1 results were seen: countries are also ranked by days alone ...'. At first use in line 101: 'By days alone (a ranking added after the part 1 results were seen), ...'

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:101 "English-language pop that lingers where the local chart turns over fast"
findings.problem: The ratio's denominator is the local median number one, so a high ratio where local hits are short is partly mechanical. The text acknowledges this for Luxembourg and in the change list, then presents the same mechanism as a finding about where her music 'lingers'. By days alone, Iceland ranks 23rd and Estonia 28th.
findings.evidence: results.json q2: Iceland ratio rank 2, rank_by_days 23; Switzerland 3 and 21; Estonia 6 and 28; Latvia 4 and 16.

But the sentence itself names the mechanism ('where local number ones are short-lived', 'where the local chart turns over fast'), so it is not hidden. Whether 'lingers' misleads is a judgment call.

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:126 "rose with each tour ... as she moved from halls to arenas" and line 81 "nearly all in arenas, from a first tour of mid-sized halls"
findings.problem: The 2019 tour already played arenas (Moda Center, American Airlines Center, Toyota Center, Altice Arena, BOK Center), so 'halls to arenas' is not supported as the explanation for the price rise. The two lines also contradict each other ('nearly all in arenas' vs 'a first tour of mid-sized halls'). Prices are nominal, with no adjustment for inflation over 2019–2025.
findings.evidence: tour.csv, When We All Fall Asleep Tour rows: Portland Moda Center 12 489 seats, Dallas American Airlines Center, Houston Toyota Center, Lisbon Altice Arena 19 469.
findings.fix: 'rose with each tour, from 59 dollars in 2019 to 114 and 149 (nominal dollars).' Drop 'as she moved from halls to arenas' and 'mid-sized halls'.
findings.note: Duplicate of [5] on halls versus arenas (2019 rows include several 11-19k arenas). The prices are nominal (59/114/149) and the text says nothing about inflation; this part checks out.

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:116 "A handful of her songs, from every album, carry most of her listening, which matches what the first question found: her durability is spread over several songs"
findings.problem: Fourteen songs carry half of her streams, not 'most', and 14 is more than 'a handful'. Q4 measures share of streams, not durability, so it cannot 'match' Q1. The TL;DR (line 50) calls BIRDS OF A FEATHER and bad guy 'her two biggest hits', but by streams lovely (3.89 bn) is second, ahead of bad guy (2.98 bn).
findings.evidence: results.json q4; songs.csv: BIRDS OF A FEATHER 4.01 bn, lovely (with Khalid) 3.89 bn, bad guy 2.98 bn.
findings.fix: 'Fourteen songs carry half of her streams.' Drop the 'matches what the first question found' clause. TL;DR: 'Her two longest-charting number ones, from 2019 and 2024, ...'
findings.note: songs.csv: BIRDS OF A FEATHER 4.01bn, lovely 3.89bn, bad guy 2.98bn, so 'her two biggest hits' (TL;DR line 50) skips lovely if 'biggest' means streams. 'Most' with 14 songs is covered in [6]. Q4 measures stream share, not durability, so 'matches what the first question found' is a non sequitur.

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:116 "The Gini coefficient over songs is 0.52"
findings.problem: The Gini coefficient is used without explanation, and the reader cannot interpret 0.52. Part 1 explains it ('0 would mean every song streamed equally and 1 that one song took everything').
findings.evidence: pop-harry-styles.html:117 has the explanation; pop-billie-eilish.html has none.
findings.fix: Add: '(0 would mean every song streamed equally, 1 that one song took everything)'.
findings.note: Line 116 gives 'Gini coefficient over songs is 0.52' with no gloss; part 1 line 117 adds 'where 0 would mean every song streamed equally and 1 that one song took everything'.

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:86 (Kaplan–Meier, 95 % bootstrap interval, Spearman's correlation, lower bound); line 41/43/44 and fig captions ("administrative count"); line 81 ("Boxscore"); line 80 ("focal song", "whose start can be seen")
findings.problem: Several technical terms appear without a plain explanation at first use. Kaplan–Meier is half-explained. 'Bootstrap interval' and 'Spearman's correlation' are not explained at all. 'Administrative count' (fact box) is jargon. 'Boxscore' is never said to be Billboard's reported attendance and gross per engagement. 'Whose start can be seen' does not say that the chart begins 1 January 2017 and 29 earlier songs are excluded. The methods section also comes before any concrete example.
findings.evidence: Text of lines 41-44, 80-81, 86; results.json q1.excluded_before_2017 = 29.
findings.fix: Line 86: 'Spearman's correlation (whether entries with more nights tend to have a higher or lower share sold, from -1 to 1)' and 'a 95 % bootstrap interval (the range the estimate takes when the songs are resampled 2 000 times)'. Line 80: 'the 165 global number ones that first charted after the chart began in January 2017 (29 older ones excluded)'. Line 81: 'Billboard Boxscore, the industry's reported tickets and gross per engagement'. Replace 'administrative count' with 'a count, no sampling error'.

Boxscore is never defined, Spearman and the bootstrap are unexplained, and 'administrative count' appears unexplained in the fact box and captions.

findings.location: texts/pop-billie-eilish.html:139 fig. 6 caption "administrative count, 116 entries" vs 118 entries elsewhere
findings.problem: The text never explains why Q5 uses 116 entries when Q3 uses 118. The two Russian 2019 shows have no gross.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:122 "Bad Bunny's tours followed income most ... the only artist whose tours played many countries across a wide range of incomes, from Honduras to Sweden."
findings.problem: Both parts of this explanation are contradicted by tickets.csv. Bad Bunny is not the only artist with many countries over a wide income range: Harry Styles (33 countries, GDP per capita 3,169 to 113,122, ratio 36) and Billie Eilish (27 countries, 3,548 to 131,592, ratio 37) both cover a wider range than Bad Bunny (27 countries, 3,003 to 78,009, ratio 26). Sweden (63,133) is also not Bad Bunny's richest host; the Netherlands (73,684) and the United States (69,585) are richer.
findings.evidence: uv run pandas on assets/pop/together/tickets.csv, grouped by artist: bad-bunny 27 countries, min 3003 (HND), max 78009, ratio 26.0; billie-eilish 27, 3548-131592, 37.1; harry-styles 33, 3169-113122, 35.7. Mean gdppc per Bad Bunny country: SWE 63133, USA 69585, NLD 73684.
findings.fix: Drop the 'only artist' explanation, e.g. 'Bad Bunny's tours followed income most, with an elasticity of 0.34 (0.23 to 0.45), across 27 countries from Honduras to the Netherlands.' If an explanation is wanted, use one the data support, such as Bad Bunny's many dates in middle-income Latin American countries.
findings.note: tickets.csv grouped by artist: bad-bunny has 27 countries from 3,003 to 78,009 (ratio 26). Harry Styles has 33 countries, ratio 35.7, and Billie Eilish 27 countries, ratio 37.1, so both cover a wider range. Bad Bunny's richest hosts by mean GDP per capita are NLD 73,684, USA 69,585 and AUS, all above SWE 63,133.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:117 "the host countries' incomes run from 3 003 dollars per person a year in Honduras to 101 733 in Ireland, a ratio of about 34"
findings.problem: The upper figure is not a GDP per capita for any year. It is the mean of Ireland's entry-level values from 2018 to 2025 (80,805 to 131,592). Honduras's figure is a single 2022 value. The sentence calls both 'incomes per person a year', but in the data the regressor actually runs from 3,003 to 131,592, a ratio of about 44. With that range the derived figures change: the cheaper ticket becomes about 2.3 times, not 2.2, and the cost in days of income about 19 times, not 16.
findings.evidence: tools/pop/together_article.py:191-195 takes tickets.groupby('country').gdppc.mean() and uses its idxmin/idxmax. tickets.csv IRL rows: 80804.11 (2018), 105190.69 (2022), 106818.92 (2023), 131592.46 (2025); mean 101733.50. HND has one row, 3003.29 (2022).
findings.fix: Either say it is an average ('Ireland's average across the tours' years, 101 733') or use the entry-level range: 'from 3 003 dollars in Honduras (2022) to 131 592 in Ireland (2025), a ratio of about 44', and recompute the 46-dollar, 2.2x and 16x figures.
findings.note: together_article.py:191 takes groupby('country').gdppc.mean(). IRL has 6 rows (80,804 x2, 105,191 x2, 106,819, 131,592) with mean 101,733.5. HND is a single value, 3,003. The article calls this 'per person a year' without saying it is an average across years.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:96 "The smallest estimate is the one without songs still charting, because those are mostly Bad Bunny's in Latin America, the strongest same-language pairs; the effect does not depend on them, but they make it larger."
findings.problem: Only 18 of the 48 still-charting pairs are Bad Bunny in Spanish-speaking countries, and that 18 includes Spain, which is not Latin America. That is 38 %, not 'mostly'. Bad Bunny accounts for 27 of the 48 in total. The check also does more than remove 'strongest pairs': all 18 Spanish same-language pairs are still charting, so the 1.9 estimate has no Spanish same-language pair at all and rests only on the English and Korean contrasts. Saying 'the effect does not depend on them' understates this.
findings.evidence: panel.csv: still==True grouped by artist and country_lang gives bad-bunny/es 18, bad-bunny/other 8, bad-bunny/en 1, billie-eilish/en 8, billie-eilish/other 9, harry-styles 3, taylor-swift 1 (48 in total). results.json m1b.es.pairs = 18, so every Spanish same-language pair is still charting.
findings.fix: Reword: 'The smallest estimate is the one without songs still charting: those include all 18 of Bad Bunny's Spanish-speaking pairs, so without them the estimate rests on the English and Korean songs alone, and it is still above one.'
findings.note: panel.csv: 48 still-charting pairs, of which bad-bunny/es = 18 (17 in Latin America plus es). That is 38 %, not 'mostly'. All 18 same-language Bad Bunny pairs are still charting, and m1b.es.pairs = 18, so the 1.9 check contains no Spanish same-language pair.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:74 "streaming lets the question be asked song by song and day by day<sup>2</sup>" (r2 Aguiar & Waldfogel 2018)
findings.problem: Aguiar and Waldfogel (2018, IJIO) estimate whether streaming displaces or stimulates music sales (sales displacement and revenue). The paper is not about streaming charts making it possible to study home or language bias song by song and day by day, so it does not support the clause it is attached to.
findings.evidence: Crossref for 10.1016/j.ijindorg.2017.06.004: 'As streaming reaches flood stage, does it stimulate or depress music sales?', IJIO 57, 278-307. The metadata matches the reference list, but the topic is sales displacement.
findings.fix: Cite a source that uses daily Spotify chart data across countries for local or home bias (for example Way, Garcia-Gathright and Cramer 2020 on local music consumption, or Aguiar, Waldfogel and Waldfogel 2021 on playlisting), or drop the citation and state the point as the author's own.
findings.note: The reference metadata is correct. The paper uses song-level Spotify streaming data across countries, so it loosely illustrates the data point, but its topic is sales displacement, not home or language bias. Whether it fits the clause is a judgement call, and I did not read the full text.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:74 "Courty and Pagliero how much of that pricing is set before a promoter knows each city<sup>4</sup>"
findings.problem: The chapter surveys pricing styles in the concert industry: uniform versus differentiated seat pricing, price discrimination and pricing under demand uncertainty. 'Set before a promoter knows each city' is a loose paraphrase that attributes a city-level claim the chapter does not make specifically.
findings.evidence: Crossref 10.1016/b978-0-444-53776-8.00013-1: 'The Pricing of Art and the Art of Pricing: Pricing Styles in the Concert Industry', Handbook of the Economics of Art and Culture vol. 2, 299-356. The metadata is correct.
findings.fix: e.g. 'and Courty and Pagliero the pricing styles promoters use, including how much prices vary across seats and shows'.
findings.note: The chapter covers pricing styles, including prices set in advance under demand uncertainty and little variation across shows. The paraphrase 'before a promoter knows each city' is loose but not clearly wrong. I did not check the chapter text.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:122 "BTS's tours priced almost the same everywhere, 0.04 (−0.29 to 0.38)"; Harry Styles, Billie Eilish intervals
findings.problem: The per-artist intervals use country-clustered SEs with few clusters: 11 for BTS and 7 for Taylor Swift. The cited guide (r5, Cameron & Miller) warns that cluster-robust intervals are unreliable with this few clusters. The article flags only Taylor Swift's interval and reports BTS's interval and its 'almost the same everywhere' reading without the caveat. The article also cites r5 only for the 73-cluster language model, not the 43-cluster price model.
findings.evidence: results.json m2c: bts clusters 11, n 24; taylor-swift clusters 7. Article line 131 invokes r5 only for 73 clusters.
findings.fix: Add: 'BTS's interval rests on 11 countries and Taylor Swift's on 7, too few clusters for the clustered intervals to be reliable' (or report wild-cluster bootstrap intervals in a future version).
findings.note: results.json m2c: BTS has 11 clusters (n 24) and Taylor Swift 7. The article caveats only Taylor Swift and cites r5 only for the 73-cluster language model.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:79 "Each pair is coded for whether the song's language is the country's main official language"
findings.problem: This conflicts with the coding the same paragraph and the design actually use: 'any country where English is an official national language'. The English list includes hk, in, ng, ph, pk, sg and za, where English is an official language but not the main one, and mt, where Maltese is the national language.
findings.evidence: docs/research/pop-measured-part6-design.md §2 English list; tools/pop/together.py COUNTRY_LANG.
findings.fix: Replace 'main official language' with 'an official national language' (and likewise in line 149, 'Language is coded by official national language').
findings.note: Line 79 says 'main official language', then 'an official national language'. COUNTRY_LANG in together.py lists hk, in, mt, ng, ph, pk, sg and za as en. Line 149 says 'official national language', which is consistent with the code, so only line 79 needs changing.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:138 "What changed after registration: Nothing."
findings.problem: The design (§3) fixes the reporting of β 'as exp(β) − 1 in percent'. The article reports the multiple exp(β) (2.9×) and never the percent (+191 %). This is a small reporting change from the registered design and is not listed.
findings.evidence: pop-measured-part6-design.md §3 'reported as exp(β) − 1 in percent'; results.json m1.pct = 1.906; the article uses 2.9× throughout.
findings.fix: Either add the percent ('2.9 times, +191 %') or list it under changes: 'β reported as a multiple exp(β) rather than exp(β) − 1 in percent; same quantity.'
findings.note: Design §3, line 39: 'reported as exp(β) − 1 in percent'. The article reports only the multiples (2.9×, 1.8×, 4.9×), and the changes section says 'Nothing.' It is a minor presentational deviation.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:154 "Every number on this page is filled in from assets/pop/together/results.json by a script."
findings.problem: Several numbers do not come from results.json. The day counts (1 152, 891, 866, 217, 141, 850–902, 332, 1 253, 14, 634, 757, 867, 105) and the incomes 3 003 and 101 733 come from panel.csv and tickets.csv.
findings.evidence: results.json contains no per-pair days or GDP values. together_article.py:191 reads pop-measured-part6-tickets.csv for the income range.
findings.fix: 'Every number on this page is filled in by a script from results.json, panel.csv and tickets.csv in assets/pop/together/.'
findings.note: together_article.py:188-195 reads the panel CSV for the per-pair days (d_<country>_<artist>) and the tickets CSV for the income range and span. results.json holds neither.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:38-41, 49-50, 96 "A hit lasts three times as long in its own language" / "That holds ... under every check" / "the effect does not depend on them, but they make it larger"
findings.problem: The pooled 2.9x headline rests mostly on one artist's still-charting pairs. All 18 Spanish same-language pairs (Bad Bunny) are still charting, so their days are lower bounds. The pre-registered check that drops still-charting pairs therefore drops every Spanish same-language pair. That check no longer tests the Spanish effect at all: what survives is essentially the English effect (1.9x, CI 1.07-3.3, about the same as M1b's English 1.8x). The article says the effect 'does not depend on them' and the tl;dr says it 'holds ... under every check'. In fact the jump from about 1.8-1.9x to 2.9x comes from one artist and one cohort of right-censored pairs. Neither the title nor the tl;dr says this.
findings.evidence: docs/research/pop-measured-part6-panel.csv grouped by still x artist x country_lang: 48 still-charting pairs, of which bad-bunny/es = 18 (= all 18 Spanish same pairs per m1b.es.pairs), bad-bunny/other 8, billie-eilish 17, others 3. results.json m1 coef 1.067 (2.9x) vs without_still_charting 0.637 (1.89x, n=300) vs m1b.en 0.569 (1.77x).
findings.fix: In the tl;dr and the dek, say the pooled 2.9x mixes a 1.8x English effect with a 4.9x effect from one Spanish song whose 18 same-language pairs are all still charting. Replace 'the effect does not depend on them' with: 'without the songs still charting, which removes every Spanish same-language pair, the multiple is 1.9 (1.07-3.3), close to the English-only estimate'. Consider changing the title from 'three times' to wording that does not generalise Bad Bunny's estimate to every language.
findings.note: All 18 Spanish same-language pairs have still=True. The without_still_charting check (n=300) gives coef 0.637 (1.89×), close to m1b.en 0.569 (1.77×). So the check drops the whole Spanish contrast, and 'the effect does not depend on them' and 'holds under every check' overstate it.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:52, 107 "Czech listeners kept the three English-language songs longer than the model expects ... treat English-language pop much as an English-speaking country would"
findings.problem: The model has country fixed effects, so the five Czech log residuals sum to zero by construction. Some songs must sit above the prediction and some below, so 'longer than expected' and 'shorter' are only relative to each other. The pattern (English songs up, BTS down) is also not specific to Czechia. Across all 'other-language' countries, the mean residual is positive for the three English artists (+0.01 to +0.15) and strongly negative for BTS (-0.28), and English songs beat non-English ones in 27 of 40 such countries. What the text presents as a Czech trait is the model's general misfit for English songs outside English-speaking countries.
findings.evidence: Czech log residuals from refitting M1: 0.151+0.496-0.357-0.581+0.292 = 0.000. Residual means over country_lang=='other': harry-styles 0.013, taylor-swift 0.099, billie-eilish 0.151, bad-bunny 0.045, bts -0.284. In 66% of 40 'other' countries the English mean residual exceeds the non-English one. tools/pop/together.py:89-91 computes these residuals from the same FE model.
findings.fix: State that the residuals are relative within Czechia and sum to zero. Compare Czechia with the average non-English, non-Spanish country, e.g. 'English songs outlast the model in most countries that speak none of the five languages; Czechia follows that pattern, more strongly for Taylor Swift'. Drop 'much as an English-speaking country would' and remove or soften the tl;dr bullet.
findings.note: I refitted M1 with OLS and artist and country fixed effects. The Czech residuals (0.151, 0.496, -0.357, -0.581, 0.292) sum to 1.9e-14. Mean residuals over 'other' countries: HS 0.013, TS 0.099, BE 0.151, BB 0.045, BTS -0.284. The mean English residual exceeds the non-English one in 27 of 40 'other' countries, so the pattern is not specific to Czechia.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:122 "BTS's tours priced almost the same everywhere, 0.04 (-0.29 to 0.38), which is why a ticket in Mexico cost them more than a week of income"
findings.problem: The BTS interval includes zero and also 0.38, which is higher than the pooled 0.22 and above Bad Bunny's point estimate. The data cannot tell whether BTS 'priced almost the same everywhere', yet the text treats the point estimate as a finding and draws a causal 'which is why' from it. 'them' wrongly refers to BTS instead of fans. The ranking 'came next ... then Billie Eilish's' also orders estimates whose intervals overlap, and Billie Eilish's includes zero.
findings.evidence: results.json m2c.bts coef 0.043, lo -0.291, hi 0.377, n=24, 11 clusters; m2c.billie-eilish lo -0.078.
findings.fix: 'BTS's estimate, 0.04 (-0.29 to 0.38), rests on 24 entries in 11 countries and is too uncertain to say whether its prices followed income; a ticket in Mexico cost its fans more than a week of income.' Say that the per-artist intervals overlap, instead of ranking them.
findings.note: m2c.bts: 0.043 (-0.291 to 0.377), whose upper bound is above the pooled 0.22. Billie Eilish's lower bound is -0.078. 'which is why' is causal, and 'them' grammatically refers to BTS. The Mexico figure itself checks out: 279 / (13,889/365) = 7.3 days.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:122 "No artist's tours came close to pricing in proportion to income."
findings.problem: Taylor Swift's interval (-0.78 to 1.19) includes 1, i.e. prices fully proportional to income. The previous sentence calls it 'too wide to read', and this sentence then reads it as excluding proportional pricing.
findings.evidence: results.json m2c.taylor-swift lo -0.784, hi 1.187.
findings.fix: 'For the four artists with readable intervals, none came close to pricing in proportion to income.'
findings.note: m2c.taylor-swift hi = 1.187, so the interval includes 1. 'No artist ... came close' contradicts the preceding 'too wide to read'.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:132 "which is one reason the estimate is a lower bound on how much prices adapt to income across regions"
findings.problem: The 'lower bound' claim is not supported by any analysis, and the next sentence gives a bias in the opposite direction. If poorer countries sell a cheaper seat mix, the average-ticket elasticity is biased up. The direction of the net bias is unknown, so 'lower bound' claims more than the design shows.
findings.evidence: No check in docs/research/pop-measured-part6-design.md §4 or tools/pop/together.py tests between- vs within-tour variation. The very next sentence at line 132 describes an upward bias from seat mix.
findings.fix: 'Regional pricing of whole legs would be absorbed by the tour effects and push the estimate down, while a cheaper seat mix in poorer countries would push it up; the data cannot say which dominates.'
findings.note: Line 132 calls the estimate a 'lower bound' with no supporting analysis. The next sentence (cheaper seat mix in poorer countries) describes a bias that inflates the elasticity, so the net direction is unknown.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:43, 51, 116 "about 6.1x the days of income" / "costs several times more of a day's pay in poorer countries"
findings.problem: The days-of-income figure is a highlighted headline number and the tl;dr calls it 'a day's pay'. It divides by GDP per capita, which is not fans' income or pay. The text admits this only at the end (line 149, 'a rough stand-in').
findings.evidence: Line 43 header stat and line 51 tl;dr use income/pay wording. The only caveat is at line 149.
findings.fix: Use 'days of GDP per head' in the header stat and the tl;dr, or add 'measured by GDP per head, a rough stand-in for fans' income' at first use (line 116).
findings.note: Line 43: 'the days of income'. tl;dr line 51: 'a day's pay'. The measure is GDP per capita, and the only caveat is at line 149.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:79 "coded for whether the song's language is the country's main official language ... English-speaking countries are those where English is an official national language"; line 91 "which fits English being the default language of global pop"
findings.problem: The text calls the coding 'main official language' and then defines it as 'an official national language'. The registered list counts India, Pakistan, Philippines, Nigeria, Hong Kong, Singapore, Malta and South Africa as English-speaking, even though English is not the main language in most of them. That coding by itself would shrink the English effect. The article explains the smaller English effect only by the post-hoc 'default language of global pop' story and does not name this alternative.
findings.evidence: tools/pop/together.py:23 and design §2 list 'au ca gb hk ie in mt ng nz ph pk sg us za' as English.
findings.fix: Drop 'main' at line 79. At line 91, add: 'Part of the gap may be coding: eight of the fourteen English-coded countries mostly speak other languages.' Label the global-pop explanation as an interpretation.
findings.note: In panel.csv the en-coded countries are au ca gb hk ie in ng nz ph pk sg us za (13; mt has no pair). Of these, 7 mostly speak other languages (hk, in, ng, ph, pk, sg, za), so the suggested 'eight of fourteen' should be 'seven of thirteen'. Misclassification as an alternative explanation for the smaller English effect is not mentioned.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:96 "those are mostly Bad Bunny's in Latin America"
findings.problem: Only 18 of the 48 still-charting pairs are Bad Bunny in Spanish-speaking countries. 27 of 48 are Bad Bunny's overall, and 17 are Billie Eilish's.
findings.evidence: panel.csv: still==True, bad-bunny/es 18, bad-bunny/other 8, bad-bunny/en 1, billie-eilish 17, others 3.
findings.fix: 'More than half are Bad Bunny's, including all 18 of his pairs in Spanish-speaking countries.'
findings.note: Duplicate of [2]. Still-charting pairs: Bad Bunny 27 (es 18, other 8, en 1), Billie Eilish 17, others 3. Only 17 of the 48 are Bad Bunny in Latin America.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:47-53 details.tldr
findings.problem: The short version gives no numbers, does not say what each result rests on beyond 'five artists', and does not say what would overturn it. It says nothing about the pooled effect depending on Bad Bunny's still-charting pairs, or the price result depending partly on Bad Bunny (0.14 without him).
findings.evidence: tl;dr bullets at lines 49-53; m2_drop_artist.bad-bunny = 0.141.
findings.fix: Add one bullet: 'The language result leans on one Spanish song still in the charts (English alone: 1.8x); the price result falls to 0.14 without Bad Bunny. More artists with songs in other languages could overturn either.'
findings.note: The tl;dr bullets (lines 49-53) contain no numbers and no fragility caveat. m2_drop_artist gives a minimum of 0.14 without Bad Bunny, and the language result depends on still-charting Spanish pairs (see [9]). The header facts do give the headline numbers.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:79 "the artist's focal song"
findings.problem: 'Focal song' is central to the language model but is never defined, and four of the five songs are never named (only Dynamite appears, at line 96). A reader cannot tell which songs the 348 pairs describe.
findings.evidence: grep of the article: no song title except 'Dynamite'.
findings.fix: At line 79 add: 'the focal song of each part: <title> (Harry Styles), <title> (Taylor Swift), Dynamite (BTS), <title> (Bad Bunny), <title> (Billie Eilish)'.
findings.note: 'focal' appears 4 times and is never defined. The only song title in the article is Dynamite.

findings.location: texts/pop-together.html:39, 41, 74, 86, 94, 138
findings.problem: Technical terms are used without explanation at first use: 'elasticity' (line 39, explained only at 86); 'fixed effects' (line 41, gloss at 85); '95 % CI' (line 41, never glossed); 'clustered by country' / 'clustered standard errors' (line 86, the reason is given but not what clustering does); 'Boxscore' (line 64/80, never explained as Billboard's touring box-office chart); 'lower bound' (line 79); 'leg totals' (line 138, never explained).
findings.evidence: Article lines as listed.
findings.fix: Add a short gloss at first use, e.g. 'income elasticity (how many percent the price rises for each 1 % of income)', 'Boxscore, Billboard's record of concert grosses', 'leg totals (rows summing several shows, excluded)'.
findings.note: Partly. The deck (line 39) already glosses elasticity ('0.22 % for each 1 %'), so that item is refuted. Boxscore is never explained, 'leg totals' at line 138 is unexplained, and '95 % CI' and clustering are not glossed.

findings.location: texts/pop-measured.html:72 (tldr) "Czech listeners keep English-language hits about as long as the world's middle and let hits in other languages pass quickly."; also :166 "Czechia's place follows language: for the three English-language artists ... for BTS and Bad Bunny well below it"
findings.problem: BTS's focal song Dynamite is sung entirely in English, yet it is the one that passed quickly in Czechia (ratio 0.60, rank 60/72). The tldr's claim that English-language hits sit mid-ranking and hits in other languages pass quickly is contradicted by Dynamite. The body sentence avoids the error only by switching from songs to artists.
findings.evidence: assets/pop/bts/results.json q2.czechia: ratio 0.6009, rank 60 of 72. docs/research/pop-measured-part6-design.md §2: "Korean (BTS; *Dynamite* is sung in English, so a second coding treats it as English)". texts/pop-together.html:96 says Dynamite is English, "which it is sung in".
findings.fix: Tldr: "Czech listeners keep the English-language hits of Harry Styles, Taylor Swift and Billie Eilish about as long as the middle of the world ranking, and let BTS's and Bad Bunny's pass quickly (though BTS's Dynamite is sung in English)." Body: "Czechia's place follows the artist's language market rather than the song's language..." or say plainly that Dynamite is the exception.
findings.note: Line 72 talks about English-language hits vs hits in other languages, but bts/results.json q2.czechia gives Dynamite ratio 0.601, rank 60.
