findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:113 "One week in eleven is about what chance produces"
findings.problem: The pre-trend bands are uniform 95 % bands that cover all 25 event weeks at once (crit 2.65 in results.json). Under such bands the chance of any week excluding zero is about 5 % in total, so one week in eleven excluding zero is not 'about what chance produces'. That reasoning only works for separate pointwise 95 % intervals. The sentence plays down the single registered pre-trend failure.
findings.evidence: results.json y1_share.crit = 2.653 (uniform critical value). estimate.py fit() uses cband=True and builds lo/hi = att ± crit·se. The article itself says at line 89 that the bands 'hold for all weeks at once'. Week −10 band is 0.0000289 to 0.000505, i.e. 0.003 to 0.050 pp.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Because the bands are uniform, even one week outside them is more than chance alone would usually produce. The weeks nearest the show are flat, but the registered rule counts it, and it is one reason the label is not 'supported'."
findings.note: results.json y1_share.crit=2.653 and estimate.py builds lo/hi = att ± crit·se from the dynamic aggregation over e=−12..+12, so these are sup-t bands covering all 25 weeks at once. Under the null the chance that any of the 11 pre-weeks excludes zero is at most about 5 %. 'One week in eleven is about what chance produces' only holds for pointwise intervals, and line 89 itself says the bands hold for all weeks at once.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:97 "A sold-out arena holds ten to twenty thousand people, so the extra streams in a week are a few per person in the hall"
findings.problem: Treatment is the week of a country's FIRST show. For half of the visited countries (the 2017 legs) that first show was in a 2,000 to 6,000 seat theatre, not an arena. Against roughly 64 000 extra streams that is about 10 to 30 streams per attendee, not 'a few'. The capacity figure also has no source in the article.
findings.evidence: docs/research/harry-styles-tour.csv, Live on Tour first shows: SF Masonic 3,188 sold; Enmore Theatre Sydney 2,446; Star PAC Singapore 4,862; Ex Theater Tokyo 3,600 over 2 nights; Eventim Apollo London 10,375 over 2 nights; Tempodrom Berlin 3,546; AFAS Live Amsterdam 5,974. 0.000835 × 76.5 M ≈ 64 000.
findings.fix: Base the sentence on the repo's own Boxscore data, e.g. "His first show in a country was often in a theatre of two to six thousand seats (arenas of ten to twenty thousand came in 2018), so the extra streams are several to a few dozen per person in the hall, or a little from many others; the data cannot say which." Cite the Wikipedia tour revision [7].
findings.note: docs/research/harry-styles-tour.csv shows the 2017 first shows were in small venues: SF Masonic 3,188; Eventim Apollo 10,375 over 2 nights; Tempodrom 3,546; AFAS 5,974; Star PAC Singapore 4,862; Enmore 2,446; Ex Theater Tokyo 3,600 over 2 nights; Spark Arena NZ 7,575. The 2018 first shows were also mostly under 11k (St. Jakobshalle 6,725; Royal Arena 10,580; HKCEC 4,097). The article gives 64 000 extra streams (0.000835 × 76.5 M), which is roughly 10 to 30 per attendee, not 'a few'. The capacity figure has no source in the article.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:107 "New Zealand (+0.314), Australia (+0.312), Belgium (+0.210), Singapore (+0.194): ... while his album was still in their charts"
findings.problem: For Australia and Singapore his raw share in the four weeks before the show was zero: he was not in their Top 200 at all. So 'while his album was still in their charts' is false for two of the four countries named. For them the jump is a re-entry into the chart, not a rise from a charting level.
findings.evidence: Recomputed from assets/concerts/panel.csv with the article.py raw_path() definition (mean y1_share over e = −4..−1, against e = 0). Australia pre = 0.000, show week = 0.312. Singapore pre = 0.000, show week = 0.194. New Zealand pre = 0.187. Belgium pre = 0.163.
findings.fix: Change to: "... all visited after the opening legs in North America and western Europe; in New Zealand and Belgium his album was still in the chart, while in Australia and Singapore the show week brought him back into a chart he had left."
findings.note: Recomputed from docs/research/concert-effect-panel.csv using the article.py raw_path definition. Pre-show mean (e=−4..−1): Australia 0.000, Singapore 0.000, NZ 0.187, Belgium 0.163. Australia was at 0 from e=−6 and Singapore from e=−6 as well. So 'while his album was still in their charts' is false for AU and SG. In both the show week was a re-entry; Singapore's lasted one week only (0.194 at e=0, 0 at e=+1).

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:72 "listening is now counted every day in every country and can follow a concert within days<sup>3</sup>"
findings.problem: Aguiar & Waldfogel (2018) study whether streaming displaces or stimulates music sales. They say nothing about concerts, or about streaming responding to concerts within days. Attributing the 'can follow a concert within days' claim to them is a misattribution. The source supports at most that country-level streaming data exist.
findings.evidence: Crossref 10.1016/j.ijindorg.2017.06.004: 'As streaming reaches flood stage, does it stimulate or depress music sales?', IJIO 57, 278-307. The topic is the sales-displacement effect of streaming.
findings.fix: Move the citation so that it only supports the data claim, e.g. "Streaming makes the question sharper, because listening is now counted every day in every country, and such country-level streaming data have already been used to measure streaming's effect on sales<sup>3</sup>; they can also follow a concert within days." Or drop r3 from this sentence.
findings.note: Crossref for 10.1016/j.ijindorg.2017.06.004 returns the title 'As streaming reaches flood stage, does it stimulate or depress music sales?' (IJIO). The paper is about sales displacement and does not cover concerts or a streaming response within days. The citation sits on the clause 'can follow a concert within days', which it does not support.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:89 "Inference uses a bootstrap that resamples countries"
findings.problem: The registered and implemented method is the multiplier bootstrap clustered by country. It perturbs country-level influence functions with random weights; it does not resample countries. The description is inaccurate.
findings.evidence: concert-effect-design.md §4: 'multiplier bootstrap clustered by country (999 draws)'. estimate.py: ATTgt(..., cband=True, biters=999, clustervar='id').
findings.fix: "Inference uses a multiplier bootstrap clustered by country (999 draws), and the bands are uniform: ..."
findings.note: Design §4 and the estimate.py docstring say multiplier bootstrap clustered by country. The code is ATTgt(cband=True, biters=999, clustervar='id'). A multiplier bootstrap perturbs influence functions with random weights and does not resample countries, so 'resamples countries' is inaccurate. Low severity.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:102 "the show lifted the songs people already knew rather than bringing new ones into the chart"
findings.problem: The same paragraph reports that the number of his songs in the chart rose by 0.29 on an average day in the show week (band 0.09 to 0.49, excluding zero). So songs did enter the chart. The Y3 result (top three songs ≈ whole effect) shows only that the extra streams went to his three biggest songs, two of which (Sweet Creature, Kiwi) were themselves often off the chart.
findings.evidence: results.json y2_songs.event e=0: att 0.288, lo 0.087, hi 0.489. y3_share_top3.summary 0.000343 against y1 0.000344.
findings.fix: "... almost the whole of the main effect: the extra listening went to his three best-known songs, some of which re-entered the chart, rather than to the rest of the album."
findings.note: results.json y2_songs e=0: att 0.288, band 0.087 to 0.489, which excludes zero. So in the show week the number of his songs in the chart rose, i.e. songs (re-)entered it. That contradicts 'rather than bringing new ones into the chart'. See also #12.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:72 "Harry Styles's first solo tour, which visited 24 countries with a Spotify chart"
findings.problem: This conflicts with line 78, which says Thailand had a show and a chart that was incomplete. Thailand is in panel.csv, so the tour visited 25 countries with a Spotify chart, 24 of them with a chart in every week of the window.
findings.evidence: assets/concerts/panel.csv has 25 countries with g>0, including Thailand (g=63). results.json dropped_unbalanced includes Thailand. shows.csv: 2018-05-07 Thailand.
findings.fix: "... which visited 24 countries with a complete Spotify chart between September 2017 and June 2018 ..."
findings.note: panel.csv has 25 countries with g>0, Thailand among them (shows.csv 2018-05-07). Thailand is listed in dropped_unbalanced, and line 78 itself says Thailand had a show and an incomplete chart. '24 countries with a Spotify chart' should say 24 with a complete chart. China (2017-11-19) has no Spotify chart, so it is correctly excluded.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:79 "and ended with South-East Asia in May and Latin America in May and June"
findings.problem: The tour did not end in Latin America. After Mexico (1 to 2 June 2018) it played a North American arena leg until 14 July 2018 (Canada and the United States, 22 dates). Only the last NEW country was in Latin America.
findings.evidence: assets/concerts/shows.csv: rows from 2018-06-05 to 2018-07-14 in United States and Canada. concert-effect-design.md §2: 'The tour ran from 19 September 2017 to 14 July 2018.'
findings.fix: "... South-East Asia in May and Latin America in May and June, before a last North American leg in June and July that added no new country."
findings.note: shows.csv lists US and Canada dates from 2018-06-05 to 2018-07-14 after Mexico (1–2 June), and design §2 says the tour ran to 14 July 2018. Line 77 correctly says Mexico was the last new country, but line 79 says the tour 'ended with ... Latin America', which is wrong.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:123 "the next parts of Pop, measured can ask the same of other artists" (also kicker line 35 "Research · Pop, measured")
findings.problem: The Pop, measured hub describes this page as 'a separate study, not a part of the series'. Calling the follow-ups 'the next parts of Pop, measured' contradicts that.
findings.evidence: texts/pop-measured.html:171: 'It is a separate study, not a part of the series.'
findings.fix: "... is open; the same design could be run on other artists' tours."
findings.note: texts/pop-measured.html:171 says 'It is a separate study, not a part of the series.' The article's kicker reads 'Research · Pop, measured' and line 123 says 'the next parts of Pop, measured can ask the same of other artists', which implies it belongs to the series.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:113 "1 has a band that excludes zero: week -10"
findings.problem: The sentence opens with a numeral ('1'), and 'week -10' uses an ASCII hyphen where the rest of the page uses a true minus sign (−).
findings.evidence: article.py builds bad_pre with f"week {r['e']}" without the n() minus-sign formatter.
findings.fix: "Of the eleven weeks from −12 to −2, one has a band that excludes zero: week −10 (0.003 to 0.050 points)."
findings.note: article.py:157 builds bad_pre with f"week {r['e']}" using an ASCII hyphen, while elsewhere it uses n()/pp() with U+2212. n_bad_pre renders '1' at the start of the clause ('Of the eleven weeks ..., 1 has a band').

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:7 and :9 (meta/og description) "A registered staggered difference-in-differences study of 50 countries: in the week of Harry Styles's first show in a country, his share of its Spotify Top 200 rose by about 75 %, and within three weeks the rise was gone."
findings.problem: The search and social-share summaries put the word "registered" next to the week-0 peak. That peak is a single event-study coefficient, singled out after the data were seen because it is the largest. The registered result, the weeks 0 to +4 summary, is not mentioned, and neither is its label 'inconclusive'. The body (line 96) says 'the headline does not swap one for the other', yet these two summaries do exactly that. 'within three weeks the rise was gone' is also stated as a finding, although the bands for weeks +1 to +3 all include zero.
findings.evidence: design §4/§6: the only labelled estimand is the 0..+4 average. results.json y1_share.label = 'inconclusive', summary 0.034 pp (−0.004 to 0.073). The deck (line 37) does mention 'inconclusive', but lines 7 and 9 do not.
findings.fix: E.g. meta: "A registered difference-in-differences study of 50 countries: the registered five-week effect of Harry Styles's first show in a country is inconclusive (+0.034 pp, CI −0.004 to 0.073); in the show week alone his chart share rose by about 0.08 pp, a spike that faded within weeks." Use the same wording for og:description.
findings.note: Lines 7 and 9 report only the week-0 coefficient as a 75 % rise and never mention the registered 0..+4 summary or its 'inconclusive' label. The deck (line 37) does mention it, so the meta and og text diverge from the body's own 'headline does not swap one for the other'. 'Within three weeks the rise was gone' rests on point estimates (+3 = 0.004); the bands from +1 on include zero, so this is not a demonstrated return. Week 0 was a registered event-study coefficient (design §4–5), so 'singled out post hoc' is somewhat overstated. Severity is arguably medium rather than high.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:102 "Restricted to his three biggest songs, the summary is 0.034 points and inconclusive, almost the whole of the main effect: the show lifted the songs people already knew rather than bringing new ones into the chart."
findings.problem: This cannot tell old songs from new ones, because Y3 is almost the same variable as Y1. Before the show, his three biggest songs already made up 99.7 % of his chart share, so Y3 has to track Y1 whatever the mechanism. Y3 is also registered as exploratory (design §3), and the text does not say so. The same claim comes back in 'What this means' (line 123: 'concentrated on songs fans already played').
findings.evidence: results.json pre_mean: y1_share 0.0011168, y3_share_top3 0.0011132. The summaries are 0.0003440 and 0.0003426. Design §3: 'Y3 (exploratory)'.
findings.fix: Replace with: "His three biggest songs already made up almost all of his chart share before the show, so restricting to them (an exploratory outcome) gives nearly the same estimate, 0.034 points; the data cannot tell whether the show also helped other songs." Remove 'concentrated on songs fans already played' from line 123.
findings.note: results.json pre_mean: y3 0.0011132 vs y1 0.0011168 (99.7 %). The summaries are 0.000343 vs 0.000344, and the event paths match to the third decimal. Y3 is therefore nearly identical to Y1 by construction and cannot separate known songs from new ones. Design §3 marks Y3 as exploratory, but line 102 does not say so, and line 123 repeats the mechanism claim ('concentrated on songs fans already played').

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:95 "The week before the show shows 0.011 points", :113 "the weeks nearest the show are flat", :90 "The weeks before the show test whether visited and unvisited countries were already drifting apart"
findings.problem: estimate.py calls csdid with its default base_period='varying'. With that setting each coefficient before the show is a one-week change (week t against week t−1), while each coefficient after the show is measured against week −1. Fig. 2 and the text read both as levels on one scale and never say this. Read as weekly changes, weeks −7 to −2 are all negative, between −0.003 and −0.020 pp per week. Added up, that is about −0.07 pp of relative decline in visited countries over six weeks, close to the size of the week-0 effect. So the weeks nearest the show are not flat, and the 'return to baseline, if anything a little below' (weeks +5 to +12 ≈ −0.022) may just continue that relative decline.
findings.evidence: tools/concerts/estimate.py:47 calls .fit(est_method="reg") without base_period. In csdid 0.4.2, att_gt.py:368 has `def fit(self, est_method='dr', base_period='varying', ...)`. results.json y1_share.event e=−7..−2: −0.0057, −0.0193, −0.0026, −0.0147, −0.0110, −0.0195 pp.
findings.fix: Say in the method section (and in the fig. 2 caption) that each coefficient before the show is a one-week change and each one after is measured against week −1. Describe the run of negative weekly changes from −7 to −2 as a mild pre-existing relative decline. Optionally re-run with base_period='universal', disclosed as a sensitivity added after registration.
findings.note: csdid 0.4.2 has att_gt.py signature fit(self, est_method='dr', base_period='varying', bstrap=True). estimate.py calls .fit(est_method='reg') without base_period, so the pre-period coefficients are short (t vs t−1) differences, and neither the text nor the fig. 2 caption says so. results.json e=−7..−2 are all negative and sum to about −0.073 pp. That cuts against 'the weeks nearest the show are flat' when read as cumulative drift. Weeks −12..−8 sum to about +0.07, which offsets this over the full pre-window.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:97 "0.083 percentage points is roughly 64 000 extra streams of his songs in that country that week, and about 1.5 million across the 24 countries together"
findings.problem: The ATT is an unweighted average over countries. Multiplying it by the mean chart size, which the US alone (520 M of a 77 M mean) pulls up, assumes the share effect is the same in large and small markets. The data show the opposite: the largest jumps were in small markets (NZ 17 M, Belgium 11 M, Singapore 15 M weekly chart streams), while the large first-wave markets (US, UK, Canada, France) had falling raw shares. The 1.5 million total is probably several times too high. Weighting the raw jumps by each country's chart size gives about 0.35 M against about 1.28 M unweighted.
findings.evidence: Computed from docs/research/concert-effect-panel.csv: show-week total streams have mean 76.5 M and median 56.5 M; US 519.7 M. Raw jump (show week minus weeks −4..−1) times each country's chart size sums to 0.35 M, versus the mean jump times the summed charts at 1.28 M.
findings.fix: Use the median chart for the per-country figure and drop the 24-country total, or label it as an upper bound that assumes the same share effect in every market. State that the estimate is an average over countries, not over streams.
findings.note: Reproduced from panel.csv. Show-week total_streams: mean 76.5 M, median 56.5 M, US 519.7 M. The raw jumps weighted by chart size sum to 0.35 M, against 1.28 M for the unweighted mean times the summed charts. The article's 1.5 M is att × mean chart × 24, which assumes a homogeneous share effect while the large markets had negative raw jumps. Raw jumps are not effects, but the homogeneity assumption behind the total is unstated.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:112 "Leaving out each visited country in turn keeps the summary between 0.020 (without Australia) and 0.042 points ... No single country carries the result." and :51 tldr "Leaving out any one country does not change the sign"
findings.problem: Leave-one-out was run only on the five-week summary, whose interval already includes zero. It was not run on the week-0 coefficient the headline rests on. Dropping Australia alone cuts the summary by 41 %, which is not 'no single country carries the result'. The descriptive section shows the jump comes mostly from the Nov–Dec 2017 cohorts and later small markets (NZ, Australia, Belgium, Singapore), while the first and largest markets (US, Canada, UK, France, Sweden) fell and five countries show zero. Neither the summary nor the deck mentions this concentration, and an unchanged sign is weak evidence of robustness for an estimate whose interval crosses zero.
findings.evidence: results.json leave_one_out: Australia 0.000202 against the full 0.000344. Raw week-0 jumps computed from panel.csv: NZ +0.314, AU +0.312, BE +0.210, SG +0.194; CA −0.126, SE −0.097, UK −0.066, US −0.041, FR −0.030; 5 countries at 0.
findings.fix: Replace 'No single country carries the result' with 'the summary keeps its sign without any one country, but falls by about 40 % without Australia; leave-one-out was not run for the show-week estimate'. In the tldr, add that the jump came mainly from the later, smaller markets and that the earliest, largest markets show none.
findings.note: estimate.py runs LOO only on fit(...)['summary'], never on the week-0 coefficient. LOO without Australia is 0.000202 vs 0.000344, a 41 % drop, which conflicts with 'No single country carries the result'. The concentration in later, smaller markets does appear in the article's descriptive section ('Where the jump was largest'), so it is disclosed in the body, but not in the tldr or the deck.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:112 "The placebo ... gives −0.180 points with a wide interval (−0.423 to 0.063) that includes zero: it finds no false effect"
findings.problem: The placebo point estimate is about twice the size of the week-0 peak and five times the summary, and its interval is roughly six times as wide as the main one. Saying it 'finds no false effect' credits the design with a pass it did not earn. The test has no power to detect a false effect of the size being claimed.
findings.evidence: results.json placebo_26w: att −0.00180, lo −0.00423, hi 0.00063. Main summary 0.00034, week 0 0.00083.
findings.fix: "The placebo ... gives −0.180 points (−0.423 to 0.063). Its interval includes zero, but it is too imprecise to rule out a false effect larger than the one reported, so it does not test the design."
findings.note: Placebo −0.00180 (−0.00423 to 0.00063): the CI width of 0.485 pp is about 6× the main summary's 0.077 pp, and the point estimate is larger in magnitude than his entire pre-show share (0.112 %). The text already calls it 'a weak test', but gives a different reason (shows pushed out of the window). 'It finds no false effect' still overstates it. Partly addressed, so lower severity.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:79 "returned to Europe in March and April 2018 for the countries it had skipped"
findings.problem: This is factually wrong, and it hides that many treated countries were visited twice. The 2018 legs went back to the UK, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Italy, Australia, Singapore, Japan, the US and Canada. The design treats only the first show and treats it as absorbing, so later visits are ignored. That was a registered choice, but readers are not told. The second visits fall outside the ±12-week window for those countries, which should be said, along with the fact that the estimate is a first-visit effect only.
findings.evidence: docs/research/concert-effect-shows.csv: UK 2017-10-29 and 2018-04-07; France 2017-10-25 and 2018-03-13; Germany 2017-10-27 and 2018-03-24; Australia 2017-11-26 and 2018-04-21; Singapore 2017-11-23 and 2018-05-03; Japan 2017-12-07 and 2018-05-10; US/Canada June–July 2018.
findings.fix: "...returned to Europe in March and April 2018, playing again in several countries and for the first time in Switzerland, Belgium, Denmark, Norway, Spain and Ireland, and then went back to Australia and Asia... Only the first show in each country is used; later visits fell more than twelve weeks after it."
findings.note: shows.csv has 2018 repeat visits to France 03-13, Netherlands 03-14, Sweden 03-18, Germany 03-24, Italy 04-02, UK 04-07, Australia 04-21, Singapore 05-03, Japan 05-10, and US/Canada in June–July. 'For the countries it had skipped' is therefore factually wrong. I checked that every second visit falls more than 12 weeks after the first (about 18–23 weeks), so the estimates are not contaminated. The article does say treatment starts at the first show, but it does not mention the repeat visits.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:72 "A tour that reaches countries at different dates is close to a natural experiment ... Recent methods for such staggered timing make the comparison clean."
findings.problem: This causal framing is stronger than the design supports. The tour order was not random: the article itself says at line 128 that promoters chose large and nearby markets first. The estimator also cannot make the comparison 'clean': it removes forbidden comparisons but still depends on parallel trends. Line 113 reports a pre-trend band that excludes zero.
findings.evidence: Line 128 says countries were not visited at random. results.json y1_share event e=−10 band 0.0029–0.0505 pp.
findings.fix: "A tour that reaches countries at different dates allows a comparison with countries not yet visited; it is not a random experiment, because the order of the tour was chosen. Recent methods for staggered timing avoid the comparisons that make a simple regression misleading."
findings.note: Line 72 says 'close to a natural experiment' and 'make the comparison clean'. Line 128 concedes that 'Countries were not visited at random: promoters chose large and nearby markets first', and the week −10 band excludes zero. The estimator avoids forbidden comparisons but still relies on parallel trends, so 'clean' overstates what it does.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:45-52 details.tldr
findings.problem: The short version gives the result but not what it rests on: a comparison with countries not yet or never visited, which assumes they would have trended alike. It does not say what would overturn it, such as a pre-show trend, coverage limited to the Top 200, or a single tour. It gives no numbers, and it presents 'back where it had been' as a finding when the bands from week +1 on include zero. The limited power is missing: the five-week interval spans about ±34 % of his pre-show share. So is the pre-trend violation at week −10.
findings.evidence: Lines 48–51 contain no number and no assumption. The power statement (±34 %) appears only at line 114, the pre-trend at line 113.
findings.fix: Add one bullet: "It rests on comparing visited countries with ones not yet visited, assuming both would otherwise have moved alike; one pre-show week breaks that pattern, and the five-week estimate could not rule out effects up to about a third of his share either way." Add the numbers: "+0.08 pp in the show week (band 0.03 to 0.14); registered five-week average +0.03 pp, inconclusive."
findings.note: Partly a misreading: tldr bullet 4 does mention 'only the Top 200 is seen, and the study covers one tour'. The rest holds: the tldr has no numbers, no identifying assumption, no power statement (±34 % is only at line 114) and no pre-trend failure, and it states 'back where it had been' although the bands from +1 include zero.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:7, 37, 39, 72, 89, 90, 96
findings.problem: Several technical terms appear without explanation at first use: 'difference-in-differences' (lines 7 and 37; never explained in plain words); 'pp' / 'percentage points' against '%' of share (line 39; readers can easily confuse +0.083 pp with +0.083 %); 'uniform band' (line 39; explained only at line 89); 'staggered' timing (line 72); 'natural experiment' (line 72); 'bootstrap' (line 89); 'placebo' (line 90); 'pre-period mean' (line 96, a raw template string); 'event window' (line 90, never defined).
findings.evidence: First occurrences found by reading the HTML top to bottom.
findings.fix: Add a one-clause gloss at first use, e.g. 'difference-in-differences (comparing the change in visited countries with the change in countries not yet visited)'. 'percentage points (0.083 pp on a share of 0.112 %, i.e. from about 0.11 % to about 0.19 %)'. Replace 'pre-period mean' with 'his share before the show'.
findings.note: Only partly valid. Several terms are glossed in place: natural experiment and staggered (line 72, same sentence), the DiD comparison (line 89), uniform bands (line 89), and placebo (line 90, 'moves every first show 26 weeks earlier'). Still unexplained: 'pre-period mean' (line 96, a raw code string), 'event window' (line 90), and the pp vs % ambiguity in the facts box (line 39) before 'percentage points' first appears at line 95.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:89 "Inference uses a bootstrap that resamples countries"
findings.problem: The code and design use the csdid multiplier bootstrap clustered by country. It reweights influence functions and does not resample countries.
findings.evidence: design §4: 'multiplier bootstrap clustered by country (999 draws)'. estimate.py: ATTgt(..., cband=True, biters=999, clustervar='id').
findings.fix: "Inference uses a multiplier bootstrap clustered by country (999 draws)..."
findings.note: Duplicate of #4. Design §4 and the code use a multiplier bootstrap clustered by country, not resampling of countries.

findings.location: texts/concert-effect.html:41 "0.112 % ... administrative count" and :96 "inconclusive: interval includes zero but is wider than ±10 % of the pre-period mean" and :113 "1 has a band ... week -10"
findings.problem: Line 41 labels a computed mean share an 'administrative count'. Line 96 pastes the code's 'why' string into the prose and repeats the sentence before it. Line 113 starts a sentence with the digit '1' and writes 'week -10' with a hyphen, while the rest of the page uses '−'.
findings.evidence: article.py fills the string from results.json y1_share.why.
findings.fix: Line 41: drop 'administrative count' (it is an estimate from the panel). Line 96: delete the pasted clause. Line 113: 'one has a band ... week −10'.
findings.note: The line 41 part follows site convention (see #8). Lines 96 and 113 are real problems. Line 96 pastes y1.why ('interval includes zero but is wider than ±10 % of the pre-period mean') right after a sentence saying the same thing. Line 113 starts the clause with the digit '1' and uses ASCII 'week -10' (article.py:157).

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:115 (fig. 2 caption) "Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood, n = 164 640 cells"; also :79 "The unit of analysis is a region on a date in a clock hour ... 164 640 cells in all"
findings.problem: 164 640 is the whole cells file: 14 regions × 10 years × 49 days (−28…+21) × 24 hours. No model in fig. 2 is fitted on it. The registered estimate uses n = 35 280 (±14 days, the 9 evening, morning and control hours), and the other rows use 34 020, 17 262, 52 920 and 28 224. At line 79 the number comes straight after the two-week windows are described, so a reader takes it as the size of the analysed sample.
findings.evidence: docs/research/dst-darkness-results.json primary.pe.n = 35280, placebo 34020, window_7 17262, window_21 52920, no_2020_2021 28224. tools/dst/prepare.py: DAYS = range(-28,22) minus 0, HOURS = 24. The design change note says 164 640 = 14 × 10 × 49 × 24. tools/dst/article.py sets n_cells = len(cells).
findings.fix: Fig. 2 caption: "n = 35 280 region-date-hour cells for the registered estimate (the 9 hours of the three groups, ±14 days)". Line 79: "... with zero where no crash was recorded; the registered model uses 35 280 such cells (the published file, 164 640 cells, also covers the wider windows used by the checks)".
findings.note: cells.parquet has 164 640 rows. results.json primary n = 35 280, and recounting the 9 hours at ±14 days in the cells gives 35 280. Line 79 puts 164 640 straight after the window description, and the fig. 2 caption gives it as n.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:98 "the morning gains about as much light as the evening loses, yet the evening effect is much the larger"
findings.problem: The article's own darkness shares contradict this. The evening goes from 17 % to 64 % dark across 3 hours, about +85 minutes of darkness. The morning goes from 47 % to 16 % across 2 hours, about −37 minutes. The evening loses more than twice as much light as the morning gains. The asymmetry argument that follows (busier evening rush, tired drivers) rests on the wrong premise.
findings.evidence: results.json sun_dark_share: evening_pre 0.171, evening_post 0.644 → 0.473 × 180 min = 85 min; morning_pre 0.469, morning_post 0.163 → 0.306 × 120 min = 37 min.
findings.fix: "The morning gains less light than the evening loses, about 37 minutes against 85 across the hour groups, and the evening effect is larger too; per minute of light the two are not directly comparable ...", or drop the asymmetry argument.
findings.note: sun_dark_share: evening 0.171→0.644 over 3 h is about 85 min of extra darkness. Morning 0.469→0.163 over 2 h is about 37 min of extra light. So 'about as much light' is false. Duplicates [11].

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:79 "In those windows the police recorded 2 768 crashes with a pedestrian ... For 0.4 % of them the hour is unknown"; facts box :42 "pedestrian crashes in the windows 2 768"
findings.problem: 2 768 counts only the pedestrian crashes with a known hour. The police recorded 2 780 in the windows, and 12 of them (0.4 %) have an unknown hour. Saying "0.4 % of them" about the 2 768 is internally inconsistent, because those 12 are already excluded.
findings.evidence: results.json missing_hour.ped: records 2780, unknown_hour 12, share 0.0043. article.py: n_ped = w.ped.sum() from cells, which contain only records with a valid hour; 2780 − 12 = 2768.
findings.fix: "In those windows the police recorded 2 780 crashes with a pedestrian, about 9.9 a day; for 12 of them (0.4 %) the hour is unknown, leaving 2 768 for the analysis." Label the facts box "with a known hour".
findings.note: Summing ped over the ±14 cells gives 2 768. missing_hour.ped is records 2780, unknown 12. So '0.4 % of them' refers to records that are already outside the 2 768.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:136 "All three are dated in the design file ... None changes the rule for reading the result." (Changes after registration)
findings.problem: Two registered outputs are changed or dropped without being listed as deviations. (a) Design §6 registers an event study (evening-minus-control by day, −14 to +14, with 95 % bands, "all reported"), and §8 promises an event-study figure. estimate.py computes it, but the article never reports or shows it. (b) §8 and the unit-change note say "The district-level map of §8 stays", but fig. 3 is a region-level map.
findings.evidence: docs/research/dst-darkness-design.md:94-95 (event study), :111-113 (outputs: event-study figure, district map), :170 ("district-level map ... stays"). results.json has an event_study block. The article contains no event-study text or figure, and fig. 3 shows 14 regions (tools/dst/article.py rush_minutes iterates over REGION).
findings.fix: Report the event study (a figure or a sentence with its result, noting its wide per-day intervals) or list its omission as a fourth deviation. Add the switch from a district map to a region map to the changes list.
findings.note: (a) design §6 and §8 register an event study and an event-study figure. estimate.py computes it, but the article has no event-study text or figure. (b) The design note says 'district-level map of §8 stays', yet fig. 3 is by region and the Changes list (3 items) does not mention it.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:111 "Its interval is so wide that it could hold no effect or a doubling"
findings.problem: The group-trend interval is 0.65 to 1.80, so it does not include a doubling (2.0).
findings.evidence: results.json group_trends.pe: lo 0.649, hi 1.799.
findings.fix: "... that it could hold no effect or an 80 % rise" (or "anything from a 35 % fall to an 80 % rise").
findings.note: group_trends.pe hi = 1.799, so the interval does not reach 2.0.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:98 "Mornings have fewer pedestrian crashes to begin with, and a smaller sample gives a wider interval."
findings.problem: Before the change, mornings have about as many pedestrian crashes as evenings: 1.78 a day in the two morning hours against 1.90 in the three evening hours. Per hour the morning has more (0.89 against 0.63). The wider morning interval comes from the post-change drop and from having two hours instead of three, not from a lower baseline.
findings.evidence: assets/dst/charts.json hours table, before per day: h6 0.75 + h7 1.029 = 1.78; h16 0.70 + h17 0.443 + h18 0.757 = 1.90. After: morning 1.21, evening 2.93.
findings.fix: "The morning group has two hours rather than three and, after the change, fewer crashes, so its interval is wider."
findings.note: Before the change, recounted from cells: morning 105+144 = 249 against evening 266, so the baselines are nearly equal. The morning's smaller total comes from the post drop (169) and from having 2 hours, not from a lower baseline.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:50 (TL;DR) "The hour from 17:00 to 18:00 ... carries most of it: from 1.90 to 2.93 such crashes a day in the three evening hours together."
findings.problem: The numbers attached to the claim about the single hour 17:00–18:00 are the totals for all three evening hours, so the sentence does not show what it asserts. The hour itself went from 0.44 to 1.34 a day, which is +0.89 of the +1.03 rise.
findings.evidence: charts.json hours table: h17 before 0.443, after 1.336; sum of h16–18 is 1.90 → 2.93.
findings.fix: "The hour from 17:00 to 18:00 ... carries most of it: from 0.44 to 1.34 such crashes a day, out of a rise from 1.90 to 2.93 across the three evening hours."
findings.note: charts.json: h17 goes 0.443→1.336 per day. The 1.90→2.93 quoted in the bullet is the sum of h16–18, so it does not support the 17:00 claim.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:105 "Czechia spans about five degrees of longitude, so dusk in Moravia-Silesia comes about twenty minutes before dusk in Karlovy Vary"
findings.problem: Czechia spans about 6.8° of longitude (12.1° to 18.9° E). It is the region centroids that span 5.2°, and that span is what produces the roughly 20-minute difference.
findings.evidence: docs/research/dst-darkness-data.json centroids: CZ-KA lon 12.74, CZ-MO lon 17.95 (5.2°). The design correction note (2 Oct) states "5.2° ... (12.74°–17.95° E)" for the centroids.
findings.fix: "The regions' centres span about five degrees of longitude, so ..."
findings.note: Centroids run from CZ-KA 12.74 to CZ-MO 17.95 E (5.2°), matching the design correction note. The country itself spans about 12.1–18.9 E (~6.8°), so 'Czechia spans about five degrees' is off. Low impact.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:73 "In Prague, sunset moves from about 17:45 to about 16:45 overnight."
findings.problem: This disagrees with the repo's own computation and with the design. sun.py gives Prague sunset 17:52 CEST on 25 Oct 2025 and 16:50 CET on 26 Oct 2025, and the design check note says 16:50 CET. The design text (§1) says 17:40 → 16:40. Three different values appear for the same quantity.
findings.evidence: Recomputed with tools/dst/sun.py altitude() at the CZ-PR centroid, altitude < −0.833°: 2025-10-25 17:52, 2025-10-26 16:50. design.md:22 "17:40 to about 16:40"; design.md:173 "sunset 16:50 CET".
findings.fix: "In Prague, sunset moves from about 17:50 to about 16:50 overnight."
findings.note: Running sun.py altitude at the CZ-PR centroid, with sunset at -0.833°, gives 17:52 CEST on 25 Oct 2025 and 16:50 CET on 26 Oct. The article says 17:45 → 16:45 and design §1 says 17:40 → 16:40. Minor, but the three values are inconsistent.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:91 "standard errors are clustered by date, so that a bad-weather day counts as one piece of evidence, not as many<sup>6</sup>"
findings.problem: Reference 6 is the pyfixest software. The superscript sits on the methodological justification for clustering, which the software does not support. The rest of the paragraph describes pyfixest only implicitly.
findings.evidence: texts/dst-darkness.html:159 r6 = "Fischer, A., and contributors. pyfixest ... version 0.60.0".
findings.fix: Move the citation to name the tool: "... estimated with pyfixest<sup>6</sup>; standard errors are clustered by date, so that ...".
findings.note: r6 is the pyfixest software, which is never named in the body text, yet the superscript sits on the justification for clustering by date. Low.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:108-120 (Checks section; no event study anywhere in the article)
findings.problem: The registered event study (design §6, plus an event-study figure promised in §8) was estimated but is not reported or mentioned anywhere, and it is not listed as a deviation. What it shows bears on the headline: before the change the evening/control day ratios are mostly below 1 (days −13 to −9: 0.49–0.63). After the change they are mostly 1.0–1.6, apart from single-day spikes at day +6 (5.45, CI 1.45–20.49) and day +14 (3.79). The morning series is degenerate (mo_m7 = 0 with a 0–0 interval; every other morning day sits at 1.7–6.7 against the day −1 reference). Leaving out a registered check that is noisy and partly odd-looking, without saying so, is selective reporting.
findings.evidence: design.md:93-94 (event study registered), design.md:111-112 (event-study figure promised); tools/dst/estimate.py:83-92 estimates it; docs/research/dst-darkness-results.json event_study keys ev_m14…ev_p14, mo_m14…mo_p14; grep of texts/dst-darkness.html finds no 'event' text.
findings.fix: Add the event-study figure, or at least a paragraph in Checks: 'The registered day-by-day event study is too noisy to read day by day (single-day intervals span roughly 0.2 to 5). Before the change the evening ratios sit mostly below 1, and after it mostly above 1, with one outlying day (+6). The morning series is degenerate because of a zero reference cell.' If it is left out, list the omission under Changes after registration.
findings.note: Reproduced from results.json: ev_m13..m9 = 0.49–0.63, ev_p6 = 5.45 (1.45–20.49), ev_p14 = 3.79, mo_m7 = 0 (0–0). Most other morning days are 1.7–6.7 (exceptions p7 1.0, p13 0.36). The article does not mention the event study, and the omission is not listed as a deviation. Same core issue as [3a].

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:98 "the morning gains about as much light as the evening loses, yet the evening effect is much the larger"
findings.problem: The article's own darkness measure contradicts this premise. The evening group (3 hours) goes from 17 % to 64 % dark, about +1.42 dark hours a day. The morning group (2 hours) goes from 47 % to 16 %, about −0.62. So the evening loses more than twice as much light as the morning gains, and part of the 'informative asymmetry' is mechanical. The behavioural explanations offered (busier evening rush, tired drivers) rest on a false comparison.
findings.evidence: results.json sun_dark_share: evening_pre 0.171, evening_post 0.644; morning_pre 0.469, morning_post 0.163. Article line 80 reports the same shares. (0.644−0.171)×3 = 1.42 h; (0.469−0.163)×2 = 0.61 h.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'The evening loses more light than the morning gains: about 1.4 of its 3 hours turn dark, against 0.6 of the morning's 2 hours turning light. So a larger evening effect is expected even before any difference in who is on the road.' Drop or soften the busier-rush and tired-driver reading.
findings.note: Same as [1]: (0.644−0.171)×3 = 1.42 h against (0.469−0.163)×2 = 0.61 h. The asymmetry argument at line 98 rests on a false equality.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:111 "It does not confirm the effect; it does not contradict it either. Its interval is so wide ... which is what the power calculation predicted"
findings.problem: This is the originally registered primary model, and its result is framed only as a matter of precision. But its point estimate falls from 1.75 to 1.08 once the evening and morning get their own trends, which is consistent with much of the jump being absorbed by the group-specific darkening trend. The deck (line 37), the meta description and the facts box say 'supported' and never mention that the originally registered model gives about 1.08.
findings.evidence: results.json group_trends.pe: ratio 1.080, CI 0.649–1.799, against primary 1.751. Design §3 (lines 56-61) was the original primary; the change note (lines 147-150) demoted it. Deck line 37: 'The registered hypothesis is supported.'
findings.fix: In Checks add: 'Its point estimate, 1.08, is also much lower than 1.75, so the trend terms absorb most of the jump, not just widen the interval.' In the deck add: 'under the amended plan; the originally registered model, with separate evening trends, is inconclusive (1.08, 0.65 to 1.80).'
findings.note: Partly addressed: line 111 reports 1.08 and tells a strict reader to treat the study as inconclusive, and the TL;DR mentions a 'stricter specification'. But the text frames the result only as imprecision, and the deck and facts box say 'supported' without saying that the originally registered model's point estimate is ~1.08. Confirmed as a framing issue.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:97 "about 176 of the 410 would not have happened in the light"
findings.problem: The counterfactual is misstated. The ratio compares after the change with before it, and the pre-change evening was already 17 % dark, while after the change it is 64 % dark, not fully dark. The estimate also includes about 25 minutes of natural darkening, and the text admits it cannot be separated. So 176 is crashes 'attributable to the clock change plus two weeks of seasonal darkening, relative to midday', not crashes that 'would not have happened in the light'. The phrase 'If the ratio is right' does not repair the wording.
findings.evidence: 410 − 410/1.751 = 175.9; sun_dark_share evening_pre 0.171, evening_post 0.644; article line 92 says the main estimate includes natural darkening.
findings.fix: 'If the ratio is right, about 176 of the 410 are the excess over what the pre-change evening would predict, around 18 a year. That excess includes the steady seasonal darkening as well as the clock hour.'
findings.note: 410 − 410/1.751 = 175.9. The pre-change evening was already 17 % dark and the post-change evening is 64 % dark, and the estimate includes natural darkening (line 92). 'Would not have happened in the light' overstates the counterfactual, even with the back-of-envelope caveat.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:103 "The clock change moves darkness and nothing else, so it can serve as an instrument"; line 104 "so the shortening days enter as darkness too, not as a nuisance"
findings.problem: Two overstatements. (1) The exclusion restriction is asserted as fact. The article itself cites Smith's sleep effect (line 73) and floats tired drivers (line 98), and the autumn change also shifts sleep and circadian timing. (2) The 2SLS model is identified only by the post × hour instruments, the same contrast as the primary model. It rescales the same before/after jump by the change in dark share and does not separate the jump from the drift. Its agreement with the main estimate is therefore not independent corroboration, as lines 104 and 125 imply. The change note's claim that H3 'separates the jump from the drift' (design.md:155) is carried into the text.
findings.evidence: tools/dst/estimate.py:94-99: instruments z6, z7, z16, z17, z18 = post × (hour == h); the controls are post + tt plus fixed effects. The confound from natural darkening sits inside post × hour, exactly as in the primary.
findings.fix: Line 103: 'The model assumes the clock change affects crashes only through darkness, which a change in sleep would violate.' Line 104: 'Because it uses the same before/after contrast, it is a rescaling of the main estimate per hour of darkness, not an independent test.'
findings.note: estimate.py: the instruments are z_h = post×(hour==h) and the controls are post + tt + FE, the same contrast as the primary. Line 103 asserts 'moves darkness and nothing else' as fact, although line 73 cites a sleep effect. Line 104 says the shortening days enter 'as darkness too', but natural darkening is inside the post×hour instrument variation, so the agreement with the main estimate is not independent.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:81 and :50 (TL;DR) "the hour from 17:00 to 18:00 is quieter than the hours around it ... After the change, that hour becomes the worst"
findings.problem: Almost all of the raw evening increase comes from one hour, 17:00 (62 → 187). Hour 16 goes 98 → 118 and hour 18 goes 106 → 105. The 17:00 baseline is anomalously low against its neighbours, so part of the measured jump may be a return from an unexplained pre-change dip. The text reports the dip as shape, not as a threat. The increase is also uneven by year: 2017 (39 → 82) and 2023 (20 → 52) contribute 75 of the +144, while 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2024 are nearly flat. No leave-one-year-out check is reported, and the summary does not say the result is concentrated in a few autumns.
findings.evidence: Tabulated from assets/dst/cells.parquet, days −14…14 without 0. Pedestrian crashes by hour, pre/post: 16h 98/118, 17h 62/187, 18h 106/105. Evening group by year, pre/post: 2016 35/49, 2017 39/82, 2018 33/33, 2019 28/33, 2020 13/15, 2021 25/36, 2022 22/36, 2023 20/52, 2024 29/32, 2025 22/42.
findings.fix: Add near the main finding: 'The pre-change 17:00 hour is unusually quiet (62 crashes against about 100 in the hours either side), so part of the jump may be a return to normal. The rise is also uneven across years: 2017 and 2023 contribute about half of it.' Report a leave-one-year-out range.
findings.note: Recounted from cells (±14, without day 0): 16h 98/118, 17h 62/187, 18h 106/105. Evening by year: 2017 39→82 and 2023 20→52 give 75 of the +144. No leave-one-year-out check is reported. The idea that the 17:00 dip is a regression-to-mean threat is interpretation, but the facts reproduce.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:110 "The placebo ratio is 0.92 (0.71 to 1.18): no effect"; :51 "A fake change two weeks earlier finds nothing"
findings.problem: An interval that includes 1 is described as a finding of no effect. By the article's own registered rule the placebo would be 'inconclusive', not 'not supported' (it is not within 0.90–1.10). Its upper bound of 1.18 means natural darkening could still account for a non-trivial share of the 1.75. The window checks point the same way: 1.55 at ±7 days, 1.75 at ±14 and 1.85 at ±21, a rise with window length that a trend contribution would produce. The text calls this 'little' movement.
findings.evidence: results.json placebo_day_-14.pe 0.917 (0.711–1.183); window_7 1.545, primary 1.751, window_21 1.851. Label rule: estimate.py:49-54.
findings.fix: 'The placebo ratio is 0.92 (0.71 to 1.18). It rules out natural darkening alone producing a jump as large as 1.75, but not a contribution of up to about 18 %. The estimate also grows with the window (1.55, 1.75, 1.85), as a trend would make it.'
findings.note: placebo pe 0.917 (0.711–1.183) is not within 0.90–1.10, so under the registered rule it would be 'inconclusive', not 'no effect'. The windows go 1.55/1.75/1.85, as the finding says. The rule formally governs H1, but the 'no effect' / 'finds nothing' wording still overstates.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:125 "An hour of darkness roughly doubles the expected number of pedestrian crashes in that hour"; facts box line 41
findings.problem: The conclusions section and the facts box state the H3 extension as measured fact. The design labels H3 an extension that 'does not change' the headline. It rests on a linear model that extrapolates from a roughly 0.47 shift in dark share to full darkness, it pools morning and evening hours while comparing against the evening mean only, and the percentage ignores uncertainty in that baseline mean.
findings.evidence: design.md:30-31, 74 (H3 an extension; the headline is H1); estimate.py:96-108 (pooled instruments for hours 6, 7, 16-18; pct = b / pre-evening mean); results.json H3: b 0.0536, base 0.0452.
findings.fix: Line 125: 'A secondary, linear model that scales the same jump by the change in darkness suggests an hour of full darkness roughly doubles the rate, an extrapolation from about half an hour of change per hour.'
findings.note: Line 125 sits under 'Measured:' and states the H3 doubling as fact. estimate.py pools instruments for hours 6, 7 and 16–18 and divides b by the pre-change evening mean (0.0452) only. Design calls H3 an extension. Fair as a framing point.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:119 fig. 3 caption "at each region's centroid"; :105
findings.problem: Undisclosed deviation. The change note of 2 October says 'The district-level map of §8 stays, computed from astronomy only', but the published map is region-level, and the Changes section does not mention this.
findings.evidence: design.md:170-171 vs article line 118-119 (fourteen regions, region centroid).
findings.fix: Either publish the district map or add to Changes: '(4) The map is drawn by region, not by district as the change note said.'
findings.note: design.md change note: 'The district-level map of §8 stays'. The fig. 3 caption is region centroids, and Changes lists only 3 items. Duplicates [3b].

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:112 "Darkness is harder on drivers too, but it is hardest on the people they cannot see."
findings.problem: The comparison of 1.28 with 1.75 is read as a mechanism (drivers cannot see pedestrians), which was not tested. The two outcomes also differ sharply in missing hours (13 % against 0.4 %, 'mostly minor damage reported later'), which may bias the non-pedestrian ratio.
findings.evidence: results.json other_crash_kinds.pe 1.284; missing_hour.other.share 0.135 vs ped 0.004; article line 79.
findings.fix: 'Crashes without a pedestrian also rise, by less (1.28). For them 13 % of the hours are unknown, so the comparison is rough.'
findings.note: Line 112 reads a mechanism ('people they cannot see') into 1.28 vs 1.75, which was not tested. missing_hour.other share 0.135 vs ped 0.004, as the finding says.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:126 "The first two weeks of November are when the evening risk jumps ... this suggests timing them to the week of the change"
findings.problem: The design measures a level change relative to midday across the change. It does not show the excess fades after two weeks, so presenting the window as the period of risk implies a transient the data do not test. The window also starts in late October, not in November.
findings.evidence: The window is days +1 to +14 after the last Sunday of October (design.md:39-41); no data after day +21 are analysed.
findings.fix: 'The evening risk jumps on the night of the change, a date known in advance, and the study cannot say whether it fades afterwards. Campaigns could start that week rather than be spread over the autumn.'
findings.note: The window runs days +1..+14 from the last Sunday of October (Oct 25–31), so it starts in late October, not 'the first two weeks of November'. The design estimates a level shift and does not test whether the excess fades after two weeks. Low.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:45-53 (details.tldr)
findings.problem: The short version gives the result but not the two main things it rests on: the model was changed from the registered one after a power calculation, and the estimate includes about 25 minutes of natural darkening. It also says nothing about what would overturn it. Bullet 3 attributes the rise to the 17:00 hour, then quotes numbers for all three evening hours (1.90 to 2.93), which do not support the 17:00 claim. The most practical sentence, on timing campaigns to the change (line 126), is missing from the box.
findings.evidence: Lines 48-51; cells give 17h 62 → 187 of a total evening 266 → 410.
findings.fix: Bullet 3: 'The hour from 17:00 to 18:00 carries most of it: 62 crashes before against 187 after across the ten autumns.' Add a bullet: 'This rests on a model simplified before the data were opened. The original specification gives 1.08 (0.65 to 1.80), so a large effect of natural darkening, or a day-trend difference between evening and midday, would overturn it.' Add a bullet: 'Practical upshot: road-safety campaigns could be timed to the week of the change.'
findings.note: Bullet 3 problem confirmed (same as [6]). The rest is partly addressed: bullet 4 mentions the stricter specification and the placebo, though not the post-registration model change or the ~25 min of natural darkening. Whether the box must carry these is an editorial judgment.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:91 "difference in differences", "Poisson regression ... pseudo-maximum likelihood", "standard errors are clustered by date"
findings.problem: Central technical terms are given in one dense paragraph with no worked example. 'Pseudo-maximum likelihood' and 'consistent ... as long as the mean is right' are not explained. A two-by-two example using the article's own counts (evening 266 → 410, midday 317 → 279) would make the ratio of 1.75 concrete before the model is introduced.
findings.fix: Before the model, add: 'In the raw counts, evening crashes rose from 266 to 410 (×1.54) while midday crashes fell from 317 to 279 (×0.88); the ratio of the two, 1.75, is the difference in differences. The model adds region, weekday and trend adjustments.'
findings.note: Numbers check: control 317→279 and evening 266→410 give a raw DiD of 1.751. But line 91 already explains DiD in plain words ('change in evening ... relative to the change in midday'). Only 'pseudo-maximum likelihood' is left unexplained. This is a style suggestion, not a defect.

findings.location: texts/dst-darkness.html:39 "95 % CI"; :103 "instrument", "fixed effects", "region-hour"; :51 "specification"; :42 "administrative count"
findings.problem: Several terms appear without explanation at first use. 'CI' is never spelled out (first use line 39). 'Fixed effects' (line 103) is never defined, although line 91 describes 'a separate level' without naming it. 'Instrument' (line 103) is described only loosely. 'Specification' (line 51) and 'administrative count' (line 42) are jargon in the reader-facing box.
findings.evidence: grep: 'CI' first at line 39 with no expansion; 'fixed effects' only at line 103.
findings.fix: Spell out 'confidence interval' at line 39 or 49. At line 91 name the levels: '(fixed effects)'. At line 103: 'an instrument, a source of change in darkness unrelated to anything else that affects crashes'. At line 51, replace 'specification' with 'version of the model'.
findings.note: grep: 'confidence interval' never appears, and 'CI' is used from the facts box on. 'fixed effects' appears only once (line 103), as 'the same fixed effects', never defined. 'specification' and 'administrative count' appear in reader-facing boxes.

findings.location: texts/eurovision.html:138 "Two countries sitting together in the European Union does not change what they give each other at all." (also deck l.40 / meta description l.7 "joining the EU earns a country no points at all")
findings.problem: The conclusion overstates a null. The registered H3 estimate is a statistically clear decline, not zero, and its label is inconclusive. Even the check that drops the 2004 cohort fails the registered 'not supported' margin.
findings.evidence: docs/research/eurovision-results.json H3: b=-0.00907, lo=-0.01354, hi=-0.00460, label 'inconclusive'. Design §5 says 'not supported' only if the CI lies within ±10% of the pre mean (±0.45 pp). The main CI of -1.35 to -0.46 pp and the without-2004 CI of -0.82 to +0.18 pp both fall outside that band.
findings.fix: E.g. 'Two countries sitting together in the EU do not give each other more points; the registered estimate is a small fall, driven mostly by the 2004 enlargement, and inconclusive by the registered rule.' Make the deck and description match: 'earns a country no extra points'.
findings.note: results.json H3 b=-0.00907 (lo -0.01354, hi -0.00460), label inconclusive; pre_mean 0.0452 so the ±10% band is ±0.45 pp. Neither the main CI nor the without-2004 CI (-0.82 to 0.18) falls inside it. l.138 says 'does not change ... at all', l.40 says 'earns a country no points', and the meta line says 'no points at all'. These overstate the result.

findings.location: texts/eurovision.html:128 "almost all of the fall comes from the 2004 enlargement ... Leaving the 2004 cohort out, the estimate is −0.32 points (−0.82 to 0.18): nothing."
findings.problem: Dropping the 2004 cohort cuts the estimate from −0.91 to −0.32 pp. That removes about 65% of the fall, which is not 'almost all'. 'Nothing' is also stronger than the registered rule allows: the CI spans −0.82 to +0.18 pp, wider than the ±0.45 pp equivalence band, so by the study's own rule it is inconclusive. Separately, 'points' should read 'percentage points'.
findings.evidence: results.json H3_checks.without_2004_cohort b=-0.00318, lo=-0.00818, hi=0.00183. H3 pre_mean=0.0452, so the ±10% band is ±0.45 pp. Ratio: 0.32/0.91 = 35% of the fall remains.
findings.fix: 'about two thirds of the fall comes from the 2004 enlargement ... Leaving the 2004 cohort out, the estimate is −0.32 percentage points (−0.82 to 0.18), indistinguishable from zero but too imprecise to rule out a small effect.'
findings.note: Without 2004: b=-0.00318 against -0.00907, so about 35% of the fall remains and 'almost all' is too strong (about two thirds). The CI of -0.82 to +0.18 exceeds the ±0.45 band, so 'nothing' contradicts the registered rule. The check also runs on a different sample (n 35071 vs 40412, stricter usable() filter). Saying 'points' for pp is minor because the previous sentence uses 'percentage points'.

findings.location: texts/eurovision.html:43 facts box "×0.98 ... 95 % CI 0.81 to 1.18 · no difference"; l.108 "a shared language's 0.91 (0.68 to 1.20): no difference"
findings.problem: The page labels the contiguity and language ratios 'no difference', but by the page's own H1 equivalence margin (0.90–1.10) neither interval establishes that. These ratios can't rule out televote-vs-jury differences of roughly ±20%. 'No difference' is also not one of the registered labels and reads like one in the facts box.
findings.evidence: results.json with_contiguity_language ct: exp(-0.2066)=0.81, exp(0.1645)=1.18. lt: exp(-0.383)=0.68, exp(0.1846)=1.20. Design §3 rule: 'not supported' only if the ratio's CI lies within 0.90–1.10.
findings.fix: Use 'no clear difference' or 'not distinguishable from 1', and in the facts box add 'check, not registered'.
findings.note: exp(ct lo/hi) gives 0.81 to 1.18 and exp(lt) gives 0.68 to 1.20. Both are wider than the 0.90 to 1.10 margin the page itself states at l.101, yet the facts box and l.108 say 'no difference'.

findings.location: texts/eurovision.html:106 "The estimate rests on 11 316 rows, the pair-rounds in which either audience gave a point."
findings.problem: The sentence calls 11 316 rows 'pair-rounds', but each row is a pair-round-audience cell. The sample is 5 658 pair-rounds, so the count is off by a factor of two.
findings.evidence: tools/eurovision/estimate.py fits on long-format data with one row per audience (n=fit._N=11316). eurovision-data.json h1_cells=17372, while fig. 1's bin cell counts in charts.json sum to 8 686 = 17 372/2 pair-rounds. Design change note: '17 372 → about 11 300 cells'.
findings.fix: 'The estimate rests on 11 316 rows (one per audience) from the 5 658 pair-rounds in which either audience gave a point.'
findings.note: The data are long format, one row per audience (prepare.py concat tele/jury, estimate.py n=fit._N=11316). The fig. 1 bin cells sum to 517+1881+3315+2056+917 = 8686 = 17372/2 pair-rounds, so 11316 rows is about 5658 pair-rounds, not 11316.

findings.location: texts/eurovision.html:169 r3 "Spijkervet, J. The Eurovision Song Contest Dataset, release 2023 ... doi:10.5281/zenodo.4036457"
findings.problem: The DOI resolves to the 2020.0 version record (published 2020-09-18), not to release 2023, which is the data actually used. The 2020 release has no 2021–2023 votes.
findings.evidence: zenodo.org/api/records/4036457: title 'Spijkervet/eurovision-dataset: 2020.0', version 2020.0, conceptdoi 10.5281/zenodo.4036456. tools/eurovision/collect.py:15 downloads from releases/download/2023.
findings.fix: Cite the concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.4036456 (all versions) or the 2023 release's own version DOI, and add the release year and author first name.
findings.note: The Zenodo API for 4036457 returns the title 'Spijkervet/eurovision-dataset: 2020.0', version 2020.0, published 2020-09-18, conceptdoi 10.5281/zenodo.4036456. collect.py:15 downloads release 2023. The citation names release 2023 but links the 2020 version DOI.

findings.location: texts/eurovision.html:144 "the decades before, when one jury or one public decided alone, are seen only in the EU test"
findings.problem: The claim is factually inaccurate for 2009–2015. In those years each country's points combined a jury and a televote (50/50); the data hold only the combined points, but neither audience decided alone.
findings.evidence: Design §2/§3: split jury/televote points exist only from 2016. Before that, Spijkervet votes.csv has total points only.
findings.fix: 'the decades before, when only a single combined set of points was published, are seen only in the EU test.'
findings.note: From 2009 to 2015 the points were a 50/50 jury and televote combination, published only as totals. 'when one jury or one public decided alone' is wrong for those years.

findings.location: texts/eurovision.html:51 TL;DR "Since 2016 every country gives Eurovision points twice: once from five professional jurors and once from its public"
findings.problem: Since 2023 the semi-finals are televote-only, so the statement doesn't hold for all rounds. The design (§3) excludes those rounds for exactly this reason.
findings.evidence: docs/research/eurovision-design.md §0 and §3: 'Rounds where only one audience voted (semi-finals from 2023) are excluded.'
findings.fix: 'Since 2016 every country gives points twice in the final (and, until 2022, in the semi-finals) ...'
findings.note: Design l.16/l.55: since 2023 the semi-finals are televote-only and are excluded. The tldr's 'every country gives points twice' (since 2016) does not hold for 2023–2025 semi-finals. Low severity.

findings.location: texts/eurovision.html:84 "the public gives 6.0 points and the jury 3.1, a difference of +2.8"
findings.problem: The rounded figures don't add up: 6.0 − 3.1 = 2.9. The difference is rounded from the unrounded values (5.98 − 3.13 = 2.85 → 2.8).
findings.evidence: assets/eurovision/charts.json gap.table row 'over 5': televote 5.98, jury 3.13, difference 2.85.
findings.fix: Write 'a difference of about +2.9', or give the components to two decimals.
findings.note: charts.json gap table, over 5: televote 5.98, jury 3.13, difference 2.85 (y1 2.848). The displayed 6.0 − 3.1 = 2.9, but the text and the bar label say +2.8. Cosmetic.

findings.location: texts/eurovision.html:91 table caption "The voting pairs with the largest televote premium, 2016–2025 (at least five rounds together)"
findings.problem: The table silently leaves out pairs without a UN diaspora figure. Switzerland→Albania (gap 8.9 over 10 rounds) would rank fourth but is missing, so the caption overstates what the table shows.
findings.evidence: assets/eurovision/pairs.csv: 'CH,AL,10,8.9,9.4,0.5,' (empty per1000), which sorts between IT,RO (9.6) and LV,RU (8.6).
findings.fix: Add to the caption: 'among pairs with a UN migrant-stock figure'.
findings.note: pairs.csv has 'CH,AL,10,8.9,9.4,0.5,' with empty per1000 and n=10≥5. A gap of 8.9 falls between IT,RO (9.6) and LV,RU (8.6), so it would be in the table. The caption does not say that pairs without a UN figure are excluded.

findings.location: texts/eurovision.html:127 "470 pairs became joint members ... 177 had too few and were dropped"
findings.problem: The counts are directed dyads (i→j), while the rest of the section uses 'pairs of countries' in the undirected sense, for example SEs clustered by pair. Read as undirected pairs, the numbers are roughly double.
findings.evidence: tools/eurovision/estimate.py: pair = i + '>' + j; treated_pairs=len(keep) over directed pairs; upair (sorted) is used only for clustering.
findings.fix: '470 directed pairs (voter → performer) ...'
findings.note: estimate.py builds pair = i+'>'+j (directed), treated_pairs=len(keep) over directed pairs, and uses upair only for clustering. The article calls them 'pairs of countries' without saying they are directed.

findings.location: texts/eurovision.html:65 meta 'data' line: "UN DESA ... 6; UNHCR 8; World Bank population 7; CEPII 9"
findings.problem: Reference r8 is cited before r7 here, so the numbering breaks first-citation order. The meta block also cites r3–r9 before r1 and r2 first appear in the body.
findings.evidence: Line 65 order: r3, r4, r5, r6, r8, r7, r9. The body (l.75, l.82–83) cites r1, r2, r3 ... r9 in order.
