findings.location: texts/lottery.html:74 "Hashes in SHA256SUMS."
findings.problem: The published checksums do not match the committed data files for 2 of the 3 files, so a reader who checks the data's integrity will find a failure.
findings.evidence: `shasum -a 256 -c assets/lottery/SHA256SUMS` gives sportka.csv FAILED, sportka_check_2025_2026.csv FAILED, eurojackpot.csv OK. The committed sportka.csv (LF) hashes to 1105adac…, the same as `git show HEAD:`. Hashing the file with CRLF line endings gives f735b0b1…, the value in SHA256SUMS. So the sums were taken on the CRLF originals before git normalised the line endings.
findings.fix: Regenerate SHA256SUMS from the committed files (`shasum -a 256 sportka.csv eurojackpot.csv sportka_check_2025_2026.csv > SHA256SUMS`), or add `assets/lottery/*.csv -text` to .gitattributes and recommit the CRLF originals.
findings.note: Reran `shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS` in assets/lottery. sportka.csv and sportka_check_2025_2026.csv FAILED, eurojackpot.csv OK. The committed sportka.csv (i/lf) hashes to 1105adac…. The same bytes converted to CRLF hash to f735b0b1…, which is the value in SHA256SUMS.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:74, 84, 89-96 (reference numbering)
findings.problem: References are not numbered by order of first citation. In the body the first citations run 2, 3, 4, 5, 1, 11, 9, 10, 7, 12, 6, 8. Counting the 'About this study' metadata first, they run 1, 9, 10, 11, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 12, 6, 8.
findings.evidence: First cites: meta line 74 cites r1, r9, r10, r11; intro line 84 cites r2–r5; Data lines 89–90 cite r1, r11, r9, r10; methods line 95 cites r7 then r12; line 96 cites r6; line 169 cites r8. All 12 references are cited.
findings.fix: Renumber by first appearance. If the metadata block counts: r1 Sazka=1, lotto.net=2, euro-jackpot.net=3, sportkasazka=4, Cook=5, Farrell=6, Walker=7, Forrest=8, Benjamini–Hochberg=9, Pedregosa=10, Gelman=11, Owen=12. Otherwise renumber from the body order.
findings.note: Read the HTML. The meta 'data' line cites r1, r9, r10, r11. The intro cites r2–r5. Methods cite r7, r12, then r6. r8 first appears in the importance-sampling paragraph. The numbering does not follow order of first citation.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:84 "Cook and Clotfelter showed that lotto sales rise with the jackpot and that the jackpot is shared among players who choose alike[2]"
findings.problem: Cook & Clotfelter (1993) is about scale economies: sales rise with population and jackpot size, and players respond to the jackpot. Prize-sharing caused by non-random number choice ('conscious selection') is the subject of Farrell et al. [3]. Crediting the sharing point to [2] looks over-attributed.
findings.evidence: AER 83(3):634–643 (NBER WP w3766 'The Peculiar Scale Economies of Lotto'). The article itself credits the concentration of winners through conscious selection to Farrell et al. in the next clause.
findings.fix: Change to: "Cook and Clotfelter showed that lotto sales rise with the jackpot and with the population of players[2], Farrell and co-authors estimated how conscious selection of numbers concentrates winners[3] …"
findings.note: Could not read the AER paper. The sentence does credit both rising sales and jackpot sharing among players who choose alike to [2], and conscious selection is Farrell et al.'s topic. Whether Cook & Clotfelter discuss sharing caused by number choice is unverified.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:158 "adds €0.069 per column at the cap" vs 163/166 "the exact difference in expected payout is known, €0.070 per column"
findings.problem: The page gives the same quantity, the gain of an unpopular over an average combination at the cap, as €0.069 in one place and as the 'exact' €0.070 in another, without saying why they differ.
findings.evidence: results.json eurojackpot.levels[120M].ev_gain_unpopular.mean = 0.06856 is the posterior mean. importance.delta = 0.06995 is computed at the plug-in N = 43 897 864 (posterior mean of N).
findings.fix: In the simulation section, add: "(the exact value at the posterior-mean sales of 43.9 million; averaging over the posterior of sales gives €0.069)".
findings.note: In results.json, levels[120M].ev_gain_unpopular.mean = 0.06856 (posterior mean) and importance.delta = 0.06995 at the plug-in N = 43 897 864. The text gives €0.069 (lines 53, 158, 208) and the 'exact' €0.070 (lines 163, 166) without explaining the difference.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:90 "cap the jackpot at €120 million. The jackpot ranged from €10.0 million to €120.2 million"
findings.problem: The reported maximum jackpot is above the stated cap and the text does not explain this, which reads as an internal inconsistency or a transcription error.
findings.evidence: results.json eurojackpot.jackpot_max = 120192955. Two lotto.net rows are at €120.19 M (also mentioned at line 198). The rules cap the jackpot at €120 M.
findings.fix: Explain the excess (for example, the advertised amount includes a rounding or carry-over transferred to tier 2), or check the two rows against the operator's records.
findings.note: results.json eurojackpot.jackpot_max = 120192955. Line 90 says the cap is €120 M and the range runs to €120.2 M. Line 198 mentions 'two draws at €120.2 million'. Nowhere is the excess over the cap explained.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:236 (r5) "Forrest, D., Gulley, O. D., Simmons, R. (2000). ... National Tax Journal 53(4), 853–863."
findings.problem: The reference has no DOI although one exists, and Crossref gives the issue as 4.1 (Part 1).
findings.evidence: Crossref: DOI 10.17310/ntj.2000.4.04, 'Elasticity of Demand for UK National Lottery Tickets', National Tax Journal 53(4.1), 853–863, 2000. Authors match.
findings.fix: Change to: "National Tax Journal 53(4, part 1), 853–863. doi:10.17310/ntj.2000.4.04".
findings.note: Crossref for 10.17310/ntj.2000.4.04 returns 'Elasticity of Demand for UK National Lottery Tickets', vol 53, issue 4.1, pages 853–863, authors Forrest, Gulley, Simmons. r5 at line 236 has no DOI and gives the issue as 4.

findings.location: assets/lottery/charts.json#counts alt: "against the expected 924" vs texts/lottery.html:120-121 "against the expected 924.5"
findings.problem: The expected count is rounded differently in the interactive chart's alt text and in the article (924 vs 924.5).
findings.evidence: results.json fairness.expected = 924.4898. The article alt text and caption say 924.5; the charts.json counts alt says 924, while its legend says 'expected, 924.5'.
findings.fix: Use 924.5 in the charts.json alt text (tools/charts/lottery.py).
findings.note: charts.json counts alt says 'against the expected 924' and its legend says 'expected, 924.5'. The article's alt text and caption say 924.5. results.json fairness.expected = 924.49. The tooltips also say 'expected 924'.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:84 "...and measures the only lever a player holds, the popularity of a combination, together with the reason a plain simulation cannot see it."
findings.problem: The introduction says the study measures how popular a combination is. Nothing measures popularity. It enters as fixed assumed values (π = 0.4 and 2.5), and lines 63, 96 and 208 of the same article say so. The intro claims more than the analysis does.
findings.evidence: tools/lottery/eurojackpot_model.py:41 sets PI = {"unpopular": 0.4, "average": 1.0, "popular": 2.5} as constants and no data feeds them. The text says at line 96 "The values π = 0.4 ... are assumptions" and at line 208 "the popularity figures are assumptions".
findings.fix: Replace with: "...and works out, for an assumed range of combination popularity, how much the only lever a player holds is worth, and why a plain simulation cannot see it."
findings.note: Line 84 says the study 'measures the only lever a player holds, the popularity of a combination'. eurojackpot_model.py:41 hard-codes PI = {0.4, 1.0, 2.5}. Lines 63, 96 and 208 say popularity is assumed. The claim is overstated, though the high severity is arguable because the caveat sits in the same article.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:48 standfirst "an unpopular combination adds €0.07 to a €2 column worth €1.29" (also meta description lines 7 and 9)
findings.problem: The standfirst and the social-card descriptions give the €0.07 gain as a plain result. It is entirely the product of an assumed popularity of 0.4. That assumption appears only in the small stat-card label (line 53) and later in the body, not in the standfirst or the descriptions.
findings.evidence: In eurojackpot_model.py:121, gain = J*p1*(share_if_won(PI['unpopular']*lam) - share_if_won(lam)), so the gain scales with the assumed PI['unpopular'].
findings.fix: "...and at Eurojackpot's cap a combination assumed to be 0.4 times as popular as average would add about €0.07 to a €2 column worth €1.29." Make the same change in the meta and og descriptions.
findings.note: The deck (line 48), the meta description (line 7) and og:description (line 9) state the €0.07 without mentioning the assumed popularity. Only the stat-card small text at line 53 carries 'assumed popularity 0.4'. Code line computing gain scales with PI['unpopular'].

findings.problem: The credible interval on the gain from an unpopular combination covers only the uncertainty in sales (the N posterior), with π held fixed. The single largest uncertainty, how popular real combinations are, is not in it. Reported as a 95 % CrI, it looks far more precise than the estimate really is.
findings.evidence: eurojackpot_model.py:116-122 computes gain over the 4 000 posterior draws of N with PI fixed at 0.4. No sensitivity over π is run or reported.
findings.fix: State it next to each interval: "the interval reflects uncertainty in sales only, with popularity fixed at 0.4". Better, add a sensitivity row (for example π = 0.2, 0.4, 0.7) to the Robustness table.
findings.note: eurojackpot_model.py computes the gain over 4 000 posterior draws of N with PI fixed. No sensitivity over π exists in the code, results.json or the Robustness table. The CrI is not labelled as covering sales uncertainty only.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:96 and 143 "the model puts sales at the €10 million minimum at 14.8 million columns ... At the €120 million cap the implied sales are 43.9 million columns"
findings.problem: Two problems. (1) The sales model is identified from win flags by assuming players pick uniformly at random, so N is a random-pick-equivalent number of columns, not sales. The body calls it "sales" and "columns sold", and only line 213 adds the caveat. (2) The dilution analysis then assumes picks are not uniform (π ≠ 1) but reuses the same N. When choices are uneven, the observed win rate implies more real columns than the uniform assumption gives, so m = πN/C, the shares and the gain are all biased. The text does not say which way.
findings.evidence: eurojackpot_model.py:47-48 uses p = 1 - exp(-N/C), the uniform-pick formula. Lines 116-122 reuse the same N with PI scaling. The caveat appears only in "What this does not show" (line 213).
findings.fix: At first use in line 143, say "effective (random-pick-equivalent) columns". In the expected-value and dilution sections, add one sentence: "Because real players do not pick uniformly, real sales are higher than this effective number, and the co-winner counts and the popularity gain here are understated by an unknown amount."
findings.note: log_post uses p = 1 − exp(−N/C), so N is a random-pick-equivalent count. The body (lines 96 and 143) calls it 'columns sold' and 'sales'. Line 213 gives a partial caveat, saying real sales 'may differ'. No section addresses the direction of bias when the same N is reused with π ≠ 1. By Jensen's inequality, non-uniform picks mean real N is at least the effective N.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:95 "The prediction test builds, for every drawing day and number, features from earlier draws only..."
findings.problem: The methods paragraph does not say that the prediction model uses only the first of the two daily draws, for both features and target. The second draw of every day is dropped, so "past draws" means past first draws. It also leaves out that the number itself is a feature. The restriction appears only in the fig. 3 caption ("the next first draw of the day"), and the tl;dr (line 60) generalises to "past draws do not predict the next one".
findings.evidence: tools/lottery/sportka_model.py:37-38 builds appearances from MAIN_T1 only. Line 51 adds num (the number) as a feature. The docstring says "first draw of each day".
findings.fix: In line 95: "For the first draw of each drawing day (the second draw is not used) and each number, the test builds features from earlier first draws only (..., the day of the week, the week of the year and the number itself)."
findings.note: sportka_model.py features() builds `app` from MAIN_T1 only, which is also the target y, and stacks `num` as a feature. Line 95 mentions neither the first-draw-only restriction nor the number feature. Only the fig. 3 caption says 'next first draw of the day'.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:59-60 tl;dr "Sportka's history shows no favoured number" and hero stat line 50
findings.problem: The short version reads absence of evidence as absence of a bias. The power analysis (line 129) shows the test detects a number favoured by about 9 % only 22 % of the time and one favoured by about 5 % only 8 % of the time. That limitation is near the main result in the body but missing from the tl;dr and the hero stats.
findings.evidence: In assets/lottery/results.json fairness.power: inclusion 1.046 gives power 0.081, 1.092 gives 0.219, and 1.18 gives 0.872.
findings.fix: tl;dr: "Sportka's history shows no large favoured number; a number drawn up to about 10 % more often would likely go unnoticed even in 32 years."
findings.note: tl;dr line 60 says 'shows no favoured number' and deck line 48 'show no favoured number'. The power results (0.08 at +5 %, 0.22 at +9 %) and the 'absence of a large bias' reading appear only at lines 129 and 213.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:153 "at the €120 million cap €1.29 ... Taxes and the booster fund's later payouts are not included."
findings.problem: The expected value at the cap treats the jackpot tier as paying exactly J. Under the post-2022 Eurojackpot rules, once the €120 M cap is reached, jackpot-tier money above the cap flows to the next tier (5+1), which raises the lower-tier value at the cap. The model omits this, and neither the expected-value section nor "What this does not show" mentions it. This needs checking against the official rules, but if it holds, the €1.29 at the cap is understated.
findings.evidence: eurojackpot_model.py:59-64 ev_column has the jackpot equal J*p1*share and the lower tiers fixed a_i*1€*(1-e^{-Nk/C}), with no cap-overflow term. common.py EJ_TIERS shares do not vary with J.
findings.fix: Check the cap-overflow rule against the official Eurojackpot rules. If it holds, model it or add to line 153 and line 213: "At the cap, jackpot-tier money above €120 M passes to the second tier; this is not modelled and makes the value at the cap somewhat higher."
findings.note: ev_column in eurojackpot_model.py computes jackpot = J·p1·share and lower tiers with fixed shares, with no cap-overflow term. Lines 153 and 213 list taxes, rollovers and the booster fund but not overflow. The rule itself (money above the €120 M cap goes to tier 2) is from my knowledge of the official rules, not checked against a document here.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:56-65 details.tldr
findings.problem: The short version states results and that popularity was assumed. It does not say what the results rest on: 124 Eurojackpot draws transcribed by a third party, a sales model that assumes random picks, a secondary source for the prize shares, and a Sportka test with low power against small biases. It also does not say what would overturn them, such as operator sales data, real combination-popularity data, or a longer Eurojackpot record.
findings.evidence: Lines 59-63 contain five sentences on findings plus "Everything is exploratory; how popular a combination was assumed, not measured." Nothing on data provenance, model assumptions or overturning evidence.
findings.fix: Add: "The Eurojackpot numbers rest on 124 draws transcribed from lotto.net and a model of sales inferred from jackpot wins; real sales figures from the operators, or data on which combinations players actually pick, could change the €0.07."
findings.note: tl;dr lines 59–63 do not mention the third-party transcription, the 124-draw base, the random-pick sales model or what would overturn the results. This is an editorial gap with low weight, since line 63 does flag that popularity was assumed.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:143 "the chance that someone wins the jackpot in a draw rises from 0.11 ... at the minimum to 0.26 ... at the cap"
findings.problem: The sentence states a rise in win chance as a result straight after saying the elasticity is not established and may be zero or negative (CrI −0.15 to 0.99). The rise exists only because the posterior mean of β is positive, and the two intervals overlap (0.04–0.21 vs 0.12–0.45).
findings.evidence: In eurojackpot_model.py:117-119, p_win_draw comes from N(J) = N0 (J/10M)^β. With β = 0 it is constant across J.
findings.fix: "...under the fitted model the chance ... would rise from 0.11 ... to 0.26 ...; with an elasticity of zero, which the data cannot exclude, it would not rise at all."
findings.note: Line 143 says the win chance 'rises from 0.11 to 0.26' right after saying β could be zero. The rise comes from N(J) with posterior β, and the CrIs 0.04–0.21 and 0.12–0.45 overlap. With β = 0, p_win_draw is constant.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:208 "the size of the share effect for real Czech players is not measured here"; line 96 "no data on Czech players' choices were available"
findings.problem: Eurojackpot is a multinational pool, so the co-winners who share a jackpot are players in every participating country. Framing the missing popularity data as Czech players' choices misstates the population whose choices set the share.
findings.evidence: The sales model N(J) (eurojackpot_model.py) counts all columns sold in the draw. C and the jackpot are pan-European.
findings.fix: Replace "Czech players" with "Eurojackpot players across the participating countries" in lines 96 and 208.
findings.note: Line 96 says 'no data on Czech players' choices' and line 208 'for real Czech players'. N, C and J in the model are pan-European draw totals, so the population whose choices matter is all Eurojackpot players.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:51, 107, 134 "test AUC 0.497"
findings.problem: AUC is the headline metric for the prediction result, in a hero stat and the tl;dr support, but it is never explained. Only the fig. 3 caption hints that 0.5 means chance. Log loss (lines 107, 134) is also unexplained, and so is what a difference of 0.00041 means.
findings.evidence: Line 51 is the first use. Line 134 uses it without definition. The only gloss is "Dashed line: 0.5, chance" in the line 137 caption.
findings.fix: At line 134: "AUC, the probability that the model ranks a drawn number above an undrawn one (0.5 is guessing, 1 is perfect)..." and "log loss, a penalty for confident wrong predictions, lower is better".
findings.note: AUC appears at lines 51, 107 and 134 with no definition. The only hint is 'Dashed line: 0.5, chance' in the fig. 3 caption. Log loss and the 0.00041 difference are also unexplained.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:52 "95 % CrI"; 109/144 "posterior predictive check", "posterior predictive p"; 118 "Cramér's V, is 0.004"; 95 "effective n", "Benjamini–Hochberg correction", "Monte Carlo null"; 118 "Monte Carlo standard error"; 84 "pari-mutuel"; 168 "common random numbers"/"paired"; 113 "registered labels"
findings.problem: Several technical terms are used without a gloss at first use. CrI first appears in a hero stat (line 52). Cramér's V is given with no reading of what 0.004 means. "Posterior predictive p" is not explained. "Registered labels" refers to a site convention the reader does not know. "Pari-mutuel" (line 84) is explained only indirectly.
findings.evidence: First uses: CrI line 52; pari-mutuel line 84; Benjamini–Hochberg, Monte Carlo null and effective n line 95; posterior predictive check line 109; Cramér's V and Monte Carlo standard error line 118; paired/common random numbers line 168; registered labels line 113.
findings.fix: Add short glosses at first use: "CrI, credible interval: the range that holds the value with 95 % probability under the model"; "pari-mutuel, where winners of a tier split its prize"; "Cramér's V, an effect size from 0 (perfectly uniform) to 1"; "posterior predictive check: simulate wins from the fitted model and compare with the real ones"; drop or explain "registered labels".
findings.note: Checked the first uses. 'pari-mutuel' (84), 'CrI' (52), 'Cramér's V, is 0.004' (118) with no interpretation, 'posterior predictive check' (109) and 'registered labels' (113) carry no gloss. 'Monte Carlo null' is partly explained at line 95.

findings.location: texts/lottery.html:62 tl;dr "Avoiding popular numbers adds a few cents"
findings.problem: The analysis models the popularity of whole combinations (π for a combination), not of individual numbers. "Avoiding popular numbers" suggests a number-level rule that the study did not analyse.
findings.evidence: eurojackpot_model.py treats PI as a combination-level multiplier on co-winners. No number-level popularity is modelled.
findings.fix: "Picking a combination few others pick adds a few cents, and only at large jackpots."
findings.note: tl;dr line 62 says 'Avoiding popular numbers'. The model applies π as a whole-combination multiplier (PI on lam in eurojackpot_model.py) and has no number-level popularity.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:167 "with the pack included the SQL-shape model scored 0.81, and without it 0.58"
findings.problem: The 0.81 AUC with the abstention pack included has no traceable source. It also does not say which SQL-shape model it refers to. 0.58 matches sql/gbm, but the SQL-shape logistic is 0.43.
findings.evidence: assets/detector/detector.json and auc.json hold only the post-exclusion fits (sql/gbm 0.577, sql/logistic 0.430). answers.csv excludes the abstention pack, so auc.py cannot reproduce 0.81. grep for 0.81 across docs/, tools/detector and assets/detector finds nothing relevant.
findings.fix: Name the model, e.g. "the SQL-shape gradient-boosting model scored 0.81 with the pack included and 0.58 without it", and either publish the pre-exclusion figure (for example a field in detector.json) or mark it "(private run log; not verifiable)".
findings.note: I grepped detector.json, auc.json and charts.json: no 0.81 AUC appears. The only 0.81x values are base rates and ap_wrong. answers.csv excludes abstention, so the 0.81 cannot be reproduced. 0.58 matches sql/gbm (0.577). The sentence does not name the model, though fig. 2 implicitly uses gbm for 'the SQL-shape model'.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:98 "Of 5 794 answers, ... The silent-failure rate ranges from 56 % to 92 % across packs and model configurations"
findings.problem: The sentence follows the 5 794-answer outcome breakdown, but the range uses a different denominator: silently wrong / (silently wrong + correct) among the 3 704 training answers. Its two ends also come from different breakdowns: 56 % is a pack (medallion) and 92 % is a model configuration (opus-docs).
findings.evidence: detector.json per_pack.medallion.silent_rate = 0.5566; by_alias.opus-docs.silent_rate = 0.9248 (n=133). The by_alias entries sum to 3 575, which is the training subset. Over all 5 794 answers, 3 839/5 794 = 66 %.
findings.fix: "Among numeric answers used for training, the silent-failure rate ranges from 56 % (medallion pack) to 92 % (opus-docs configuration)."
findings.note: per_pack.medallion.silent_rate is 0.557 and by_alias.opus-docs is 0.925. Both are computed on trained numeric answers, not on the 5 794 in the preceding sentence. One end is a pack and the other an alias. Excluded packs (abstention would be ~100 %) are silently left out of 'across packs'.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:98 "asks each question three times" (and :104 "agreement across the three repeats")
findings.problem: Not every training answer has three repeats. 15 rows have n_repeats = 1: 9 sonnet/SaaS and the 6 Llama answers. Their agreement features are trivially 'all agree', and they enter the 'correct when all repeats agree' share.
findings.evidence: answers.csv: Counter of n_repeats = {3: 3689, 1: 15}. The single-repeat rows are ('sonnet','saas'): 9 and ('ollama-llama3-1','taxi'): 6. The Llama row shows n_distinct_sql=1, repeats_agree=1, n_repeats=1.
findings.fix: Add: "15 training answers (9 Sonnet on SaaS, 6 Llama) have a single repeat, so their agreement features are trivially 1." Alternatively, exclude them from the agreement rule and say so.
findings.note: answers.csv: n_repeats is 3 for 3 689 rows and 1 for 15 (sonnet/saas 9, ollama-llama3-1/taxi 6). All 15 have repeats_agree=1. The text says 'three times' with no exception.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:69 TL;DR "Agreement across repeated runs does not make an answer measurably more likely to be correct."
findings.problem: Read alone, this bullet contradicts the main result. The only combination that beats chance (0.64, CI 0.51–0.77) uses the agreement features, and its lane is 86 % correct against an 18 % base rate. The bullet is true only of the plain 'all repeats agree' rule.
findings.evidence: auc.json models.agreement/gbm reading 'above chance'. shares.agree_minus_base_pp is 2.7 pp (−4.6 to 9.2), which is the rule, not the model.
findings.fix: "That all repeats agree does not, on its own, make an answer measurably more likely to be correct (21 % vs 18 %)."
findings.note: TL;DR bullet 3 is unqualified, while the only above-chance model is agreement/gbm (0.64, 0.51–0.77). The body (line 137) limits the claim to the plain rule ('self-consistency on its own'), but the bullet does not.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:180 "so a 6 % miss and a 2 000 % miss count alike"
findings.problem: The 6 % and 2 000 % error sizes are presented as if they were in the data but cannot be traced. answers.csv has the answer value but no true value or relative error, and detector.json has no error-size field.
findings.evidence: answers.csv columns: file, alias, lang, pack, qid, trap, group, repeat, outcome, value, ... There is no truth or error column.
findings.fix: Either cite the source of the error range (for example the private run reports, marked not verifiable) or make it clearly hypothetical: "a small miss and a twentyfold miss count alike".
findings.note: answers.csv has no truth or error column, and grep finds the 6 %/2 000 % figures only in this sentence, so they cannot be traced. The sentence can be read as illustrative, but if it is meant as observed it is unsourced. The private run reports could hold the figures; I could not check them.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:145 "All six transfer intervals include 0.5"
findings.problem: The text gives values for only four of the six transfers (trained on e-commerce and on taxi). The two trained on SaaS are never stated, so readers cannot check "all six" from the text.
findings.evidence: auc.json transfer_sql_gbm.saas.ecommerce 0.536 (0.42–0.69) and saas.taxi 0.505 (0.13–0.87); neither appears in the paragraph (they are shown only in fig. 2).
findings.fix: Add: "trained on SaaS, it scores 0.54 on e-commerce (0.42–0.69) and 0.51 on taxi (0.13–0.87)".
findings.note: Line 145 gives only the e-commerce-trained and taxi-trained transfers. saas→ecommerce (0.536, 0.42–0.69) and saas→taxi (0.505, 0.13–0.87) from auc.json are not in the text, which still says 'all six'.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:197 r7 "Lei, F., Chen, J. et al. (2024). Spider 2.0 ... arXiv:2411.07763"
findings.problem: The reference gives only the arXiv preprint, while r2, r5 and r6 name the peer-reviewed venue. Spider 2.0 was published at ICLR 2025, so the r7 entry is inconsistent with them and incomplete.
findings.evidence: arXiv API for 2411.07763 confirms the title and authors (Fangyu Lei, Jixuan Chen). The paper appeared at ICLR 2025 (oral).
findings.fix: "Lei, F., Chen, J. et al. (2025). Spider 2.0: ... ICLR 2025. arXiv:2411.07763."
findings.note: r7 cites the arXiv preprint dated 2024 with no venue. r2, r5 and r6 give venues. Spider 2.0 appeared at ICLR 2025 (oral). OpenReview API was blocked by a challenge, but the venue is well established.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:70 (tldr) "What an answer's SQL looks like does not carry over from one warehouse to another."; also :145 "What the model can learn is what the traps of a particular warehouse look like" and :180 "the transfer result suggests it would also learn the warehouse"
findings.problem: These sentences say SQL shape works within a warehouse and fails to transfer. The data show no SQL-shape signal anywhere. The pooled SQL-shape AUCs are 0.43 and 0.58, both indistinguishable from chance. The within-pack AUCs are noise (e-commerce, SaaS) or anti-predictive (taxi). The transfer intervals are wide enough to be uninformative, for example e-commerce to taxi is 0.13–1.00. So 'does not carry over' and the mechanism 'learns the warehouse's traps' are asserted, not measured. This is absence of evidence presented as a finding.
findings.evidence: auc.json transfer_sql_gbm: e-commerce diagonal 0.29 [0.10,0.52], SaaS 0.67 [0.34,0.90], taxi 0.12 [0.00,0.36]. All six off-diagonal intervals include 0.5. The article's own table (lines 116-117) shows the SQL-shape models at 0.43 (0.32–0.55) and 0.58 (0.37–0.75).
findings.fix: tldr: 'The shape of an answer's SQL did not predict silent failure, either within a warehouse or from one warehouse to another; the transfer intervals are too wide to say more.' Line 145: drop 'What the model can learn is what the traps of a particular warehouse look like', or mark it as a hypothesis the data do not test. Line 180: replace 'the transfer result suggests' with 'whether it would generalise across warehouses is untested'.
findings.note: auc.json within-pack: e-commerce 0.29 [0.10,0.52] and SaaS 0.67 [0.34,0.90] are both chance, taxi 0.12 is below chance. Pooled sql 0.43/0.58 are chance. There is no evidence that the model learns within-warehouse traps, so 'What the model can learn is what the traps of a particular warehouse look like' and 'would also learn the warehouse' are unsupported. 'Does not carry over' asserts a null, not a measured failure to transfer.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:98 "asks each question three times, in fifteen languages"; :105 "so all fifteen languages of a question are held out together"
findings.problem: Most questions do not come in fifteen languages. In the training data only 29 of the 87 questions have 15 languages. 42 have a single language: all 23 benchmark v0 questions and all 19 medallion questions. The 10 taxi questions have 8 languages each, and 6 e-commerce questions have 4–10. The text describes the design as uniform when it is not. A reader will overestimate how many answers stand behind each question cluster.
findings.evidence: answers.csv grouped by (pack, group) and counting distinct lang gives: benchmark_v0 1 language x23, medallion 1 x19, taxi 8 x10, saas 15 x9, ecommerce 15 x20 plus 4/5/6/6/8/10.
findings.fix: Line 98: 'asks each question three times, in up to fifteen languages'. Line 105: 'so every language version of a question is held out together (fifteen for SaaS and most e-commerce questions, eight for taxi, one for benchmark v0 and medallion)'.
findings.note: I grouped answers.csv by (pack, group) and counted distinct languages. benchmark_v0 has 1 language for 23 questions, medallion 1 for 19, taxi 8 for 10, saas 15 for 9, ecommerce 15 for 20 and 4–10 for the other 6. Lines 98 and 105 say fifteen for all.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:64-73 (details.tldr)
findings.problem: The short version leaves out the limitation that matters most for the one positive result: the 3.4 % lane is 126 answers, and 120 of them come from one question (e-commerce Q09). It also never says what would overturn the result. Separately, bullet 3 ('Agreement across repeated runs does not make an answer measurably more likely to be correct') sits badly next to bullet 1. The only above-chance model in bullet 1 is built on the agreement features. A reader is left unsure whether agreement helps or not.
findings.evidence: auc.json shares.best_lane_questions = {ecommerce:Q09: 120, benchmark_v0:Q09: 6}. Best model = agreement/gbm (selection.best). The lane caveat appears only at lines 135 and 175.
findings.fix: Bullet 1: 'Used as a filter, the best model forwards 3.4 % of answers (86 % correct), but 120 of those 126 answers repeat one question, so the lane may not recur.' Bullet 3: 'The plain rule "all repeats agree" barely raises the share of correct answers (21 % vs 18 %); only a boosted model on the agreement features beats chance, and only just.' Add: 'A lane that survives on new questions or another warehouse would overturn the negative reading.'
findings.note: The TL;DR omits that 120 of the 126 lane answers are ecommerce:Q09 (auc.json best_lane_questions). The bullet 3 vs bullet 1 tension is real (see 3). The 'what would overturn' part is a softer, editorial point.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:168 "two packs with fewer than 100 numeric answers (benchmark bronze v0 and TPC-DS) were excluded"; :82 registration line "two exclusions were decided after first results"
findings.problem: The registration line says both exclusions came after first results. The change log gives the effect only for the abstention exclusion (0.81 with the pack, 0.58 without). For the second exclusion, the 100-answer threshold, it gives neither the reason the threshold was chosen nor the effect on any AUC. The threshold also falls just under the two smallest packs that were kept (106 and 111 answers), so a reader cannot rule out that the cut-off was tuned. That is an undisclosed deviation.
findings.evidence: Robustness table lines 157-158: benchmark v0 has 111 answers, medallion 106. Bullet at line 168 has no effect size. The registration line at 82 counts it as post hoc.
findings.fix: Add to the line 168 bullet: why 100 was chosen, how many answers the two packs had, and the best AUC with them included (or 'not computed').
findings.note: The line 168 bullet gives no rationale for the 100 cut-off, no answer counts for benchmark_bronze_v0 or tpcds, and no effect on any AUC. The kept packs have 111 and 106 answers. The registration line counts both exclusions as post hoc.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:145 "the taxi value is treated as an artefact of the design, not as a finding about taxi SQL" vs :156 robustness table reading "anti-predictive"
findings.problem: The leave-group-out class-balance explanation is offered without a citation and without a check, such as a permutation null or a stratified split. It is then used to set aside the only interval that excludes 0.5 in fig. 2. The same artefact could also be pulling the pooled SQL-shape logistic regression down to 0.43, which the text calls noise. The robustness table labels the taxi value 'anti-predictive', which contradicts the body's verdict that it is an artefact.
findings.evidence: auc.json: taxi within-pack 0.122 [0.00, 0.364], 191 one-class resamples dropped. auc.py has no permutation test or alternative split.
findings.fix: Either run a label-permutation null within taxi and report it, or write 'possibly an artefact of ...; not tested'. Make the robustness table's 'reading' cell match the text, e.g. 'below chance, likely CV artefact (untested)'.
findings.note: Line 145 calls the leave-group-out artefact 'known' without a citation, and auc.py has no permutation or alternative-split check. The claimed table-vs-text contradiction is overstated: the body also says 'anti-predictive' before attributing it to the artefact. The core point (an untested explanation used to set the result aside) stands.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:56 (deck) and :60 "best held-out AUC ... 0.5 is chance"; first defined at :105 "area under the ROC curve"
findings.problem: AUC is the central measure and is never explained in plain words. The deck and facts box use it, and line 105 only expands the acronym. A reader without that background cannot judge what 0.64 means. A plain reading would help: the probability that a random wrong answer scores higher than a random correct one.
findings.evidence: Searched the text. No sentence explains what AUC means beyond 'area under the ROC curve' and '0.5 is chance'.
findings.fix: At line 105 add: 'the AUC is the chance that a randomly chosen wrong answer gets a higher risk score than a randomly chosen correct one; 0.5 is a coin flip, 1 is perfect.'
findings.note: Line 105 only expands the acronym and the facts box gives only '0.5 is chance'. No sentence gives a plain-language reading of AUC.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:98, :105, :125, :132, :145, :58-59
findings.problem: Several technical terms appear without explanation at first use. Line 98: 'slowly changing dimension', 'soft deletes', 'pack', 'harness'. Line 105: 'logistic regression', 'gradient boosting', 'nested cross-validation', 'bootstrap', 'clusters'. Line 125: 'average precision (AP)', 'Brier score'. Line 132: 'GroupKFold'. Line 136: 'pp'. Line 145: 'leave-group-out cross-validation'. Lines 58-59: 'administrative count'.

Replace 'GroupKFold' in the caption with 'five-fold cross-validation grouped by question'.

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:105 "The first feature set is agreement across the three repeats"
findings.problem: 15 answers (9 SaaS, 6 taxi) have only one repeat. For them the agreement features are trivially 'all agree, one distinct value', yet they are counted as agreeing in the 21 % self-consistency figure and in the agreement rule. The text says every answer has three repeats.
findings.evidence: answers.csv n_repeats: 3 for 3 689 answers, 1 for 15. All 15 have repeats_agree=1 (4 correct, 11 silently wrong).

findings.location: texts/silent-detector.html:136 "its high-confidence lane forwards ..." / :180 "accounts neither for the selection"
findings.problem: The script already computes the bootstrap distribution of the maximum of the eight AUCs, 0.56–0.84 (selection.max_of_eight_lo/hi). The text never reports it, and line 180 says only that the interval does not account for selection. The ranks-first-in-43 % figure is reported, but that number is not a selection correction either.
findings.evidence: auc.py:139 computes max_of_eight_lo/hi. auc.json selection: max_of_eight_lo 0.562, max_of_eight_hi 0.837. Neither appears in the text.
findings.fix: Report it, or drop it from the script. If kept, add a null benchmark, e.g. the max of eight AUCs under permuted labels, so the reader can see what 0.64 would look like by chance after selection.

Caveat: that interval is not a null benchmark either, so the fix needs a permutation null to be meaningful.

findings.location: texts/thesis.html, hypotheses table row H1, label 'not supported'; and the next paragraph: 'the gap in persistence between bus and tram is a quarter of the smallest effect the design could reliably detect, so the two modes cannot be ordered with this design'
findings.problem: The H1 label does not follow from the result the page reports. A difference that is a quarter of the minimum detectable effect means the design was underpowered to order the modes. That is a non-detection, not evidence against the hypothesis. The page applies the opposite logic to H3, where a null with a failed placebo is labelled 'inconclusive' because 'the null therefore does not establish that no gradient exists'. Under the page's own reasoning, the between-mode part of H1 is inconclusive. Only the within-route finding (incoming delay raises persistence, 'expected sign') bears on the hypothesis, and it points towards support, not against it.
findings.evidence: No design file or registered decision rule for this study exists in docs/research/ (grep for thesis/delay/0.727 finds only ask/eval.json, ask/golden.json and docs/style/audit-2026-09-29.json). The page says the labels are 'this summary's reading of the reported results'. Its own text gives the underpowered result for H1 and the inconclusive rule for H3.
findings.fix: Relabel H1 'inconclusive (between modes underpowered)', or split it: 'between modes: inconclusive, gap ≈ ¼ of the MDE; within route: expected sign'. If 'not supported' is kept, give the thesis's reason, e.g. an equivalence bound.
findings.note: Line 113 labels H1 'not supported'; line 118 says the bus–tram gap is a quarter of the MDE and the modes 'cannot be ordered with this design'. That is a non-detection. H3 gets 'inconclusive' for a non-informative null. The within-route result has the 'expected sign'. No thesis design file exists in docs/research/.

findings.location: texts/thesis.html:129 'The levels in crowns do depend on them and are reported as a bracket: at a thirty-minute horizon about 204 CZK a year for a bus passenger and about 60 for a tram passenger, and 182 and 40 when held out of sample on the date split.'
findings.problem: The sentence says the crown levels depend on the value of time and the reliability ratio and are therefore 'reported as a bracket'. The two pairs it then gives differ by sample (in-sample against held out on the date split), not by calibration. A reader will take 204–182 CZK and 60–40 CZK as a range over the calibration uncertainty, which it is not. The calibration constants themselves are stated as not listed.
findings.evidence: In the same paragraph, the dependence on calibration is the stated reason for the bracket, but the second pair is labelled 'held out of sample on the date split'. Nothing in the repo gives the calibration constants or a calibration range.
findings.fix: Drop 'reported as a bracket'. Write: 'The levels in crowns depend on them; at the thesis's calibration and a thirty-minute horizon they are about 204 CZK a year (bus) and 60 (tram) in sample, and 182 and 40 out of sample on the date split.'
findings.note: Line 129 says the crown levels depend on VoT and the reliability ratio and 'are reported as a bracket'. The two pairs it gives (204/60 and 182/40) are in sample against out of sample on the date split, not a calibration range. The calibration constants are stated as not listed (line 103).

findings.location: texts/thesis.html facts box and body: 121 197 794 records; 0.727 / 0.715; half-life ≈ 33 min; 5.6 % / 2.3 %; 204 / 60 / 182 / 40 CZK; 691 bus routes, 41 tram routes, 3 metro clusters
