The page discloses that the thesis is not public, but the numbers cannot be checked here. The 121 197 794 count appears only in other site pages (texts/delayed.html, the front page as '121 million', cv/index.html), never in a data file. One half-life ('≈ 33 min') is given for both modes without saying whether it is pooled or applies to each.
findings.evidence: grep over the repo (excluding .git and .claude) for 0.727, 121 197 794, 204 CZK, 5.6 % and half-life: the hits are other HTML pages, ask/eval.json, ask/golden.json and docs/style/audit-2026-09-29.json (which itself flags 'No uncertainty anywhere'). Nothing under docs/research, assets/ or tools/ relates to the thesis.
findings.fix: Add a small source file, e.g. docs/research/thesis-results.json, with each figure, the thesis table or page it comes from, and the half-life for each mode. Or state in the half-life line whether 33 min applies to both modes or is pooled.
findings.note: No thesis results, design or output file in docs/research/. tools/delay-atlas/aggregate.py only aggregates a local DuckDB and holds no results. The 0.727 hits in bts-results.json are unrelated decimals. 121 197 794 appears only in HTML pages and the ask/ files. Line 59 gives one 'half-life ≈ 33 min' for two sums (0.727, 0.715), and line 123 does not say whether it is pooled.

findings.location: texts/thesis.html, reference list and first citations: the body cites #r2, #r3, #r4, #r5 before the first #r1
findings.problem: References are not numbered in order of first citation. The thesis is r1 but is first cited after r2–r5, in 'how much of their dispersion a traveller who watches a live feed can forecast [1]'. All seven references are cited.
findings.evidence: Order of first citations extracted from the href list: r2, r3, r4, r5, r1, r6, r7.
findings.fix: Either renumber so that Noland & Small is 1, Bates et al. 2, Fosgerau & Karlström 3, Carrion & Levinson 4, the thesis 5, Brakewood & Watkins 6 and Delayed 7, or cite the thesis [1] in the first sentence of the section, e.g. after the opening framing.
findings.note: Line 92: the first citations run r2, r3, r4, r5, then r1 (at 'can forecast [1]'), then r6. r7 is first cited at line 97. Factually correct. Severity is low.

findings.location: texts/thesis.html:114 (H2 row: "opposite sign: conventional metrics overstate the cost for a traveller who observes the state") and :128
findings.problem: The H2 result is presented as an empirical finding against the proposal's prediction, but it is mostly true by construction. By the law of total variance, the variance conditional on an observed state can never be larger than the unconditional variance, so 'conventional metrics overstate the cost for a traveller who observes the state' holds for any series with a forecastable component. What the proposal predicted was a compounding multiplier above one. Line 128 says that multiplier is 'reported only for metro, where three route clusters deny it inference', so on bus and tram the estimand the proposal named was never estimated. It was replaced by a conditional-variance comparison, and the page does not mark this as a change of outcome measure.
findings.evidence: Line 114 gives the prediction as 'a multiplier above one'. Line 128 says the multiplier is reported only for metro and is not inferable there. Line 103 defines the value as the gain from conditioning on the state, which is non-negative by construction. The metro multiplier's value is not given anywhere on the page. No design file or code exists to check against: docs/research/ has no thesis design file and tools/ has no thesis folder.
findings.fix: In the H2 row and at line 128, say that the multiplier named in the proposal was estimated only on metro, where it allows no inference (and give its value), and that on bus and tram the thesis switched to a conditional-variance comparison, which cannot come out the other way. Relabel H2 as 'not testable as stated on bus and tram (estimand changed)' instead of 'not supported: opposite sign'.
findings.note: By the law of total variance, E[Var(Y|state)] ≤ Var(Y), so 'overstate for a traveller who observes the state' holds in sample by construction. Out of sample it can fail, which is a minor caveat. Line 128 says the proposal's multiplier is reported only for metro with no inference and gives no value. Lines 114/119 present the result as H2 failing 'on its sign' without flagging the change of estimand.

findings.location: texts/thesis.html:113 and :118 (H1 labelled "not supported"; "the gap in persistence between bus and tram is a quarter of the smallest effect the design could reliably detect, so the two modes cannot be ordered with this design")
findings.problem: H1 is labelled 'not supported', which reads as a refutation. The page's own explanation, though, is that the design is underpowered: the gap is a quarter of the minimum detectable effect and 'the two modes cannot be ordered'. That makes H1 inconclusive, the label H3 gets, so the two labels are applied inconsistently and the H1 label claims more than the analysis supports.
findings.evidence: Line 118 says the gap is a quarter of the minimum detectable effect and that the modes cannot be ordered. Line 113 says 'not supported'. Line 115 labels H3 'inconclusive' on similar grounds.
findings.fix: Relabel H1 'inconclusive (underpowered for the mode comparison)' and give the minimum detectable effect, or say it is not available.
findings.note: Duplicate of [0]. Checked lines 113, 115 and 118: 'not supported' against 'cannot be ordered with this design', and the MDE is not given (stated at line 118).

findings.location: texts/thesis.html:123 ("Because the delay level is far more persistent than its increment, the thesis locates the memory in a slowly moving, observable state rather than in accumulating shocks")
findings.problem: The stated reasoning does not tell the two explanations apart. A process built from accumulating shocks (a random walk or near-unit-root process) also has a highly persistent level and weakly correlated increments. So 'level more persistent than increment' fits the compounding view just as well. The rejection of compounding at line 128 rests on this sentence.
findings.evidence: Lines 123 and 128 together carry the argument that the series is 'a level plus a short-memory autoregression' and not compounding shocks. No other evidence for that distinction appears on the page.
findings.fix: Either give the evidence that actually tells them apart, for example that the AR(2) sum of about 0.72 is well below one, so shocks decay instead of accumulating, or say that the page does not reproduce the thesis's test.
findings.note: Line 123 infers 'a state rather than accumulating shocks' from 'level far more persistent than its increment'. A random walk shows the same pattern. The discriminating fact (AR(2) sum about 0.72, well below 1) is on the page (line 102), but the argument does not use it.

findings.location: texts/thesis.html:67 (tldr: "about 204 CZK a year by bus and 60 by tram") vs :129 ("182 and 40 when held out of sample")
findings.problem: The short version and the deck give the in-sample crown figures. The out-of-sample tram figure is a third lower (60 to 40), and the summary does not mention that. Line 129 also says the levels 'are reported as a bracket', but each mode gets only a single number, so no bracket is shown.
findings.evidence: Line 67 uses 204 and 60. Line 129 gives 182 and 40 out of sample. No low and high values appear anywhere on the page.
findings.fix: In the short version, give the out-of-sample values (or both, for example '182–204 CZK bus, 40–60 tram'). Either show the bracket's ends, meaning the range over the value of time and the reliability ratio, or drop the word 'bracket'.
findings.note: tldr line 67 gives only 204/60 (in sample). The out-of-sample tram figure of 40 (line 129) is a third lower and is not mentioned there. No bracket endpoints appear anywhere. This overlaps with [1].

findings.location: texts/thesis.html:113 ("within a route, higher incoming delay raises persistence") and :118 ("the effect of incoming delay on persistence has the expected sign")
findings.problem: 'Raises' and 'effect' are causal words applied to an observational within-route association. This within-route result is also not the comparison H1 predicted, which was an ordering across modes by infrastructure segregation, yet it sits in the H1 row without being marked as secondary or exploratory.
findings.evidence: Line 113 states H1 as 'infrastructure segregation orders persistence across modes'. The within-route result appears in the same row as a reported result.
findings.fix: Write 'within a route, persistence is higher when incoming delay is higher (an association, not part of the H1 prediction)'.
findings.note: Line 113 'higher incoming delay raises persistence' and line 118 'the effect of incoming delay' use causal wording for an observational within-route result. They sit in the H1 row, whose prediction is a cross-mode ordering, without being marked secondary.

findings.location: texts/thesis.html:60 and :103 ("commuter-tier reliability cost")
findings.problem: Both headline shares (5.6 % and 2.3 %) are expressed relative to a 'commuter-tier reliability cost', but the page never explains what a tier is or what the commuter tier is. Line 129 refers to 'the tiers' sharing calibration constants without defining them. This is the denominator of the main figure.
findings.evidence: The term appears at lines 60, 103 and 129. Searching the page finds no definition.
findings.fix: At first use, add one clause saying what the tiers are (for example, traveller types with different trip frequencies or schedule penalties) and what the commuter tier assumes.
findings.note: grep finds 'tier' only at lines 60, 103 and 129 ('commuter-tier', 'the tiers share their calibration constants'). There is no definition of the tiers or of the commuter tier.

findings.location: texts/thesis.html:59 and :101-102 ("AR(2) sum 0.727 · 0.715 ... half-life ≈ 33 min"; "What the time index counts ... not reproduced here")
findings.problem: Without the time step, the persistence figure cannot be interpreted. A coefficient sum of 0.727 means a very different speed of decay if t counts consecutive stops, five-minute windows or trips. The page also gives one half-life (about 33 min) for two different sums, so the reader cannot link the coefficient to the minutes.
findings.evidence: Line 101 says the time index is not reproduced. Line 59 gives one half-life for both modes.
findings.fix: State the unit of t (it is in Chapter 6), or say plainly that the 33-minute half-life is the only interpretable figure and the sum depends on a time step not given here. Say whether the half-life differs between bus and tram.
findings.note: Line 101 says the time index is not reproduced. Line 59 gives one half-life for both sums. (tools/delay-atlas/aggregate.py describes the thesis measure as using 5-minute bins, but the page does not say so.)

findings.location: texts/thesis.html:115 and :118 (H3: "a socioeconomic gradient in persistence"; "education is entangled with the structure of the network")
findings.problem: The page never says what the socioeconomic gradient is measured on. 'Education' appears for the first time in the explanation of the failed placebo, with no prior mention of an area-level education measure, and the placebo test itself is not described. Without that, a reader cannot judge why a failed placebo makes the null uninformative.
findings.evidence: Line 115 says 'socioeconomic gradient'. Line 118 introduces 'education' without definition. Neither the placebo nor the positive control is described.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: what unit carries the socioeconomic variable (for example, share of graduates in the districts a route serves), what the placebo was and what result would have counted as a pass.
findings.note: 'socioeconomic' appears only at line 115. 'education' first appears at line 118 inside the placebo explanation, with no prior definition. Neither the placebo nor the positive control is described.

findings.problem: Technical terms are used without explanation at first use: 'impulse responses' (101), 'dynamic panel estimators with fixed effects' (101), 'seasonal part' and 'forecastable state' (103: seasonal within the day or across the calendar?), 'positive control' and 'placebo' (115), 'minimum detectable effect' (118), 'reliability ratio' (129), 'turn-up-and-go service' and 'headway regularity' (134).
findings.evidence: Searching the page finds no gloss for any of these terms at the lines given.
findings.fix: Add a short gloss for each in brackets, for example 'reliability ratio (the value of one minute of standard deviation relative to one minute of mean travel time)' and 'headway regularity (even gaps between vehicles, which matter when passengers do not consult a timetable)'.
findings.note: Spot-checked 'reliability ratio' (lines 103, 129), 'placebo' and 'positive control' (115), 'minimum detectable effect' (118 gives it only as 'smallest effect the design could reliably detect', a partial gloss), and 'turn-up-and-go'/'headway regularity' (134). None is glossed. Low severity.

findings.location: texts/thesis.html:123 ("Interday correlation is far lower, so the persistence is a within-day property")
findings.problem: The page states the comparison but gives no figure for interday correlation, so 'far lower' cannot be checked.
findings.evidence: No interday figure appears anywhere on the page.
findings.fix: Give the interday correlation, or say it is not reproduced here.
findings.note: 'Interday' appears only at line 123 ('far lower'), with no figure and no note that the figure is not reproduced.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:89 "Of 22 requirements ... one, availability over a long period, as not yet verifiable."
findings.problem: The thesis contradicts itself on which requirement could not be verified, and the article picks one version without saying so. Section 3.5 (Table 3.3 and the N1-N10 table) names N6, scalability for data volumes over 100 TB, as the one 'Neověřeno' item, and its partly met items are N9, N10 and one functional requirement. Appendix A names NF2A, availability of at least 99.5 %, which needs long-term testing, and its partly met items are 1C, NF1B and NF4C.
findings.evidence: Thesis PDF (itspy.cz .../it_spy_2025_diplomova_prace_52.pdf), from the text extraction: p.74-75, 'Jediný neověřený požadavek se týkal škálovatelnosti systému pro extrémní objemy dat (nad 100 TB)'; requirement table row 'N6 Škálovatelnost pro objemy dat nad 100 TB  Neověřeno'; Appendix A row 'NF2A Dostupnost minimálně 99,5 % času  Neověřeno  Vyžaduje dlouho-[dobé]'. The 22/18/3/1 totals match Table 3.3.
findings.fix: Either say 'one (long-term availability per the appendix; the main text names scalability above 100 TB) could not be verified', or drop the named item and keep only '18 met, 3 partly met, 1 not verifiable'. A short line in 'What I would do differently' could also note that the thesis's two requirement tables disagree.
findings.note: dp.txt l.3299-3301: the only unverified requirement is scalability above 100 TB (also Table 3.5, row N6 'Neověřeno'). Appendix l.4316: 'NF2A Dostupnost minimálně 99,5 % ... Neověřeno, Vyžaduje dlouho[dobé]'. The article picks the appendix version without saying the two disagree. The 22/18/3/1 totals match Table 3.3.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:84 "a month's logs went from about 12 hours of processing to about 15 minutes" (also facts box :48, meta :7 and :9)
findings.problem: The 12-hour baseline is an estimate and does not cover the same work as the 15 minutes. Requirement 1E calls it 'odhadovaných 12 hodin' (an estimated 12 hours). The thesis's own IT SPY leaflet footnotes it as '12 hodin = stahování dat z 30 zdrojů za měsíc', the time to download a month of data from the 30 sources. Table 2.1 instead gives '> 12 hodin' for KNIME and '15-20 minut' for optimised Python, both for logs from one day ('za 1 den'), not one month. Writing '12 hours of processing' for a month presents an estimated download time for 30 sources as a measured processing time, so the 48x speed-up is not like for like.
findings.evidence: dp.txt line 900: '1E. Snížení celkové doby analýzy z odhadovaných 12 hodin na méně než 15 minut'; leaflet it_spy_2025_informaci_letak_52.pdf: '* Původních 12 hodin = stahování dat z 30 zdrojů za měsíc'; Table 2.1: 'Zpracování logů za 1 den ... > 12 hodin  15-20 minut'.
findings.fix: Write e.g. 'The thesis reports that a month's logs took about 15 minutes, against an estimated 12 hours for the old process (which only fetched logs from the 30 analysed sources).' In the facts box, write '15 min, against an estimated 12 h before · as reported'. Optionally add the scope mismatch to the critique paragraph.
findings.note: Requirement 1E (l.900) calls the 12 h 'odhadovaných' (estimated). The leaflet footnote says '12 hodin = stahování dat z 30 zdrojů za měsíc', i.e. download time. Table 2.1 (l.1858) gives '>12 h' (KNIME) and '15-20 min' for one day of logs. Only l.1250 supports 'a month, 12 h to 15 min'. The article's 'processing' label rests on inconsistent sources.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:94 "The accuracy figures rest on one hand-labelled test set, and the thesis does not report its size or an interval..."
findings.problem: The critique leaves out the most important weakness of the evaluation. The thesis ran ENV on the labelled set 'with different values of the parameter θ' and computed precision, recall and F1 'for each configuration'. It then reports a single 96.0 %, which is apparently the best θ chosen on the same test set, with no held-out data. The article's line 89 describes the result as a plain comparison against the labels. The thesis does say annotation was done by 'experienced analysts' (plural), but it gives no agreement figure, so the labeller point stands.
findings.evidence: dp.txt lines 2747-2751 (p.62-63): '3. Automatická analýza - Takové záznamy byly zpracovány algoritmem ENV s různými hodnotami parametru θ. 4. Výpočet metrik přesnosti - Pro každou konfiguraci byly vypočteny metriky...'; line 3326: 'Manuální anotaci těchto záznamů zkušenými analytiky.'
findings.fix: Add to the critique: 'The threshold θ was tuned on the same labelled set the F1 is reported on, so 0.960 is an optimistic, in-sample figure; I would tune on one split and report on another.'
findings.note: l.2747-2751: ENV was run 'with different values of θ' and the metrics were computed 'for each configuration'. l.2659 sets θ = 0.5 'empirically'. No held-out split is described anywhere, so the F1 is in-sample and tuned on the test set. The article's critique (l.94) does not mention this. The annotators were 'zkušenými analytiky' (l.3326) and no agreement figure is given.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:84 "made the files 70 to 85 % smaller and loading up to 90 % faster than CSV"
findings.problem: The figure matches section 3.1.7, but the thesis gives other figures for the same quantity. Table 3.1 says 70–75 % smaller, and its 'up to 90 %' applies only to reading a subset of columns (a whole file reads 40–60 % faster). The leaflet says 75 %. 'Loading up to 90 % faster' overstates the general case.
findings.evidence: dp.txt line 2447: 'Velikost souboru 100% 25-30% 70-75% úspora'; Table 3.1 rows 'Čtení celého souboru ... 40-60% rychlejší', 'Čtení podmnožiny sloupců ... 90-95% rychlejší'; line 2568-2570: '70–85 %', 'až o 90 %'; leaflet 'Velikost dat 100% 25% 75% úspora'.
findings.fix: Write e.g. 'about 70 to 85 % smaller and, when reading only the needed columns, up to 90 % faster to load than CSV'.
findings.note: The article matches §3.1.7 (l.2568-2570: 70–85 %, up to 90 %). Table 3.1 (l.2447-2449) instead gives 70–75 % smaller, 40–60 % faster for a whole file and 90–95 % only for a subset of columns. The leaflet says 75 %. Low severity: the article quotes the thesis faithfully, but 'up to 90 %' is the best case for reading a subset of columns.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:47 facts box "0.960 against 0.791" vs :89 body "F1 score of 96.0 % ... 79.1 %"
findings.problem: The same F1 values are shown as proportions in the facts box and meta descriptions but as percentages in the body.
findings.fix: Use one format throughout, e.g. 96.0 % and 79.1 % in the facts box and meta descriptions.
findings.note: Facts box and meta use 0.960/0.791; the body (l.89) uses 96.0 %/79.1 %. Cosmetic only.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:54 "Universities keep far more logs than anyone reads; this thesis built a way to read them all." (also deck line 44 "built a pipeline to read the logs of more than 2 200 university systems")
findings.problem: The summary says the tool reads all 2 200+ sources, but nothing in the note shows it was run on, or validated across, all of them. The only evaluation is on 'a sample of log lines from several systems' (line 89), and the 12 h to 15 min figure does not say how many sources a 'month's logs' covers. The problem section (line 78) says the thesis 'set out to' read all of them, but the summary presents that aim as done.
findings.evidence: Line 78 states the goal ('set out to build a tool that could read all of them'). Line 89 limits the test to 'several systems'. No sentence anywhere reports coverage achieved, such as how many sources were processed or how many failed to parse. There is no design file under docs/research and no tools/ directory for this study, and the IT SPY page (itspy.cz) shows only metadata, so the claim cannot be checked against anything else.
findings.fix: Rewrite bullet 1 as: 'Universities keep far more logs than anyone reads; this thesis built a pipeline meant to read all of a university's 2 200+ log sources, and tested its accuracy on a sample from several of them.' If the thesis reports how many sources were actually processed, give that number.
findings.note: The TL;DR says 'built a way to read them all'. The thesis (l.557) says the design 'umožňuje postupné zapojení většiny z více než 2 200 zdrojů' (allows gradual connection of most). Requirement 1A is only the ability to connect. The thesis reports no achieved coverage, so the bullet overclaims.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:51-58 details.tldr
findings.problem: The short-version box does not give the result, what it rests on, or what would overturn it. Bullet 3 says 'far better' with no numbers (F1 0.960 vs 0.791). It does not say this rests on one hand-labelled test set of unreported size with no interval. It does not say that a comparison against standard parsers (Drain, Spell on Loghub) could overturn it. Bullet 4 points readers to the end instead of stating the caveat.
findings.evidence: The numbers appear only in the facts block (line 47) and the body (line 89). The unknown test-set size, the lack of an interval and the weak regex baseline appear only in the last section (line 94).
findings.fix: Replace bullets 3 and 4 with: 'On one hand-labelled test set from several systems, the method scored F1 0.960 against 0.791 for regular expressions. The thesis does not report the test set's size or an uncertainty interval, and regular expressions are a weak comparison: the result would need re-testing against standard log parsers such as Drain on the public Loghub datasets. The figures are as reported in the thesis and were not re-run.'
findings.note: TL;DR bullet 3 says only 'far better', with no figures. The test-set caveats appear only at l.94. The numbers do appear in the facts box just above, so this is an editorial gap rather than a factual error.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:48 facts "15 min from 12 hours" and line 7 meta description "cut a month's processing from 12 hours to 15 minutes"
findings.problem: The speed-up is a headline figure, but the note never says what the 12 hours measured: which earlier tool or process, how many sources, how much data, on what hardware. The caveat that it bundles three changes (parallelism, Parquet, the algorithm) comes only at line 94, far from the headline and the meta description.
findings.evidence: Line 84 says only 'a month's logs went from about 12 hours of processing to about 15 minutes'. Neither the baseline nor the data volume is defined anywhere in the note.
findings.fix: At line 84 add: 'The 12-hour baseline is [the earlier process / a single-threaded run of the same algorithm on CSV] on [N sources / X GB]; the gain combines parallelism, Parquet and the new algorithm, and the thesis does not separate them.' Add a short note under the facts entry: 'combined effect of three changes'.
findings.note: Line 84 and the facts box give no baseline definition (tool, sources, volume). The thesis is itself inconsistent on this (see [1]: download of 30 sources vs processing). The three-changes caveat appears only at l.94. Overlaps [1].

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:89 "It reached a precision of 97.3 %, a recall of 94.8 % and an F1 score of 96.0 %"
findings.problem: The note never says what is being counted, so the metrics cannot be interpreted. They could be per token (fixed vs variable), per line or per pattern. It also does not say who built the regular-expression baseline, or whether it was written before or after the test set was seen. A baseline written by the author can make the comparison look better than it is.
findings.evidence: Line 89 says lines were labelled by 'marking which parts are fixed and which vary' and gives the percentages, but names no unit of evaluation. Line 56 says 'found the changing parts', which suggests token level, but the note never states it.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: 'Precision and recall are computed over [tokens / lines / patterns]: precision is the share of parts the method marked as variable that really vary, and recall is the share of truly variable parts it caught. The regular-expression baseline was [written by the author for these systems / the IT centre's existing rules].'
findings.note: The article names no unit of evaluation. The thesis (l.3424) defines precision as parts identified as dynamic that really were dynamic, i.e. token or part level. The regex baseline is the author's own RegexBasedLogAnalyzer (Listing 3.8, l.2763-2778), which the article does not say.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:47 "pattern detection, F1 on a hand-labelled test set" and line 89 "precision ... recall ... F1 score"
findings.problem: The central accuracy terms F1, precision and recall are used in the facts block and the body without being explained. F1 is the headline number.
findings.evidence: F1 first appears at line 47 (and at line 7 in the meta description). Precision and recall first appear at line 89. Neither line defines them.
findings.fix: At first use in the body, add: 'Precision is how often a part the method called variable really was; recall is how many of the truly variable parts it found; F1 combines the two into one score between 0 and 1.'
findings.note: F1, precision and recall are never glossed in the article (l.7, 47, 89).

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:83 "The thesis used the Extended Nagappan–Vouk algorithm"
findings.problem: The note explains the original Nagappan–Vouk idea but never says what 'Extended' adds. That extension is the thesis's own method and the thing being evaluated.
findings.evidence: Line 83 describes only the original frequency-by-position heuristic from reference [2]. No sentence describes the extension or who made it.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: 'The extension [what it changes, e.g. how it handles lines of different length or sets the frequency threshold] is [the thesis's own / from source X].'
findings.note: The article does not say what 'Extended' adds or who extended it. The thesis (l.1503-1505) attributes the ENV extension to Daniel Tovarňák, Masaryk University (Tovarnák, 2017). That source is missing from the article's references; it cites only Nagappan & Vouk 2010.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:78 "make unusual ones easy to find" and line 83 "millions of lines collapse into a few thousand patterns"
findings.problem: Two problems in the setup. The problem section names finding unusual events as a goal, but the note never reports whether that goal was met or tested, so readers may assume it was. And 'millions of lines' and 'a few thousand patterns' are given as fact with no figure or source.
findings.evidence: None of the sections after line 78 mention anomaly detection again. No pattern count appears in the facts block or the body.
findings.fix: Either give the thesis's actual line and pattern counts with the citation, or write 'in principle, many lines collapse into far fewer patterns'. Add: 'Finding unusual events was left to the IT staff browsing the dashboard and was not evaluated.' (or whatever the thesis actually did).
findings.note: 'A few thousand patterns' has no support: grep finds no pattern count in the thesis ('miliony záznamů denně', l.832, supports only the line volume). The thesis presents anomaly detection only as a goal or future work (abstract l.49), and the article sets it as a goal (l.78) without reporting that it was not evaluated.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:47,56,84,94 terms: "regular expressions" (47), "SSH" (84), "parallel processing across cores" (84), "Drain and Spell" (94), "baseline" (89)
findings.problem: Several technical terms are used without explanation at first use. 'Regular expressions' matters most because it is the comparison method behind the headline number.
findings.evidence: Line 47 and line 56 use 'regular expressions' with no gloss. Line 84 uses 'SSH' and 'parallel processing across cores'. Line 94 names Drain and Spell without saying what they are.
findings.fix: Gloss them at first use: 'regular expressions (hand-written text-matching rules)', 'over SSH (a secure remote connection)', 'Drain and Spell, two widely used automatic log parsers'.
findings.note: Regular expressions, SSH, 'parallel processing across cores', Drain and Spell are all unglossed at first use (l.47/56, 84, 94). Low-severity readability point.

findings.location: texts/thesis-logs.html:44 deck "more than 2 200 university systems, of which about 30 were being analysed" vs line 46 "log sources"; line 47 "0.960" vs line 89 "96.0 %"
findings.problem: The note switches units and formats for the same quantities. It says 'systems' in the deck and 'sources' elsewhere, and gives F1 as 0.960 in the facts block but 96.0 % in the body. 'Of which about 30 were being analysed' also leaves unclear whether it means before or after the thesis.
findings.evidence: Lines 44, 46 and 78 use different nouns. Lines 47 and 89 use different number formats.
findings.fix: Use 'log sources' throughout and one format for F1 (0.960). In the deck, write 'of which the university's security tools analysed about 30 before the thesis'.
findings.note: Deck l.44 says 'systems'; facts l.46 and body l.78 say 'sources'. 'Of which about 30 were being analysed' is ambiguous in time, while l.78 makes clear it means before. The F1 format point duplicates [4].

findings.location: texts/thesis-eu.html:78 "It drew on the literature on coalitions in the Council, which finds that governments mostly vote their own interest<sup>3</sup>"
findings.problem: The sentence gives Häge (2013) a finding the paper does not report. Häge builds an agent-based model in which consensus in the Council emerges as an unintended by-product of governments trying to form blocking coalitions. 'Governments mostly vote their own interest' is at most an assumption of that model, not its finding. The paraphrase is copied from the thesis's own summary (thesis p. 8: 'státům jde ve většině případů pouze o svůj vlastní zájem'), so the article repeats an over-reading.
findings.evidence: Crossref abstract for 10.1017/S0007123412000439: 'consensual decisions may emerge as an unintended by-product of government representatives' desire to form blocking coalitions ... the model's predictions correspond closely to the observed consensus rates.' The abstract does not claim that governments mostly vote their own interest. Thesis PDF (insis.vse.cz/zp/73222), lines ~154-156 of the extracted text, has the paraphrase.
findings.fix: Reword to what the source supports, for example: 'It drew on the literature on coalitions in the Council, which explains the Council's high rate of consensus as a by-product of governments forming blocking coalitions<sup>3</sup>.' Alternatively, attribute the self-interest reading to the thesis rather than to Häge.
findings.note: Crossref abstract (10.1017/S0007123412000439) reports that consensus emerges as a by-product of governments trying to form blocking coalitions. It does not report that governments mostly vote their own interest. The line-78 paraphrase repeats thesis p.7 (zp.txt l.155-157: 'státům jde ve většině případů pouze o svůj vlastní zájem'), which over-reads Häge.

findings.location: texts/thesis-eu.html:88 "In the headlines, the phrase \"Franco-German\" moved from a quarter to two-thirds of the sample." (with line 83: "compared news headlines ... in 2014–2015 and 2020–2021")
findings.problem: The thesis gives the 25 % and 67 % shares for the single years 2014 and 2020, not for the two-year windows that line 83 names. It also does not say what the percentage is a share of. 'Of the sample' implies a share of all 8,421 headlines, which the thesis does not state.
findings.evidence: Thesis text: 'toto spojení v roce 2014 zaznělo v 25 %, v roce 2020 už dominovalo ... na 67 %' (results section, Graf 15/16). The samples were 3,368 headlines for 2014–2015 and 5,053 for 2020–2021 (section 4.2).
findings.fix: For example: 'the phrase \"Franco-German\" went from about a quarter of the 2014 headlines to two-thirds of the 2020 ones, as reported.'
findings.note: Thesis zp.txt l.1052-1053 gives 25 % for 2014 and 67 % for 2020, both single years. It does not say what the percentage is a share of. 'A quarter to two-thirds of the sample' reads as two-year windows over all headlines, which goes beyond the source.

findings.location: texts/thesis-eu.html:67 "Named the best thesis of the Faculty of International Relations in the university's ... ESOP 2021 competition"
findings.problem: ESOP 2021 named a separate 'nejlepší fakultní práce' (best faculty work) for each work type. At the Faculty of International Relations, the seminar-paper category had its own winner (Walica). The award here was best faculty work in the bachelor's-thesis category, so 'the best thesis of the Faculty' is slightly broader than the source. Line 78 repeats the claim ('best thesis of its faculty').
findings.evidence: The vse.cz ESOP 2021 page (created 22. 11. 2021) lists 'Seminární práce' then 'Bakalářské práce'. Under the bachelor's heading, Fakulta mezinárodních vztahů: 'Bc. Šandová Barbora – Francouzsko-německé partnerství v rámci Evropské unie – nejlepší fakultní práce'. Under the seminar heading, FMV: 'Bc. Walica Marek ... – nejlepší fakultní práce'.
findings.fix: 'Named the faculty's best bachelor's thesis in the university's Excellent Student Theses (ESOP) 2021 competition', with the same change on line 78.
findings.note: The local ESOP page copy (thesiseu/esop.html) has 'nejlepší fakultní práce' winners under separate headings. Under 'Seminární práce', FMV: Walica Marek. Under 'Bakalářské práce', FMV: Šandová Barbora. So the award was best faculty bachelor's thesis, not best thesis of the faculty. This affects lines 67 and 78.

findings.location: texts/thesis-eu.html:88 "In the European Parliament, agreement rose on several topics, most on foreign and security policy, and no topic showed a fall" (also tldr line 55)
findings.problem: The note reports the EP topic-agreement rise as a finding, but the underlying number is implausible. In the thesis, Franco-German agreement on foreign and security policy goes from about 1.2 % before to about 64 % after. A jump that size almost certainly reflects how the data were coded or how VoteWatch's topic labels changed, not behaviour. The 2019 EP election also replaced the whole Parliament exactly at the split point. The note mentions neither, and the tldr repeats the rise without qualification.
findings.evidence: Thesis PDF (insis.vse.cz/zp/73222), p. 29: 'Největší rozdíl zaznamenaly zahraničně-bezpečnostní otázky (Graf 8), z necelých 1,2 % před podepsáním, souhlasí po podepsání v téměř 64 %'. Thesis p. 28 says VoteWatch added topic categories in 2018 ('před rokem 2018 v systému tyto ...'). The EP term changed in July 2019, inside the 'after' window (2019 to April 2021).
findings.fix: Give the magnitude and flag it. For example: 'agreement on foreign and security policy went from about 1 % to 64 %, a jump too large to be behavioural; it more likely reflects changes in VoteWatch's topic coding and the new Parliament elected in May 2019, which falls exactly at the split.' In the tldr, add 'possibly an artefact of coding and the 2019 election'.
findings.note: Thesis l.907-909 gives foreign and security policy agreement going from under 1.2 % to almost 64 %. The note does not give this magnitude, which is implausible as behaviour. The May 2019 EP election falls right after the January 2019 split, and the note mentions 'an election' only generically on line 93. One correction to the evidence: the '2018' category remark (l.799-802) is about the Council (budget control and general development), not EP topics. So the VoteWatch-recoding claim is speculation, while the election confound and the magnitude are solid. Severity 'high' is arguable.

findings.location: texts/thesis-eu.html:56 tldr "Both national parliaments voted far more often in favour of EU items after the treaty"; line 88 "The largest changes were national"; facts lines 47-48
findings.problem: The largest change the note reports does not measure Franco-German convergence. It is each chamber's own approval rate on EU-related items. The thesis itself warns that the mix of motions may differ between periods. In the Bundestag, opposition motions that are routinely rejected make a 71 % rejection rate likely, so the share of opposition motions on the agenda can drive the rate. The bases are also small: 45 Bundestag items after. None of this appears near the finding or in the tldr. The 'What I would do differently' paragraph raises agenda composition only for EU-institution topic agreement.
findings.evidence: Thesis p. 33: 'Samozřejmě je nutné myslet i na skladbu jednotlivých usnesení a zda jednoduše nebyly jednotlivé návrhy pro obě země výhodnější'. Bundestag: 129 items in total, 84 before and 45 after, 71 % rejected before. Assemblée nationale: 499 items, 376 before and 123 after.
findings.fix: After line 88's national sentence, add: 'These are each chamber's own approval rates on a small number of items (45 Bundestag items after the treaty), not a measure of the two countries voting together, and they move with how many opposition motions were tabled.' In the tldr, replace bullet 3 with: 'Both national parliaments approved more EU items after 2019, but that measures each chamber on its own, on few items, and depends on what was tabled.'
findings.note: The facts block and l.88 report each chamber's own approval rate (Bundestag 84 → 45 items, 71 % rejected before; AN 376 → 123 items). The note never says this does not measure France and Germany voting together. Line 93's 'a change in what was put to a vote' only partly covers the agenda issue. The thesis itself flags agenda composition (l.1040-1042). The opposition-motion mechanism is the auditor's conjecture and was not verified.

findings.location: texts/thesis-eu.html:83 "computed correlations between countries' voting records"; line 88 "The correlation between their voting records stayed near zero, −0.088 before and −0.084 after"
findings.problem: The note does not say how the correlation was coded, and the coding matters. The thesis code maps 'Against', "Didn't vote" and missing values all to 0. Abstention is also 0 according to the thesis text. The thesis prose says absences were dropped, but the code fills them with 0. The coefficient therefore mixes participation with position. Council votes are also nearly all 'yes', so there is almost no variance. That is why a near-zero correlation sits next to 82–100 % topic agreement in the same paragraph. The note presents both numbers without explaining how they fit together.
findings.evidence: Thesis appendix 3 (p. 47): df.replace(["Didn't vote"],int(0)); df.fillna(0). Footnote 17 (p. 23): 'pokud proti nebo se zdržely "0"'. p. 23 text: 'Pokud jedinec na hlasování chyběl ... řešena vynecháním'. Line 88 gives 100 % agreement on foreign policy and 86 %→82 % on agriculture, with r ≈ −0.09.
findings.fix: Add one sentence after the correlation figures: 'Votes were coded yes = 1 and everything else (no, abstain, absent) = 0. Almost every Council vote is a yes, so the correlation has little to work with, and near zero here does not mean the two disagree; the topic-agreement shares are the more meaningful figure.'
findings.note: Appendix code (l.1548-1551) maps Against and 'Didn't vote' to 0 and fills NaN with 0. Footnote 17 (l.760) maps abstain to 0. The prose (l.733-734) says absences were dropped, which contradicts the code. The note does not describe the coding. I did not verify that Council votes are near-all-yes (the data are not kept), but the gap between 100 % topic agreement and r≈−0.09 is unexplained in the note.

findings.location: texts/thesis-eu.html:93 "they show which countries' votes predicted France's or Germany's, which is a different and weaker claim"
findings.problem: This correction still overstates what the code computed. The thesis code fits a random forest that predicts Germany's vote from every integer column, and the target column 'ger' is apparently among them. It then explains a single validation row: row_to_show is left at the last index of a loop over columns. The plotted 'Shapley values' are therefore a SHAP force plot for one vote from a model that may include its own target. They are not a summary of which countries predict Germany's or France's votes.
findings.evidence: Thesis appendix 4 (p. 48): y = (data['ger'] == 1); nazvy = [i for i in data.columns if data[i].dtype in [np.int64, np.int64]]; X = data[nazvy]; for index,x in enumerate(df): row_to_show=index; predikce = val_X.iloc[row_to_show]; shap.force_plot(..., predikce).
findings.fix: Rewrite: 'The "Shapley values" are SHAP attributions from a random-forest model, plotted for a single vote; the feature set appears to include the very country being predicted, so they say little even about prediction, and nothing about coalition value.'
findings.note: Appendix 4 (l.1578-1597): y = data['ger']==1, and X takes every int64 column, which very likely includes 'ger' itself. The loop over enumerate(df) iterates column names, so row_to_show ends at the last column index. SHAP is then computed and force-plotted for that one validation row. Line 93 of the note ('which countries' votes predicted France's or Germany's') overstates what the code produces.

findings.location: texts/thesis-eu.html:93 "a change in what was put to a vote, an election or the pandemic in 2020 could explain as much as the treaty"
findings.problem: The note names the main confounds only generically and only in the final section. The split date (January 2019) almost exactly matches the May 2019 European Parliament election, which replaced every MEP. The Bundestag and Assemblée elections (2017) fall inside the 'before' window. The treaty also entered into force only in January 2020, so part of the 'after' period predates it. None of this is said next to the findings or in the tldr. The tldr's only caveat is the missing comparison country.
findings.evidence: Facts line 46: '2014–2018 → 2019–April 2021'. The thesis data window is 1 Apr 2014 to 3 Apr 2021 (p. 22). Treaty signed 22 Jan 2019; in force 22 Jan 2020.
findings.fix: In the line 88 section, add: 'The split also coincides with the 2019 European Parliament election, which changed every MEP, and the treaty only entered into force in January 2020.' In the tldr, add 'and the split coincides with a new European Parliament'.
findings.note: Line 93 names 'an election' and 'the pandemic' only generically. The split is January 2019 (facts l.46), the EP election was in May 2019, and the treaty entered into force on 22 January 2020. The note does not mention any of these next to the findings or in the TL;DR. Partly addressed, but the specific coincidence with the EP election is not stated.

findings.location: texts/thesis-eu.html:88 "the correlation between French and German members stayed near zero"
findings.problem: The note smooths over a fall. In the thesis, the EP correlation moved from 0.063 to −0.024, and the thesis text describes this as a decrease ('klesl', 'se ... snížila'). The note's tldr reports only the EP topic-agreement rise. That gives readers the positive measure and leaves out the measure that moved the other way.
findings.evidence: Thesis p. 29: 'korelovali ... v hodnotě 0,063'. Thesis p. 31: 'Korelační koeficient klesl na hodnotu -0,024'. Conclusion p. 36: 'Vzájemná korelace se po podepsání smlouvy však snížila'.
findings.fix: Give the figures: 'the correlation between French and German members went from 0.06 to −0.02, near zero either way'.
findings.note: Thesis l.926 gives 0.063 before and l.958 gives −0.024 after (described as 'klesl'). The conclusion (l.1121-1122) says the correlation 'se ... snížila'. The note's line 88 says only 'stayed near zero', with no figures. That is accurate but leaves out the decline, while the TL;DR reports only the EP rise.

findings.location: texts/thesis-eu.html:88 "In the headlines, the phrase \"Franco-German\" moved from a quarter to two-thirds of the sample"
findings.problem: The headline sample came from Google News searches that included the query 'Franco-German cooperation', and the results were retrieved in 2021 for both periods. The phrase share therefore depends on how the query was worded and on what Google News still showed for 2014 in 2021. The note does not say so, and it reports the share as a finding.
findings.evidence: Thesis footnote 15 (p. 22): queries 'Franco-German cooperation', 'France, Germany, EU', 'French, German cooalition in the EU'. Headlines were translated on 15 April 2021 (p. 35).
findings.fix: Add: 'the headlines came from Google News searches that themselves used the phrase, retrieved in 2021, so the share mostly reflects the search, not the press.'
findings.note: Footnote 15 (l.716-717) lists the queries, including 'Franco-German cooperation'. So the share of the phrase in the headlines is partly driven by the query, and the note does not say so. 'Mostly reflects the search' in the proposed fix overstates it: the same queries were used for both periods, so the change over time is less affected than the levels.

findings.location: texts/thesis-eu.html:51-58 details.tldr
findings.problem: The short version states results but does not say what they rest on: the number of Council and EP votes or of national items, the yes = 1 / other = 0 coding, or the fact that the EP split coincides with an election. It also does not say what would overturn the national-parliament result, for example a difference-in-differences against other large member states, or holding the agenda fixed. The most useful practical sentence, that the inference should have been designed before collecting data (line 93), is left to the end.
findings.evidence: Lines 54-57 contain four bullets: the claim, Council/EP, national parliaments, and the no-comparison caveat. No N, no coding, no falsifier. The thesis gives N: Council 1,588 records, EP 2,788, Assemblée 4,865 (499 on the EU), Bundestag 1,310 (129 on the EU).
findings.fix: Add a bullet: 'Rests on 1,588 Council and 2,788 EP roll calls and 499 / 129 EU items in the two parliaments; a comparison against other large-country pairs, or holding the agenda fixed, could erase the national-parliament change.'
findings.note: The TL;DR (l.54-57) has no N, no coding and no falsifier. The Ns exist in the thesis (l.739-742: Council 1,588, EP 2,788, AN 4,865, Bundestag 1,310). This is a real omission but an editorial one. The TL;DR does carry the key caveat (no comparison country). Low priority.

findings.problem: Several technical terms are used without explanation: 'difference-in-differences' (line 93), 'scaling of roll calls' (line 93; this means NOMINATE-type ideal-point estimation), and 'roll calls' (line 68). findings.location: texts/football.html:54 deck "alone among small peers its Big-5 count fell without recovering"; :7/:9/:45 meta description "its Big-5 count fell in 2014/15 without recovering"; :116 "Croatia fell in 2003/04 and recovered eleven seasons later and Norway fell in 2004/05 and recovered seventeen seasons later, while every other small peer's later step is a rise"
findings.problem: The comparative headline rests on dated steps that are statistically indistinguishable from no change. The Czech fall's interval reaches 1.02. Croatia's fall (0.51–1.16) and rise (0.80–1.69), and Norway's fall (0.27–1.39) and rise (0.37–2.24), all include no change, with posteriors of only 0.22–0.30. The other small peers' 'later rises' have posteriors of 0.08–0.24, and all of their intervals include 1. Denmark and Switzerland fail the convergence rule and have no dated steps at all, so 'every other small peer' silently leaves them out. The deck and the meta description state 'fell ... without recovering' as a fact, with no caveat.
findings.evidence: docs/charts/nations.json long_run.countries: CRO fall 2003-04 p=0.30 ×0.75 (0.51–1.16), rise 2014-15 p=0.27 ×1.31 (0.80–1.69); NOR fall 2004-05 p=0.26 ×0.67 (0.27–1.39), rise 2021-22 p=0.22 (0.37–2.24); SVK, AUT, HUN and POL steps p 0.08–0.24, all intervals include 1. The convergence table on docs/nations/index.html marks Denmark and Switzerland 'fails: no dated steps'. The atlas's own nations page says 'a step whose interval includes no change is not distinguishable from none'.

Drop 'alone among small peers' and 'without recovering' from the deck and the meta and og descriptions. At :116, give each peer step its posterior and interval. Say that none excludes no change, and that Denmark's and Switzerland's fits fail convergence and carry no dated steps.

findings.location: texts/football.html:121-126 "three channels, the under-21 share of home minutes, home-league strength (the mover-based estimate) and the median age of the first move" and the table (league strength +5.1 for Norway, +1.7 for Denmark; age at first move 0.0)
findings.problem: The league-strength channel has a negative coefficient in the ridge fit: a weaker home league goes with more players per million. That is why Norway and Denmark get positive 'league strength' contributions. The text never says so, and readers will assume a stronger league helps. The age channel also uses a different measure from the one in the prose. It is the median age at the first top-9 season among recent entrants, which is 22 for all three countries, so it is zero by construction. The text at :115 gives first-move ages of 24, 23 and 22.5, which leaves the 0.0 column unexplained and apparently contradicted.
findings.evidence: The atlas's nations page (docs/nations/index.html, takeaway 2) says: 'The league-strength coefficient in this fit is negative (−56.5 per unit of the league multiplier): a weaker home league goes with more players ... The export-age channel is zero by construction: Czechia, Norway and Denmark share the same median age at the first top-9 season among recent entrants (22).' The article's :115 reports 'median age of 24, against 23 for Denmark and 22.5 for Norway'.
findings.fix: Add to :121: "In this fit the league-strength coefficient is negative (−56.5 per unit of the multiplier), so a peer with a weaker home league than Czechia's gets a positive contribution. The age channel uses the median age at the first top-9 season among recent entrants, which is 22 in all three countries, so it is zero by construction. It is not the first-move age given above."

findings.location: texts/football.html:115 "Czech players aged 21 or younger get 6.4 % of Czech First League minutes ... The Czech share was 10 % in 2020/21." and :66 tldr "Czechia gives its own under-21s the smallest share"
findings.problem: The 6.4 % is a floor, because FBref leaves some rows without a nationality. The ceiling is 7.6 %. Setting 6.4 % against the 2020/21 value implies a decline, but the share was 11.1 % in 2024/25, and the six-season trend interval includes zero (−1.26 to +0.48 pp a season). Neither point is stated.
findings.evidence: The atlas nations page, takeaway 3, gives shares of 10.3, 8.6, 9.0, 7.9, 11.1 and 6.4 %, an OLS trend of −0.39 pp (90 % CI −1.26 to +0.48), and says 'The last season's share is a floor ... at its ceiling of 7.6 %'.
findings.fix: "... get 6.4 % (a floor; at most 7.6 %) of Czech First League minutes ... The share moved between 7.9 % and 11.1 % over 2020/21–2024/25, and the six-season trend (−0.4 pp a season, 90 % CI −1.3 to +0.5) does not exclude zero."
findings.note: youth_panel.json: CZE x 0.1106 in 2024/25 and 0.0635 in 2025/26. The atlas nations page says the last share is a floor with ceiling 7.6 % and gives a trend CI of -1.26 to +0.48. The article sets 6.4 % against 10 % in 2020/21 without either point.

findings.location: texts/football.html:62-70 details.tldr
findings.problem: The short version does not give the headline result (2.39 per million, seventh of nine, against Denmark at five times the density) or the Big-5 drop (26 → 6 → 10). It does not say what the per-head ranking is 'robust' to (only a 450-minute floor), and it says nothing about what would overturn the findings. The first bullet is meta-information about editions.
findings.evidence: The tldr bullets are 'The atlas has six national editions...', 'Czechia gives its own under-21s the smallest share...', 'The per-head ranking is robust; the dating ... is not', 'Everything here is description'. The 450-minute check is the only robustness check of the ranking (:100).
findings.fix: Replace with: "Czechia has 2.39 players per million in Europe's nine strongest leagues, seventh of nine; Denmark has five times that. • The ranking holds with a 450-minute floor; Czechia would need 35 players to move up or 17 to move down. • The Czech Big-5 count fell from 26 (2007/08) to 6 (2015/16) and is 10 now; the model's dating of the fall to 2014/15 has posterior 0.58, and its size does not exclude no change. • Czechia gives its own under-21s the smallest share of home-league minutes of eight countries (6.4–7.6 %). • All of this is description from one season's counts; it does not show why."
findings.note: TL;DR l.62-70 has no 2.39 / seventh-of-nine figure and no 26->6->10. 'Robust' rests only on the 450-minute floor check (l.100). The first bullet is about editions. This is a clarity and editorial judgment, but it is accurate as a description.

findings.location: texts/football.html:59, :116, :128 "90 % HDI"; :59 and :116 "posterior probability"; :94 "local-level model with two step changes"
findings.problem: The central statistical terms behind the headline break result are never explained: HDI, posterior probability of a season, and local-level model. The header card leads with 'posterior probability 0.58 · level ×0.59, 90 % HDI 0.37–1.02', and a general reader cannot tell that this means the fall may be zero.
findings.evidence: The terms first appear at :59 in the header card. The text has no gloss anywhere.
findings.fix: At :94: "A local-level model (a smoothly drifting average) with two step changes at unknown seasons ... gives, for each season, the probability that the step falls there (the posterior probability), and a 90 % highest-density interval (HDI), the range that holds the size of the step with 90 % probability." In the header card, add 'interval includes no change'.
findings.note: HDI, posterior probability and local-level model appear at l.59, 94 and 116 with no gloss anywhere on the page.

findings.location: texts/football.html:121 "ridge regression ... linear Oaxaca–Blinder split"; :95 "PCA", "K-means", "hierarchical Poisson model"; :137 "log predictive density", "R-hat", "divergences"; :142 "Spearman 0.74"; :115 "regular under-21 starters"; :131 "style projection", "quality projection", "rung"
findings.problem: Technical terms appear without explanation at first use. 'Style projection' and 'quality projection' in the fig. 3 caption are not tied to the names used in the Method section. 'Regular under-21 starters' is never defined.
findings.evidence: There is no gloss at any of the listed lines.
findings.fix: Give a short gloss at each first use. For example: Oaxaca–Blinder, 'splitting the fitted gap into the part each channel accounts for'; ridge, 'a regression that shrinks coefficients to cope with few countries'; PCA, 'reduced to the two directions with the most variation'; K-means, 'grouped into clusters of similar players'. Define 'regular starter' (minimum minutes or starts), and at :95 name the two runs 'style' (raw rates) and 'quality' (UEFA multipliers).
findings.note: Checked: no gloss for ridge, Oaxaca-Blinder, PCA, K-means, R-hat, log predictive density or Spearman. 'Regular under-21 starters' (l.115) is never defined. Fig. 3 says 'style/quality projection' while the Method says 'raw rates' / 'multiplying by a league factor'. The caption does give these in parentheses, so that part is partly addressed.

findings.location: texts/football.html:54 deck and :57 header "Big-5"
findings.problem: 'Big-5' is used in the deck and the header stats before it is defined at :94, as 'the first five of the nine'.
findings.evidence: The first use is at :54 ('its Big-5 count fell'). The definition is at :94.
findings.fix: In the deck: "... in the Big-5 (England, Spain, Italy, Germany, France) ..."
findings.note: 'Big-5' first appears in the deck (l.54) and the facts (l.57). It is defined only at l.94 ('the first five of the nine').

findings.location: texts/football.html:100 "Czechia has 26 players in the nine leagues, 2.39 per million, seventh of nine peers."
findings.problem: There are eight peers plus Czechia. 'Seventh of nine peers' implies nine peers and contradicts the deck's 'against eight peers'.
findings.evidence: :54 says 'against eight peers: Czechia ranks seventh of nine'.
findings.fix: "... 2.39 per million, seventh of nine countries."
findings.note: l.100 says 'seventh of nine peers', while the deck says 'against eight peers ... seventh of nine'. The l.100 wording is inconsistent.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:113 "Finland and Sweden show only rises over the same seasons<sup>1</sup>" and :145 "over the three fits the largest R-hat is 1.007 and there is one divergent transition, in Finland's<sup>1</sup>"
findings.problem: Reference 1 is the live atlas, and the live atlas has since withdrawn the Finland result. The page presents Finland's two dated rises as a valid comparison, but at atlas HEAD 335cb08 (1 Oct 2026, "Q2 convergence rule, Finland undated") Finland's fit fails the convergence rule and its steps are no longer dated. A reader who follows r1 now finds the opposite of what the sentence cites it for.
findings.evidence: assets/hockey/q2_break_model.json is byte-identical to `git show d1f9f88:outputs/q2_break_model.json`, so the article's numbers are correct for d1f9f88 (FIN: two 'up' steps, n_divergences 1). At HEAD 335cb08, FIN diagnostics are {pass: False, stage: 2, n_divergences: 1}. Live hockey.bsandova.com now reads: "Finland fails (one divergent transition after both stages), so its two steps (1999/00 and 2018/19) are no longer dated." Other HEAD changes include Finland's five-league count (425 to 426) and NL unidentified (22 to 21).
findings.fix: Either cite the d1f9f88 build explicitly in r1 (not the live URL), or update to the current build. For example: "Sweden shows only rises over the same seasons; Finland's fit has a divergent transition and the atlas does not date its steps." Then re-check the 22-of-365 NL figure against the current outputs.
findings.note: assets/hockey/q2_break_model.json is byte-identical to atlas d1f9f88:outputs/q2_break_model.json. At atlas HEAD 335cb08, FIN diagnostics are pass False, stage 2. The live hockey.bsandova.com text now reads 'Finland fails ... its two steps (1999/00 and 2018/19) are no longer dated'. r1 says 'build of 29 September 2026' but links to the live site, which now contradicts line 104 ('Finland and Sweden show only rises', cited to r1).

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:103 "...the football atlas's series model, in PyMC13."
findings.problem: The superscript after "PyMC" points to r13, which is the author's own atlas repository, not PyMC. PyMC itself is never cited. Only its version number appears inside r13.
findings.evidence: r13 = "Šandová, B. (2026). czehockey-player-pool-atlas, v0.1.0. Software ... PyMC 5.28.5." uv.lock at d1f9f88 does contain pymc 5.28.5, so the version is correct, but there is no reference entry for PyMC (e.g. Abril-Pla et al. 2023, PeerJ Computer Science 9:e1516, doi:10.7717/peerj-cs.1516).
findings.fix: Add a PyMC reference (Abril-Pla, O., et al. (2023). PyMC: a modern, and comprehensive probabilistic programming framework in Python. PeerJ Computer Science 9, e1516. doi:10.7717/peerj-cs.1516) and cite it after "PyMC". Keep r13 for the atlas code, and renumber in order of first citation.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:145 "runs at d1f9f88 with 247 software tests passing and 16 skipped"; also :151 "about six minutes"
findings.problem: The test counts and the runtime cannot be traced to any output in either repo.
findings.evidence: Neither the bsandova.com repo nor the atlas repo at d1f9f88 (README.md, outputs/) records 247 passed / 16 skipped or a runtime. `git grep -c 'def test_' d1f9f88 -- tests` gives 226 test functions; parametrisation could make 263, but nothing records it.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:98 "at least 20 of 82 games, pro-rated to the league-season's schedule, the 95th percentile of skater games"
findings.problem: As written, "the 95th percentile of skater games" reads as a description of the 20-game threshold. In the code, the 95th percentile is how the schedule length (82 for the NHL) is estimated; the threshold is 20/82 of that length.
findings.evidence: src/analysis/common.py:96-101 at d1f9f88: "The league-season's schedule length, read off the data as the 95th percentile of ... games". The pro-rated values 12 (48 games), 17 (~70) and 14 (56) follow from 20/82 × schedule.
findings.fix: "...at least 20 of 82 games, pro-rated to the league-season's schedule length (read off the data as the 95th percentile of skater games played)..."
findings.note: Line 90 places the appositive 'the 95th percentile of skater games' right after 'threshold ... schedule'. At d1f9f88, src/analysis/common.py schedule_length() takes the 95th percentile as the schedule length, and games_threshold = round(20/82 x schedule). The wording is ambiguous, and the proposed fix matches the code.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:116 "No Czech player aged 21 or under reached the threshold" vs :117-124 table "Under-21 skaters' share" and :125 "Under-21 here means aged 20 or less"
findings.problem: Two neighbouring passages use different age cut-offs. The cohort paragraph uses age 21 or under (q3 band ≤21), while the youth table and the facts box call age 20 or under "under-21" (q4). A reader can easily take the two as the same group.
findings.evidence: q3_cohort_gaps.json definitions: age_bands ["≤21", ...], age = season start year minus birth year. q4_youth_ice_time.json definitions.u21: "age ... of 20 or less". All the numbers match their own source (F ≤21 shortfall 6.05; Extraliga mean 0.0795/0.0547).
findings.fix: Label the youth measure "aged 20 or under" in the facts box and the table caption, or call the q3 band "aged 21 or under" every time and the q4 measure "U21 (20 or under)".
findings.note: q3 age_bands '≤21' (age = season start year minus birth year) is used at line 109 as 'aged 21 or under'. common.py U21_MAX_AGE = 20 drives the table and the facts-box 'under-21', which line 117 defines as 20 or less only after the table. Each number matches its own source, but adjacent passages use two cut-offs. Same issue as finding 14.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:59 facts box "most probable season of the fall 2009/10 · posterior probability 0.09 · level ×0.83, 90 % HDI 0.56–1.14"
findings.problem: The facts box calls the step "the fall", but its 90 % HDI includes 1 (no change), and the box omits the 0.80 probability that the step lowers the level. Taken out of context, the box overstates how certain the decline is.
findings.evidence: q2_break_model.json CZE steps[1]: delta_factor {median 0.831, lo 0.561, hi 1.140}, p_down 0.80375, modal 2009/10 prob 0.0931. The body text (line 113) does give p_down 0.80.
findings.fix: Add "P(lower) 0.80" to the facts-box small text, or relabel the row "most probable season of the second step".
findings.note: Facts box line 54 gives modal 2009/10 at 0.09 and ×0.83 (HDI 0.56–1.14) but not p_down 0.80375. That figure appears only in the body at line 104. Low severity: the box's own HDI already shows the uncertainty.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:178 r5 link https://api.nhle.com/stats/rest/en/skater/summary
