findings.location: texts/hockey.html:99 "Counting the five leagues, Czechia has 53 players, 4.86 per million, 5th of 10 against a peer median of 3.55"
findings.problem: The five-league measure counts each peer's home league but leaves out Czechia's. Finland's Liiga, Sweden's SHL, Switzerland's National League and Germany's DEL are all among the five leagues, while the Czech Extraliga (and the Slovak, Latvian, Danish, Norwegian and Austrian home leagues) is not. So the rank compares Czechs abroad with Finns and Swedes at home plus abroad. The text gives the 5th-of-10 rank and the peer median as if it were a like-for-like comparison and never mentions the asymmetry.
findings.evidence: assets/hockey/q1_per_million.json headline.nations: FIN top5 = 425, of which Liiga 314; SWE 408, of which SHL 251; CHE 248, of which NL 233; DEU 198, of which DEL 189; CZE 53 with no Extraliga column (line 90 defines the Extraliga as the home league, outside 'NHL + rung 2').
findings.fix: Next to the five-league figure, add: "This count includes the home leagues of Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and Germany but not the Czech Extraliga, so it measures Czechs abroad against those four nations' whole pools; it is not a like-for-like rank." Alternatively, report the five-league rank with each nation's home-league players excluded.
findings.note: q1 headline by_league: FIN Liiga 314 of 425, SWE SHL 251 of 408, CHE NL 233 of 248, DEU DEL 189 of 198. CZE has 53 with no Extraliga, because line 90 defines the Extraliga as the home league outside the five. Neither line 99 nor Limits mentions the asymmetry. It also feeds the q3 cohort medians at line 109, which use rung 1+2 players.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:54 facts "most probable season of the fall 2009/10 · posterior probability 0.09 · level ×0.83, 90 % HDI 0.56–1.14"; line 104
findings.problem: The fall step's 90% interval includes 1 (no change), and its modal season holds only 9% of the probability. Even so, a fall season is a headline fact in the facts box. The body describes the step as 'the fall' without saying that its interval includes no step at all. The rise is reported the same way: "The model dates a rise to 1998/99 (... 90 % HDI 0.73–1.97)" also has an interval that includes 1.
findings.evidence: q2_break_model.json CZE steps: step 1 delta_factor 0.728–1.970, p_down 0.147; step 2 delta_factor 0.561–1.140, p_down 0.804, modal prob 0.093.
findings.fix: Drop the 'most probable season of the fall' fact, or relabel it, e.g. "no single fall season: the most probable, 2009/10, holds 9 %, and the step's 90 % interval (×0.56–1.14) includes no change". In the body, write "the model's first step is most likely in 1998/99, though its interval includes no change" instead of "dates a rise".
findings.note: Narrowed. For the fall, the body does give P(lower) 0.80 and says 87 % of the probability is spread over 2008/09–2023/24, so the body's treatment of the fall is adequate. 'The model dates a rise to 1998/99' is overstated: the modal probability is 0.39, the HDI 0.73–1.97 includes 1, and P(up) 0.853 is not stated. The facts-box part duplicates finding 5.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:104 "The fitted level is 23.1, 43 % of its 2002/03 peak of 53.1."
findings.problem: The fitted level is computed with the breaks fixed at one pair of seasons (1998/99, 2009/10), and that pair has a joint probability of only 0.04. The text presents it as the model's level, marginalised over break seasons like the rest of the model, and does not say it depends on that pair.
findings.evidence: q2_break_model.json CZE fitted.at_pair = ["1998/99","2009/10"]; top_candidates[0] prob 0.041.
findings.fix: "Holding the steps at the most probable pair (1998/99 and 2009/10, joint probability 0.04), the fitted level is 23.1, 43 % of its 2002/03 peak of 53.1."
findings.note: q2 CZE fitted.at_pair is ['1998/99','2009/10'], and top_candidates[0] has prob 0.041. Fitted median values: last 23.1, max 53.095 at index 7 (2002/03). Line 104 does not say the level is conditional on that pair.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:62 tldr "The per-head ranks hold under other thresholds; the dating of the decline does not."
findings.problem: The body never tests the dating of the decline under other thresholds, so this sentence has nothing to rest on. The body shows only that the posterior over the fall season is diffuse. The short version also states none of the decline numbers (58 → 20) and does not say what would overturn the result.
findings.evidence: Line 127 tests threshold sensitivity only for the 2025/26 ranks. q1/q2 outputs hold no threshold sensitivity for the break model.
findings.fix: Replace it with: "Czech NHL players fell from 58 in 2001/02 to 20 in 2025/26, a gradual decline: the model cannot date a single break (the most probable season holds 9 %). The rank rests on league-published nationality and Eurostat population; it holds when any NHL game counts."
findings.note: Line 62 sets 'the per-head ranks hold under other thresholds' against 'the dating of the decline does not', which implies the dating was tested under thresholds. The q1/q2 outputs hold no threshold sensitivity for the break model, and the body (line 104) shows only that the posterior is diffuse. The rest of the proposed rewrite is optional.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:90 "at least 20 of 82 games, pro-rated to the league-season's schedule, the 95th percentile of skater games"
findings.problem: As written, the sentence says 20 games is the 95th percentile of skater games played, which cannot be right. A reader cannot tell how the threshold was derived (for example, whether 95 % of skater games come from players above it).
findings.evidence: q1_per_million.json definitions.threshold uses the same ambiguous phrase "(95th percentile of skater games played)".
findings.fix: State the rule explicitly, e.g. "20 games, the cut that keeps the players who together account for 95 % of skater games" (if that is what the code does), and check the wording against the atlas code.
findings.note: Same ambiguity as finding 3 (line 90, and q1 definitions.threshold). Its proposed fix is wrong: common.py uses the 95th percentile of games played to estimate the schedule length, not as a 95 %-of-games cut. Use finding 3's fix.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:109 "No Czech player aged 21 or under" / "forwards aged 21 or under" vs line 117 "Under-21 here means aged 20 or less"
findings.problem: 'Under-21' has two meanings in adjacent paragraphs: aged 21 or under in the cohort shortfall, and aged 20 or less in the ice-time table and the facts box.
findings.evidence: Line 109 uses '21 or under' twice; line 117 defines under-21 as 20 or less; the line 53 facts label says 'under-21'.
findings.fix: Use one label per definition, e.g. 'U21 (aged 20 or less)' for the ice-time table and facts, and 'aged 21 or under' for the cohort paragraph, with the definition placed before the table, not after it.
findings.note: Duplicate of finding 4. Line 109 uses '21 or under' (q3 band ≤21), while the facts box at line 53 and the table caption say 'under-21' and line 117 defines that as 20 or less, placed after the table.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:54, 94, 104, 127 (HDI, posterior probability, Poisson local-level model, step changes 'marginalised', R-hat, divergent transition, 'level ×0.83')
findings.problem: These central model terms are used without explanation at first use. 'HDI' appears in the facts box before the model is introduced. 'Level ×0.83' is never glossed as the level after the step divided by the level before. R-hat and 'divergent transition' are given with no hint of what a good value is.
findings.evidence: Line 54 first uses HDI and 'level ×0.83'; line 94 is the only sentence on the model; line 127 gives R-hat 1.007 and one divergence without explanation. The q2 definitions.delta_factor gloss is not carried into the text.
findings.fix: At line 94 add: "It treats each season's count as noisy around a slowly drifting level and lets that level jump twice, averaging over which seasons the jumps fall in; '×0.83' means the level after a jump is 0.83 times the level before, and the 90 % HDI is the range holding the most credible 90 % of values." At line 127 add "(R-hat near 1 means the chains agree)".
findings.note: In texts/hockey.html, HDI (lines 54, 104), 'level ×' and R-hat/divergent (line 127) are never glossed. q2 definitions.delta_factor ('level after the step divided by level before') is not carried into the text. football.html uses the same unglossed convention, so this is site-wide.

findings.location: texts/hockey.html:109 "The largest shortfall against the peer median is forwards aged 21 or under, 6.1 players"
findings.problem: The unit and construction of the 'shortfall' are unclear. It is given in players (6.1), yet the peer median is a per-million rate, presumably rescaled to Czech population. The next sentence switches to per-million figures, and the 'median of 0' for defencemen aged 30 or over is left unexplained.
findings.evidence: Line 109 mixes '6.1 players' with '1.37 per million against 0.66' and gives no definition.
findings.fix: "Shortfall = (peer median per million − Czech rate) × Czech population, in players."
findings.note: q3 definitions.shortfall = '(peer median - Czechia) per million x Czech population'. Line 109 gives '6.1 players' and then switches to per-million figures ('0.66', 'median of 0') with no definition in the text. Low severity.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:104 and table rows 108-113, "not supported when the 95 % bootstrap interval lies wholly on the other side of the threshold"
findings.problem: The registered reading rules call for 95 % bootstrap intervals on statistics the verifiers never compute. Prague 2 needs a "BSS against climatology with its interval above 0", but no BSS interval exists. The rules also need intervals on Klementinum bias, on the paired MAE differences (Prague 3), on Spearman rho and the spread share (Surf 1), and on the share of positive errors (Surf 3). So under the current code most claims can never be labelled "not supported", and Prague 2 cannot be read at all as written.
findings.evidence: weather/verify.py:134 computes only mae_tmax_ci; the ensemble block (lines 156-178) has brier/bss but no CI and no paired model differences. surf/verify.py:195-197 computes only mae_swell_ci95 and p_surfable_given_yes_ci95. grep for 'paired|diff' in both verifiers finds nothing.
findings.fix: Either state in the text that only the MAE intervals exist so far and that the other claims are read on point estimates (supported or inconclusive only), or list the missing intervals (BSS, bias, paired MAE difference, rho, spread share, positive-error share) next to the eight-week rule as not yet coded.
findings.note: surf/verify.py only bootstraps mae_swell_ci95 (l.195) and p_surfable_given_yes_ci95 (l.197). weather/verify.py only has mae_tmax_ci (l.134). The ensemble blocks have BSS but no CI, and no paired differences exist. So the Prague 2 rule 'BSS interval above 0' cannot be evaluated.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:85, "takes swell, wave height and wind from three wave models (Météo-France MFWAM, DWD GWAM, DWD EWAM)"
findings.problem: Wind does not come from the three wave models. The collector takes it from a separate Open-Meteo Forecast API call (single default model), shared by all three wave models.
findings.evidence: surf/collect.py:79-89: the marine call takes wave variables with models=MFWAM,GWAM,EWAM, and a separate WEATHER call takes wind_speed_10m/wind_direction_10m with no model list. docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-14-surf-forecast-design.md:12-13 lists the wind source separately as well.
findings.fix: "takes swell and wave height from three wave models (...) and 10 m wind from the Open-Meteo Forecast API".
findings.note: surf/collect.py fetch_forecast: wind comes from a separate WEATHER call with no models param and is attached to every wave model. The spec at l.12-13 lists it separately as well.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:85, "its mean period at least 8 s"
findings.problem: The surf design spec registers a different period threshold (mean period >= 9 s) from the one the article and code use (8 s). The article does not disclose the change, and it presents 9 s only as a robustness alternative (8.5 %).
findings.evidence: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-14-surf-forecast-design.md:32-33: "Surfable (v1, adjustable): daily max swell height 1.0–2.5 m, mean period >= 9 s"; surf/verify.py:42 RULE p=8.0, which is also 8.0 at commit 425195f.
findings.fix: Add one clause, e.g. "(the design note of 14 September 2026 said 9 s; the code used 8 s from the first run)", or correct the spec.
findings.note: The spec says 'mean period >= 9 s' while the code says RULE p=8.0. Both were committed together in 425195f (14 Sep 22:17), and the text does not disclose the difference.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:123, r4 "Richardson, D. S. (2000) ... Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society 126."
findings.problem: The reference is missing its issue and page range.
findings.evidence: Crossref for 10.1002/qj.49712656313: volume 126, issue 563, pages 649-667, published 2000-01. The DOI resolves (302 to rmets.onlinelibrary.wiley.com).
findings.fix: "... Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society 126(563), 649–667."
findings.note: Crossref returns volume 126, issue 563, pages 649-667. The reference gives only '126'.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:85, "the live page turns the probability of such a day into a booking rule, treating each day of a trip as surfable with the same probability<sup>4</sup>"
findings.problem: The citation sits on the simplification (every trip day has the same probability), which is the page's own assumption, not something Richardson (2000) states. Richardson supports only the cost-loss/economic-value framing of a probability-based decision.
findings.evidence: Richardson 2000 (QJRMS 126:649-667) covers the skill and relative economic value of the ECMWF EPS in a cost-loss framework. It says nothing about multi-day trips or equal daily probabilities.
findings.fix: Move the citation to "turns the probability of such a day into a booking rule<sup>4</sup>" and leave the equal-probability clause uncited, as the author's own simplification.
findings.note: The sup 4 marker sits at the end of the equal-probability clause. That clause is the author's own simplification; Richardson 2000 covers cost-loss economic value, not multi-day trips.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:91, "with period, minimum temperature, precipitation and Spearman's rank correlation alongside"
findings.problem: The sentence reads as if both verifiers compute Spearman's rank correlation, but only the surf verifier does. The Prague verifier has no rank correlation.
findings.evidence: grep 'spearman' finds it only in surf/verify.py:63,194. weather/verify.py:132-140 computes MAE/bias/RMSE tmax, MAE/bias tmin, precipitation MAE/bias and the contingency table.
findings.fix: "... with period and Spearman's rank correlation (surf), minimum temperature and precipitation (Prague) alongside."

findings.problem: The count of 6 + 6 = 12 is right, but the live Prague page this article links to still says five tests, so the two pages contradict each other.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:40, JSON-LD "image": "https://bsandova.com/assets/og/surf.jpg"
findings.problem: The structured-data image differs from the og:image and twitter:image (assets/og/forecast-verification.jpg). It is left over from the pre-merge surf page.

findings.fix: Set the JSON-LD image to https://bsandova.com/assets/og/forecast-verification.jpg.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:85-86 and :94 "The surf instrument runs at 06:10 UTC" / "The Prague instrument runs at 06:40 UTC" / "the rain window closes at 06:00 UTC, before the run"
findings.problem: The run times are the cron schedule, not when forecasts are actually fetched. The collectors run about 5 to 8 hours late. So 'issue time' is really early afternoon UTC: lead-0 temperature and surf daylight windows are mostly past, and lead-1 forecasts come from later model cycles than the text implies. The lead-0 reasoning and the claim that persistence uses only values known at issue time both rely on the 06:xx timing, and nothing says the timing varies.
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/surf.yml:4 cron "10 6 * * *", weather.yml:4 cron "40 6 * * *"; `git log -- weather/data/forecasts surf/data/forecasts` commit hours: 12 at 11 UTC, 9 at 12, 6 at 13, 1 at 14, 1 at 15, and only 3 before 09 UTC (e.g. weather-collector 2026-09-28 14:26:13 +0000, surf 2026-10-01 13:02:09 +0000). The forecast JSON files store no fetch timestamp.
findings.fix: State that the jobs are scheduled at 06:10/06:40 UTC but have run between about 07 and 15 UTC (mostly 11 to 14). Record the fetch time (or the model run time) in each forecast file, and define issue time from it. Re-examine the lead-0 rule with the real run times, and say that lead-1 skill reflects later model cycles than a 06 UTC user would see.
findings.note: The crons are 10 6 and 40 6, but commit hours touching the forecasts dirs (UTC) are mostly 11-13 (12/9/7) with only 3 before 09. Forecast JSON 'issued' holds only a date such as '2026-10-02', with no fetch time. Caveat: commit time is a proxy for fetch time.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:104 "supported when the condition holds, not supported when the 95 % bootstrap interval lies wholly on the other side of the threshold, inconclusive otherwise"
findings.problem: The reading rule is lopsided. A point estimate on the predicted side is enough for 'supported', but 'not supported' needs the whole interval on the other side. At 30 pairs over 8 weeks the intervals will be wide, so a claim can almost never be refuted, only supported or left inconclusive. Prague 2's 'about zero by lead 6', read as 'interval containing 0', makes the same mistake: a wide interval counts as a hit, so absence of evidence is scored as support.
findings.evidence: Text line 104 and table rows lines 108-113. Prague 2 rule (line 112): "containing 0 at lead 6". With n≈30 and 8 weekly blocks, intervals on a BSS or a share will usually straddle any threshold.
findings.fix: Make the rule symmetric: supported only when the interval lies wholly on the predicted side, refuted when it lies wholly on the other side, inconclusive otherwise. For 'about zero', state an equivalence margin (e.g. interval within ±0.1).
findings.note: Line 104: 'supported when the condition holds' uses the point estimate, while 'not supported' requires the whole interval on the other side. Prague 2 scores 'interval containing 0 at lead 6' as a hit, so a wide interval counts as support.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:93 and :104-113 "Intervals come from a block bootstrap by ISO week" / reading rules that use "the 95 % bootstrap interval"
findings.problem: The reading rules need intervals the code never computes. The verifiers bootstrap only the MAE of swell height, P(surfable | yes) and the Prague tmax MAE. There is no interval on Spearman's ρ, on the spread shares (≤0.3 m, >0.5 m), on the share of positive errors, on bias, on the BSS or Brier differences, or on the paired MAE differences of Prague 3. The verifier computes no spread share and no paired difference at all. The text discloses only the eight-week rule as 'not yet in the code'.
findings.evidence: surf/verify.py:195,197 (only mae_swell_ci95 and p_surfable_given_yes_ci95); weather/verify.py:134 (only mae_tmax_ci); the ensemble block weather/verify.py:167-178 has no bootstrap; surf quality computes only disagreement_gt_1m (surf/verify.py:240-248), not the 0.3/0.5 m spread shares.
findings.fix: Next to the 'fourth rule is not yet in the code' sentence, add: 'Neither are the intervals, spread shares and paired differences the reading rules use; until they are coded, only Surf 2's MAE and Prague 1 can be read from the live output.' Or implement them before the reading dates.
findings.note: Same code check as [0]. Surf quality has no 0.3/0.5 m spread-share metric (only swell_max_spread per day), and there are no paired differences. The text marks only the eight-week rule as not yet in the code.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:85 "A day is surfable when ... its mean period at least 8 s"
findings.problem: The design spec written the same day sets the surfable rule at mean period ≥ 9 s. The code and the published text use 8 s, and no deviation is disclosed. The change came after the 92-day back-fill was visible, and at 9 s the summer base rate was about 2 % (the changelog lists 2 % as an alternative). Changing a threshold after seeing data needs a note.
findings.evidence: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-14-surf-forecast-design.md: "'Surfable' (v1, adjustable): daily max swell height 1.0–2.5 m, mean period ≥ 9 s"; surf/verify.py:42 RULE p=8.0; f815c6b:texts/surf.html already says 8 s and "Only eleven of the 92 days had a mean period of 8 s or more".
findings.fix: Add one sentence and a changelog entry: 'The design of 14 September set the period at 9 s; it was lowered to 8 s before publication, after the 92-day analysis showed about 2 % of days clearing 9 s.' Keep 9 s as the named robustness variant.
findings.note: The spec/code discrepancy (9 s vs 8 s) is real and undisclosed. However, the spec and the 8 s code were committed in the same commit 425195f, so the claim that the threshold was changed after seeing the back-fill cannot be shown from git.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:85 "forecast and truth share a model family" and :91 "The share f_i of models calling the event"; table rows :108-110
findings.problem: For MFWAM, the surf truth is the same model's own analysis, so MFWAM is not just 'the same family': it is self-verification. The verifier flags this (self_verification), but the text does not. MFWAM is still included in the Surf 1 ρ>0.9 'every model' test, in the Surf 2 and 3 MAE and sign tests, and as one of the voters in the Brier share. EWAM is empty beyond lead 3, so at leads 4 to 6 the 'share of models' is a two-model vote that can only be 0, 0.5 or 1. The Surf 2 'spread' at leads 5 to 6 is likewise a two-model spread, not three.
findings.evidence: surf/verify.py:40 TRUTH_MODEL="meteofrance_wave", :187 self_verification flag; :184 votes include every model with a non-null value; text line 99: "EWAM, which returns nothing beyond lead 3, has 43 % empty cells".
findings.fix: State: 'MFWAM is scored against its own analysis (self-verification); GWAM and EWAM are the cross-model tests.' In the Surf 1 to 3 rules, either drop MFWAM or report it separately, and say that at leads 4 to 6 the vote share and spread come from MFWAM and GWAM only.
findings.note: TRUTH_MODEL is meteofrance_wave and the self_verification flag is set at l.187. The text says only 'share a model family'. Votes append whatever records exist (l.184), so with EWAM empty beyond lead 3 the share comes from 2 models at leads 4-6.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:91 "its skill against climatology and persistence"
findings.problem: The surf climatology reference is never described; only Prague's (1991–2020, ±15 days) is. In the code, the surf climatology is one constant: the in-sample surfable share over the whole analysis file. That window starts in mid-June, so it is dominated by summer (nortada) days, and it includes the target days being verified. For autumn targets this is a poorly matched reference that can inflate BSS against climatology.
findings.evidence: surf/verify.py:145 surfable_share over all analysis days; :205 base = that share used for every target; surf/data.json climatology ericeira: 110 days, 2026-06-14 to 2026-10-01, share 0.145.
findings.fix: Add: 'For surf, climatology is the share of surfable days in the back-filled analysis since 14 June (in-sample, summer-weighted), not a seasonal reference; skill against it is optimistic for autumn targets.' Or use a trailing or out-of-sample base rate.
findings.note: l.145: surfable_share is computed over all analysis days. l.205: that share is used as the base for every target, so it is in-sample, the window starts 14 June, and the text never describes the surf climatology.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:94 "all twelve tests pass"
findings.problem: The sentence sits next to the three corrections and suggests they are tested. No test checks any of them: persistence at issue − 1, no precipitation score at lead 0, or the ensemble excluding best_match. The weather test world contains only best_match and icon_seamless, so after the fix its 'ensemble' is a single model.
findings.evidence: grep of surf/tests/test_verify.py and weather/tests/test_verify.py: no assertion on persistence dates, lead-0 mae_precip absence or ensemble membership; weather/tests/test_verify.py:19 models = ["best_match", "icon_seamless"].
findings.fix: Say 'the twelve existing tests still pass; none tests the three corrections directly', or add tests for them.
findings.note: Neither test file asserts persistence dates, the absence of lead-0 precip or ensemble membership. weather test models are ['best_match','icon_seamless'] (l.19).

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:91 "with period, minimum temperature, precipitation and Spearman's rank correlation alongside"
findings.problem: The sentence implies Spearman's correlation is computed for both instruments, but weather/verify.py computes none. It also leaves out that the Prague verifier computes temperature MAE against climatology and persistence.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:85 "Its truth is the MFWAM analysis of the target day"
findings.problem: 'Analysis' is the central term of the surf half (the truth) and is never explained. A reader does not know it means the model's best estimate of the current sea state, assimilated from observations, rather than a measurement. The design spec explains it; the article does not.
findings.evidence: First use at line 85; no gloss anywhere in the text.
findings.fix: 'Its truth is the MFWAM analysis of the target day: the model's own best reconstruction of that day's sea state, not a measurement.'
findings.note: Line 85 introduces 'MFWAM analysis' without a gloss, and no definition appears elsewhere in the article.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:91-93, :99
findings.problem: Many technical terms appear without explanation at first use: lead day (line 49/85), MAE, bias, RMSE (line 91), Spearman's rank correlation (91), probability of detection and false-alarm ratio (91), persistence (91, only defined at 94), climatology for surf (91), block bootstrap by ISO week (93), 'descriptive' (93), 'the gate' (99, never named as a term), spread (108), lapse-rate correction (86), best_match (86).

findings.note: MAE, RMSE, POD/FAR, block bootstrap, 'descriptive' and 'the gate' are undefined at first use. Persistence is explained only at line 94, after its first use at line 91. This is an editorial judgement, and a few items (best_match, lapse-rate) are partly glossed in context.

findings.location: texts/forecast-verification.html:58-66 details.tldr
findings.problem: The short version gives the truth source but not its consequence: surf scores will look better than against a buoy. It does not say what the six predictions rest on, or what outcome would count against them. 'no number shown before changed' is ambiguous next to a changelog listing several changed numbers (base rate, test count, caption). The most useful practical sentence for a visitor to the live pages, that no interval shown there should be read yet, is buried in line 94.

'Six predictions, each with a pass/fail rule, are read once 30 pairs span eight weeks (November).' 'Until then, no interval on the live pages should be read.' 'The three corrections of 29 September changed no published skill number (none had passed the gate).'

findings.problem: This is stated as fact, but it is an expectation. Analysis-based truth usually flatters the error scores, but the text has no buoy comparison to show that it does here.

findings.location: texts/cutover.html:96 "about 3.3 million trips in one parquet file"
findings.problem: The parquet file holds about 3.48 million trips, not 3.3 million. 3.3 million is the count left after the demo drops non-positive fares, so the sentence gives the post-filter count as the file size. The Limits section (line 122, "7 280 aggregated rows built from about 3.3 million trips") is right, because there the filtered count is the one meant.

The worked-example sentence calls the file's size 'about 3.3 million trips', which is the count after filtering. The Limits sentence ('built from about 3.3 million trips') is fine.

findings.location: texts/cutover.html:96 "The legacy version ... converts miles to kilometres at the end ... declares an absolute tolerance of 10^−6 on kilometres for the different order of multiplication"
findings.problem: The stated reason for the km tolerance does not match the code. Both versions sum trip_distance first and then multiply by 1.609344 once (pandas: g["km"] = g["km"] * MILE; SQL: sum(trip_distance) * MILE), so the order of multiplication is the same. The km differences come from pandas and DuckDB summing floats in a different order or with a different algorithm. Saying only the legacy side converts "at the end" suggests the SQL side converts per row, which it does not.
findings.evidence: tools/demos/cutover_demo.py lines 35 and 45. Recomputed: km differs in 3,281 of 7,280 rows, max |diff| 4.2e-10, well inside 1e-6.
findings.fix: "declares an absolute tolerance of 10^−6 on kilometres, because pandas and DuckDB add floats in a different order (the largest difference in the demo is 4 × 10^−10)", and drop "converts miles to kilometres at the end" or say both versions do it.
findings.note: cutover_demo.py: legacy does g['km']*MILE after groupby sum; new does sum(trip_distance)*MILE. Both convert after summing, so the order of multiplication is the same. Recomputed km: 3,277 rows differ, max 4.22e-10. The count varies by about 0-4 between runs because DuckDB's parallel sum is not deterministic, so any fix should not print an exact km count.

findings.location: texts/cutover.html:105 "Across all 343 rows the largest absolute difference is 3.6 × 10^−12"; line 114 "Re-running ... 10^−9 gave PASS, and with 10^−12 it gave FAIL"
findings.problem: No published artefact supports these numbers. report-1.json holds only 20 fare samples, whose largest difference is about 1e-13, and the 29 September re-runs with 10^−9 and 10^−12 were not saved. A reader cannot check either claim from the reports the article points to. The values themselves are correct.
findings.evidence: assets/cutover/report-1.json samples max |old-new| is about 1.1e-13 (zone 82, 995.82). Recomputed from the parquet: fare max |diff| = 3.637978807091713e-12 over 343 mismatches, so 1e-9 passes and 1e-12 fails, consistent with the text.
findings.fix: Have the demo script print or save the max fare difference and the two re-runs (for example a report-tol.json), or say these numbers come from re-running the demo and are not in the published reports.
findings.note: report-1.json columns.fare holds only 20 samples (e.g. 995.82 vs 995.8199999999999, diff ~1e-13) and no max-diff field. No file for the 1e-9/1e-12 re-runs exists in assets/cutover/ (only report-1/2 plus a stale report.html/json). Recomputed max fare diff = 3.637978807091713e-12 over 343 rows, so the numbers are right but cannot be checked from the published files.

findings.location: texts/cutover.html:91 "The sixth step is the verdict: PASS only when the schema is clean, the key is unique, neither side has keys the other lacks, ..."
findings.problem: The PASS conditions leave out NULL keys. The code adds reason key_nulls when either side has a NULL key, so a table with a unique key that contains a NULL still fails. The list as written suggests it would pass.
findings.evidence: ~/Documents/Coding/cutover/src/cutover/compare.py: `if keys.old_nulls or keys.new_nulls: reasons.append("key_nulls")`; passed = not reasons.

findings.location: texts/cutover.html:154 r8 "design in the spec" (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-14-cutover-design.md)
findings.problem: The cited design spec contradicts the article on two method points without saying so. It gives the tolerance as abs(a-b) <= abs_tol + rel_tol*abs(b), the summed form the change log says was corrected. It also says time-zone-aware timestamps are compared as UTC instants, but the article (line 92) and the code treat different time zones as a type change. A reader who follows r8 finds a method that differs from the page.

findings.fix: In r8, add "(pre-release design; the tolerance and time-zone handling differ in 0.1.0, as described above)", or update the spec.
findings.note: Spec line 57 gives `abs(a-b) <= abs_tol + rel_tol*abs(b)`, the summed form the change log says was corrected. Spec line 91 says tz-aware timestamps are compared as UTC instants, which contradicts the article's 'time zones are a type change'. r8 links the spec with no caveat. Duplicates the time-zone point in #12.

findings.location: texts/cutover.html:130 "The script downloads the 59 MB parquet file"
findings.problem: The demo script's own docstring says "~50 MB" and says it writes report.{html,json}, which conflicts with the article's 59 MB and with the report-1 and report-2 files the article links. The article is right (59.16 MB), but the source it tells readers to run says otherwise.
findings.evidence: tools/demos/cutover_demo.py docstring lines 1-6; ls -la tools/data/yellow_tripdata_2025-01.parquet = 59,158,238 bytes.
findings.fix: Correct the script docstring to "~59 MB" and report-1/report-2.{html,json}. The article needs no change.
findings.note: The docstring says '~50 MB' and 'writes assets/cutover/report.{html,json}'. The code writes report-1/report-2, and the file is 59,158,238 bytes. The fix belongs in the script docstring, not the article. Also, stale assets/cutover/report.html and report.json are still present.

findings.location: texts/cutover.html:107 "declares an absolute tolerance of 10^−6 on kilometres for the different order of multiplication"
findings.problem: The stated reason for the km tolerance is wrong. Both pipelines sum trip_distance first and multiply by the mile factor afterwards, so the order of multiplication is the same. The real difference is pandas versus DuckDB summation order. The text also never says that this tolerance, set before the first run, hides 3 280 exact km mismatches. That is ten times as many as the 343 fare mismatches the article reports as a finding.
findings.evidence: tools/demos/cutover_demo.py: legacy does groupby sum, then g["km"] * MILE. new does sum(trip_distance) * MILE. Both multiply after the sum, despite line 107 saying the legacy 'converts miles to kilometres at the end' as if only it did. I re-ran both aggregates on tools/data/yellow_tripdata_2025-01.parquet: km has 3 280 of 7 280 rows not exactly equal, max abs diff 4.2e-10; fare has 343 not equal, max 3.64e-12.
findings.fix: Change to: "declares an absolute tolerance of 10^−6 on kilometres, because pandas and DuckDB add the distances in a different order; without it, 3 280 rows differ in km by at most 4.2 × 10^−10." Also correct the legacy description: both versions convert to kilometres after summing.
findings.note: Duplicate of #1 on the multiplication order: confirmed from the code. The point about km mismatches being hidden is also true: about 3,277-3,281 rows differ at max 4.2e-10 against 343 for fare. Use 'about 3 300' or 'over 3 000', not an exact count, because it is not deterministic.

findings.location: texts/cutover.html:61 facts card "33 / 33 daily partitions with identical fingerprints" and :121
findings.problem: The headline 33/33 fingerprint result covers only day, zone and trips. Fare and km both carry tolerances, so the fingerprints leave them out. The 33/33 figure therefore says nothing about the two money and distance columns. The facts card, the run-2 paragraph and the TL;DR never say this, so a reader takes 33/33 as a full-row identity.
findings.evidence: assets/cutover/report-2.json: partitions.excluded_columns = ["fare","km"]. compare.py _partitions: hashed = key + columns without a tolerance. Line 101 states the general rule, but lines 61, 121 and 122 never apply it to the demo.
findings.fix: Change the facts card to: "33 / 33 daily partitions with identical fingerprints over day, zone and trips (fare and km, compared within tolerance, are not hashed)". Add the same clause after the run-2 output.
findings.note: report-2.json partitions.excluded_columns = ['fare','km']. The fingerprint paragraph states the general rule (tolerance columns are left out of the hash), but the facts card, the run-2 output and the run-2 paragraph never say that 33/33 covers only day, zone and trips.

findings.location: texts/cutover.html:122 "any difference below half a cent is rounding and any larger one is a real change"
findings.problem: The half-cent tolerance was chosen after the 343 mismatches were seen, and it is about 10^9 times larger than the largest difference actually observed (3.6e-12). The article's own re-run shows that 10^−9 also passes. With fare left out of the fingerprint, run 2 cannot detect a real fare change below 0.005 per zone-day. The text presents 0.005 as the intended contract and does not mention this blind spot.
findings.evidence: My recomputation gives max fare diff 3.64e-12. Line 122 reports that 1e-9 passes. report-2.json excludes fare from the fingerprints.
findings.fix: Add: "The tolerance was set after run 1. Any genuine fare change smaller than half a cent per zone and day would also pass; a tolerance of 10^−9 passes too and leaves less room."
findings.note: The text calls 0.005 'the intended contract' but it was declared in run 2, after the 343 mismatches. Fare is in report-2 excluded_columns, so fingerprints do not cover it. The article's own re-run shows 1e-9 passes. A real fare change of less than half a cent per zone-day would pass, and this is not stated. Low severity, because the run sequence is visible.

findings.location: texts/cutover.html:64-71 details.tldr
findings.problem: The short version leaves out the main practical limit: the tool has never run on more than 7 280 aggregated rows, so the scale at which it stays practical is unknown. It also does not say that the demo's PASS needed a tolerance declared after the first run. Both points appear only in the Limits section and in the run-2 paragraph.
findings.evidence: Line 132: 'no benchmark on larger inputs has been made, so the size at which the tool stops being practical is unknown.' The TL;DR's 4 bullets say nothing about scale or tolerances.
findings.fix: Add a bullet: "Its largest run so far is 7 280 rows; behaviour on large tables is untested. The demo passed only after a half-cent fare tolerance was declared."

findings.location: texts/quotecheck.html:98 "FOUND* means the phrase occurs as two adjacent halves ... at most twelve folded characters between them ... a splice of two fragments from different parts of a book fails because the halves are not adjacent"; also deck line 56 and meta description line 7 "tolerant of extraction noise but not of rewording"
findings.problem: The FOUND* rule accepts any quotation that leaves out up to 12 folded characters from the middle of a source sentence, as long as each remaining half is at least 12 characters. Dropping a negation or qualifier ("not", "never", "only", "no longer") is a rewording that turns the meaning around, and the tool reports it as FOUND*. FOUND* counts as found: Match.ok is True and the CLI exits 0. The article says only that distant splices fail. It never mentions that short omissions pass, so the deck's claim that the tool is 'not tolerant of rewording' says more than the code does.
findings.evidence: src/quotecheck/find.py:58-65 (interleaved branch: prefix found, remainder within MAX_GAP=12, which returns status 'interleaved'), find.py:24-25 (ok includes 'interleaved'), cli.py:67 (exit 0 if all ok). Run: check('the committee concluded that the new procedure is safe for routine clinical use in children', 'The committee concluded that the new procedure is not safe for routine clinical use in children.') -> status='interleaved', similarity=1.0. Likewise 'Officials said the bridge would be reopened...' against '...would never be reopened...' -> 'interleaved'. The only test of this rule (tests/test_fold_and_find.py:69-72) covers a splice whose halves are far apart.
findings.fix: In Method (line 98), add: "Because the gap may hold any twelve folded characters, a quotation that silently drops a short word from the middle of a sentence, such as 'not' or 'never', is also reported FOUND*. The context line shows the dropped text, and a FOUND* should be read before it is accepted." Repeat this in Limits (line 127) and soften the deck to "tolerant of extraction noise; it reports rewording as DRIFT, except that a short omission inside a sentence passes as FOUND*". A better option is to change the code so FOUND* requires the gap to be digits or punctuation, or a known running head, and to add a test for an omitted 'not'.
findings.note: Reproduced at v0.1.0. check('the committee concluded that the new procedure is safe for routine clinical use in children', '...is not safe...') returns status='interleaved', similarity=1.0. In find.py, ok counts interleaved as found, and the CLI exits 0. The article and the deck ('not of rewording') never say that a short omission inside a sentence passes as FOUND*. The only test of this rule covers halves that are far apart.

findings.location: texts/quotecheck.html:98 "FOUND* means the phrase occurs as two adjacent halves"
findings.problem: The code tests only one split: the longest prefix that occurs anywhere, at its first occurrence. If that prefix also appears earlier in the source, or the remainder is not adjacent to that first occurrence, the search stops (the 'break') and no shorter split is tried. A genuine quotation interrupted by a page number can then fall to DRIFT or ABSENT, which is a false alarm of the kind the article says the rules exist to prevent. The text describes a general search for two adjacent halves.
findings.evidence: src/quotecheck/find.py:58-65: ja = flat.find(needle[:h]) (first occurrence only); after the first prefix is found, the loop breaks whether or not the remainder matched.
findings.fix: Either describe it accurately in Limits ("FOUND* tries only the longest matching opening and its first occurrence, so an interrupted quotation whose opening words recur earlier in the book can be missed") or change the loop to try every occurrence and every split.
findings.note: Reproduced. In find.py, the loop takes the first occurrence of the longest matching prefix and then breaks. A source that holds 'If a man has any genuine talent he should be ready.' earlier, followed by the genuine '...he 4 should be ready to make almost any sacrifice...', returns status='absent' for the Hardy quotation. That is a false alarm on a genuine interrupted quotation, and the article does not mention it.

findings.location: texts/quotecheck.html:98 "In batch mode the tool extracts every blockquote line and every quoted run of six or more words"
findings.problem: Batch extraction is narrower than described. Inline quotations count only inside double quotation marks (straight or curly), not single marks. Blockquotes are checked line by line, and any blockquote line under six words is skipped. A multi-line blockquote is never checked as one passage, so a quotation spliced across two lines of a blockquote is checked as two separate pieces that may each pass.
findings.evidence: src/quotecheck/batch.py:17-18 (_INLINE matches only ["“]...["”] with at least 20 characters; _BLOCK matches one line), batch.py:31 (blockquote lines under MIN_WORDS skipped).

findings.note: The overlap with [2] is confirmed (double quotes only, at least 20 characters, blockquote lines need 6+ words). The new point is also confirmed: _BLOCK uses ^...$ with re.M, so each blockquote line is checked on its own and a multi-line blockquote is never checked as one passage. A splice across two lines could pass as two separate FOUND results.

findings.location: texts/ai-over-data.html:83 "over 5 794 answers the silent-failure rate ranges from 56 % to 92 % depending on the model and the pack [7]"
findings.problem: The 56–92 % range does not come from the Quaesitor pages that r7 cites, and it is not computed over 5 794 answers. The Quaesitor measurements page publishes per-model silent-failure rates of 20 % to 80 % per warehouse (Table 2, share of cells including declined answers). The 56–92 % figure is from the silent-detector data (assets/detector/detector.json). That figure divides silently wrong answers by numeric answers only (correct plus silently wrong), over the 3 704 training answers. It also mixes two levels of grouping: 56 % is the lowest pooled pack rate (medallion 0.557, per_pack) and 92 % is the highest model-configuration rate (opus-docs 0.925, by_alias). Broken down by model and pack, answers.csv gives 50 % to 92.5 % (opus/medallion 0.50, opus-docs/ecommerce 0.925). Over all 5 794 answers the silent share is 3 839 / 5 794 = 66 %.
findings.evidence: grep finds no '56 %' or '92 %' in texts/quaesitor/*.html. texts/quaesitor/measurements.html:70 says 'silent-failure rates ran from 20 % to 80 % per model', and Table 2 at lines 111-118 gives 70/58, 67/40, 50/20, 80/70, 55/50. In detector.json, per_pack.medallion.silent_rate = 0.5566, by_alias['opus-docs'].silent_rate = 0.9248, trained_on = 3704, and per_pack n sums to 3704. silent-detector.html:98 carries the same 56–92 % sentence but cites detector.json (r8). Recomputing from answers.csv grouped by alias and pack gives a minimum of 0.50 and a maximum of 0.925.
findings.fix: Either cite the Quaesitor figure as published: 'across five warehouses the share of answers that were silently wrong ranged from 20 % to 80 % per model [7]'. Or keep the detector figure and attribute it correctly: 'of the 3 704 numeric answers, 56 % to 92 % were silently wrong depending on the pack or model configuration [8]'. Drop 'over 5 794 answers' from the rate sentence.
findings.note: No '56 %' or '92 %' on any texts/quaesitor/*.html page. measurements.html gives '20 % to 80 % per model'. The 56–92 sentence comes from silent-detector.html ('across packs and model configurations'). In detector.json, per_pack medallion = 0.557 (lowest pack) and by_alias opus-docs = 0.925 (highest alias), with trained_on = 3704 and answers = 5794. So the range mixes two groupings, uses the 3 704-answer denominator rather than 5 794, and is attributed to r7 instead of r8.

Calling it a 'public benchmark' overstates this.

findings.location: texts/ai-over-data.html:83 "Quaesitor, a public benchmark run on public models ... over 5 794 answers the silent-failure rate ranges from 56 % to 92 % depending on the model and the pack"
findings.problem: The page calls Quaesitor a public benchmark. Its own pages describe exploratory research that was not pre-registered, with data and code that are private and not verifiable, run by a service that is now retired. The 56–92 % range also leaves out the low-rate warehouses that the Quaesitor measurements page reports: 20 % to 80 % per model on 10 to 80 cells, too few to describe precisely. Because the range is quoted without the exploratory label or the small-cell caveat, it reads as a firm benchmark result.
findings.evidence: texts/quaesitor/measurements.html: "status: exploratory research; the service is retired", "registration: not pre-registered", "data ... (private; not verifiable)"; tldr: "silent-failure rates ran from 20 % to 80 % per model, on 10 to 80 cells each, which is too few for more than a description". The 56–92 % range comes from texts/silent-detector.html ("across packs and model configurations").
findings.fix: "Quaesitor, an exploratory harness I ran on commercial models rather than on the work system (not pre-registered; its run data are private) ... silent-failure rates ranged from 56 % to 92 % on the planted-trap packs, and from 20 % to 80 % on smaller warehouses with too few cells for more than a description."

findings.location: texts/ai-over-data.html:83 "A follow-up study found no run-time signal that separated wrong answers from right ones well (best held-out AUC 0.64)"

findings.location: texts/ai-over-data.html:76 "Each step is a typed node, so a run can be replayed from its trace" vs line 89 "Every run now writes fourteen fields ... and never a name or a raw tool output"
findings.problem: The two statements contradict each other. A trace that never stores raw tool outputs and keeps only 14 summary fields cannot replay a run, because the warehouse results each node consumed are missing. What the page can support is that the sequence of steps is reconstructable, not that the run can be replayed.
findings.evidence: Line 76 and line 89 as quoted. Neither the trace fields nor any other passage mentions storing tool outputs elsewhere.
findings.fix: Change to "so the sequence of steps and tools in a run can be reconstructed from its trace", or say where the inputs needed for a replay are kept.
findings.note: Line 76 says a run 'can be replayed from its trace'. Line 89 says traces never hold raw tool output. But line 89 lists the fourteen fields only partly ('among them'), so the SQL or the node inputs could be stored. Re-running the read-only queries would count as a replay without the raw outputs. The tension is real, but I could not confirm a contradiction.

findings.location: texts/brand-reflection.html:114 "Claim A is indeterminate: one of the three coherent spots is unmeasurable ... and the measurable totals, 3 813 for two coherent spots against 3 210 for two muddled ones, compare unequal sets."
findings.problem: The reason given for 'indeterminate' is partly wrong. View counts are cumulative, so Lidl's missing increment is at least 0. Adding it could only raise the coherent total above 3 813, which already beats 3 210. The missing spot therefore cannot reverse claim A's direction. What actually makes claim A indeterminate is the 119-day window instead of the registered 30 days, plus the unrecorded 30-day values.
findings.evidence: PREDICTIONS.md (fe5bb00), Claim A: the sum of increments of spots 1, 2 and 3 > the sum for spots 4 and 5. Table rows 108–112: 44 + 3 769 = 3 813 and 1 364 + 1 846 = 3 210, with Lidl Δ ≥ 0. The arithmetic and the 119-day count (18 May → 14 Sep) both check out.
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "Claim A is indeterminate: the check ran at 119 days instead of the registered 30, so the 30-day increments were never measured. The two measurable coherent spots gained 3 813 views against 3 210 for the muddled pair, and Lidl's missing increment could only add to the coherent side, but over the wrong window."
findings.note: Table: 44+3769=3813 vs 1364+1846=3210. Lidl's increment is >=0, so the missing spot cannot reverse A on the 119-day window. 'Compare unequal sets' is therefore not a valid reason for indeterminacy; only the window deviation (which the text also names) is.

findings.location: texts/delayed.html:63 facts 'source history 121 197 794 vehicle-location records' and line 87 'the same Golemio history of 121 197 794 vehicle-location records ... The record uses five days of it, counted as stop events'
findings.problem: The unit of the 121 197 794 figure contradicts the cited software. The repository README (r2) describes the same source period as '~121 million stop events'. The extraction script reads a stop-time table (stop_times_history_modeling), not vehicle positions. 121.2 M records over the 178 days from 15 March to 8 September is about 681 000 a day, which is the scale of the record's own daily stop-event totals (413 000-811 000). So the 121 M look like stop events, and the changelog's claim that 'vehicle-location records' is the thesis's unit, separate from stop events, cannot be checked. The phrase 'five days of it, counted as stop events' suggests a unit conversion that the code does not do.
findings.evidence: README.md at 798f726: 'Source period: 15 March – 8 September 2025 (~121 million stop events)'. extract_sonification_data.py: FROM stop_times_history_modeling, count(*) per bin. tools/data/sonification_days.json day totals: 431672, 412695, 802163, 810652, 810798. 121197794/178 = 680 887. texts/thesis.html:58 gives 'Prague vehicle locations'.
findings.fix: Settle on one unit across the thesis page, this note and the README. If the 121 197 794 rows are the stop-time history that the five days are drawn from, call them stop events (stop-time records) in both places and remove 'vehicle-location records'. If they really are vehicle positions, say that the record is drawn from a different, derived stop-time table and do not call it 'the same history'.
findings.note: README@798f726 line 16: '~121 million stop events'. The extraction script reads stop_times_history_modeling. 121 197 794/178 days is about 681k a day, the same scale as the day totals of 413k-811k. The page's own data line (:77) says 'stop-time history', but :57/:87 say 'vehicle-location records' and 'counted as stop events'. That contradicts the cited README. Which unit the thesis really used cannot be checked from here.

findings.location: texts/delayed.html:97 "Each mode is an instrument whose volume follows its number of stop events in the window" and :106 "the later the network runs, the higher the line"
findings.problem: Both mappings are scaled to each day's own maximum, and the text does not say so. Volume is sqrt(events / that mode's busiest window of the day). The lead's pitch is the smoothed delay divided by the day's maximum smoothed delay. So Easter Monday at its peak is as loud as the Typical Tuesday, and the lead reaches the same top note at 58 s (Easter) as at 373 s (Meltdown). 'The later the network runs, the higher the line' holds only within one day. Comparing days by ear (loudness, melody height) is not supported. Only the key carries an absolute between-day comparison.
findings.evidence: index.html@798f726 line 239: `act[m.key][i]=Math.sqrt(d.n[i]/mx)` with `mx=Math.max(1,...d.n)` per day. Lines 267-268: `act["město"][i]=wmax?wsm[i]/wmax:0`. The lead degree is `Math.round(al*(leadScale.length-5))`. Smoothed maxima recomputed: Easter 57.8 s, Meltdown 372.6 s.
findings.fix: Line 97: 'whose volume follows its stop events in the window relative to that mode's busiest window of the day (square-root scaled)'. Line 106: 'smoothed surface delay relative to the day's own peak; the line is highest at each day's worst moment, so pitch compares moments within a day, not days with each other.' Add one tldr bullet: 'Loudness and melody are scaled to each day's own peak; only the key compares days.'
findings.note: index.html:237-239: mx = max(1, ...d.n) per day per mode, act = sqrt(n/mx). Line 268: city act = wsm/wmax. Line 603: lead degree = round(al*(len-5)). wmax: Easter 57.8 s, Meltdown 372.6 s. Both mappings are per-day relative, and :97/:106 do not say so.

findings.location: texts/delayed.html:65 tldr "The rush-hour choruses and the keys come from thresholds set by hand, not from a finding."
findings.problem: The short version calls the choruses 'rush-hour'. Because the threshold is relative to each day's maximum, the chorus marks each day's own worst stretch, which is a rush hour only on the Typical Tuesday. Three of the five tracks have no morning-rush chorus: the Meltdown (15:20-18:25 only), Easter Monday (13:30-19:30 and late evening) and Summer Sunday (12:05-19:35 and 21:20-22:35). The tldr also leaves out what the five days rest on: hand-picked dates whose ranking computation is not in the repository (said only at :88).
findings.evidence: Player logic recomputed from tools/data/sonification_days.json (see the chorus finding). Line 88: 'The dates are fixed in the script, and the computation that ranked the days is not in the repository.'
findings.fix: Replace the bullet with: 'A chorus marks each day's own worst stretch (above 68 % of that day's peak delay): the two rush hours on the typical Tuesday, the afternoon on the other days. That threshold and the key cut-offs were set by hand.' Add: 'The five dates are hard-coded; the ranking that picked them is not published.'
findings.note: Player choruses: Easter 13:30-19:30 (+21:05-22:15), Summer 12:05-19:35 and 21:20-22:35. Neither is a rush hour. 'Rush-hour choruses' (:65) is therefore wrong for those days. The finding overstates the case: Back to School 07:15-11:50 covers the morning rush, and the Meltdown's 15:20-18:25 is the evening rush. So rush-hour choruses are not limited to the Typical Tuesday. The core problem holds. The omission of the date-selection caveat from the tldr is editorial.

findings.location: texts/delayed.html:103 "bus delay sets the detune in cents"; :102 "tram delay detunes the plucks"
findings.problem: The text does not say that the detune is capped. It is delay/180 clamped to [0, 1], so early running gives no detune and every delay above 180 s sounds the same. On the Meltdown the bus mean is 193 s, so the chords stay at the cap for much of the day and the instrument cannot tell 200 s from 400 s. The detune is also multiplied by a listener-adjustable 'drama' slider.
findings.evidence: index.html@798f726 line 311: `const delayNorm=(k,i)=>Math.min(1,Math.max(0,getD(k,i,"delay")/180));`. Stab detune is `45*dn*drama` and pluck detune `30*delayNorm(...)*drama`; `drama` is set from a slider at line 660. The Meltdown bus event-weighted mean is 193.5 s.
findings.fix: Add to :97: 'detune rises with delay from 0 to 180 s and stays flat above that; early running adds none.'
findings.note: index.html:311: delayNorm = clamp(delay/180, 0, 1). Stab detune 45*dn*drama (:588), pluck detune 30*delayNorm*drama (:577), drama slider 0-300 % (:152, :660). Recomputed Meltdown bus mean: 193.5 s. The text does not mention the cap or the slider.

findings.location: texts/delayed.html:67 tldr "Early running counts as negative delay, so a day with early departures sounds brighter."
findings.problem: The aggregates are arrival delays, not departures. Early running makes a day 'brighter' only through the daily mean that sets the key; it has no effect on the detune, which is clamped at 0.
findings.evidence: extract_sonification_data.py@798f726 averages `current_stop_arr_delay`. delayNorm clamps negative values to 0 (index.html line 311).
findings.fix: 'Early arrivals count as negative delay in the daily mean, so they can move a day into a brighter key.'
findings.note: The extraction script averages current_stop_arr_delay, so the delays are arrivals, not departures, and :87 itself says 'early arrivals'. delayNorm clamps negative delays to 0, so early running cannot change the detune. The lead also does not sound when al <= 0.02. Early running therefore affects brightness only through the daily mean that sets the key.

findings.location: texts/second-brain.html:78-80, h2 "A gap between NIST AI 600-1 and the extraction literature" and "The link that made this visible came from a different shelf."
findings.problem: The article frames the example as a gap between NIST AI 600-1 and the extraction literature, which the vault's linking brought in from 'a different shelf'. It never says that NIST AI 600-1 itself cites both extraction papers the article relies on. So the gap is not between NIST and that literature. At most, NIST cites the literature but does not turn its decoding findings into a suggested action.
findings.evidence: I downloaded nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf and ran pdftotext. Its reference list contains 'Carlini, N., et al. (2021) Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models. Usenix' (line 3342 of the extracted text) and 'Carlini, N. et al. (2023) Quantifying Memorization Across Neural Language Models. ICLR 2023' (line 3344). These are the article's r7 and r8.
findings.fix: Retitle the section to something like "Decoding settings missing from NIST AI 600-1's memorisation actions". After the r7/r8 sentence, add: "NIST AI 600-1 cites both of these papers in its references; what it does not do is carry their decoding settings into any suggested action." Change the deck, meta description and TL;DR in the same way, so none of them describes a gap between NIST and 'the extraction literature'.
findings.note: NIST pdftotext lines 3342 and 3344 list Carlini 2021 (Extracting Training Data) and Carlini 2023 (Quantifying Memorization), which are the article's r7 and r8. The article never says this, and its h2, meta description and JSON-LD all frame a 'gap between NIST AI 600-1 and the extraction literature'.

findings.location: texts/second-brain.html:79, "Its suggested actions accordingly concern red-teaming for training-data output (MS-2.10-001) and the curation of training data (MG-3.1-004)."
findings.problem: The text calls MG-3.1-004 only 'curation of training data'. But that action also asks for output-side measures against reproducing training data, which is the same kind of control as decoding settings. It also skips a training-data deduplication action that NIST lists in the same block. Leaving these out makes NIST look narrower than it is and makes the gap look larger.
findings.evidence: In NIST AI 600-1, MG-3.1-004 reads: 'Take reasonable measures to review training data ... and where appropriate, remove it. Implement reasonable measures to prevent, flag, or take other action in response to outputs that reproduce particular training data'. The text next to MS-2.10-003 reads 'Verify deduplication of GAI training data samples' (extracted text lines 2251-2256 and 2725-2730).
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "Its suggested actions concern red-teaming for training-data output (MS-2.10-001), deduplication of training data, and reviewing training data plus 'reasonable measures to prevent, flag, or take other action in response to outputs that reproduce particular training data' (MG-3.1-004); none of them names decoding settings."
findings.note: NIST line 2256 is MS-2.10-003 'Verify deduplication of GAI training data samples', in the same MS-2.10 block as MS-2.10-001. MG-3.1-004 includes the output-side measure 'prevent, flag... outputs that reproduce particular training data'. The article mentions neither, which makes NIST look narrower than it is.

findings.location: texts/second-brain.html:80, "The research literature supports the general point: Carlini and colleagues recovered memorised training text from GPT-2 and compared sampling strategies in doing so"
findings.problem: The text never says what 'the general point' is. The paragraph is about decoding as a way to reduce memorisation, so a reader will take it to mean that decoding settings mitigate leakage. Carlini et al. (2021) do not show that. They compared sampling schemes as an attacker, and their temperature-decay sampling was used to find more memorised text, not less. Carlini et al. (2023) use greedy decoding to define what counts as extractable, which is a measurement convention, not a mitigation result. The cited papers support only the weaker claim that the decoding choice changes how much memorised text comes out.
findings.evidence: From the article text: the sentence cites r7 and r8 as support for Raschka's framing of decoding 'with the stated aim of reducing training-data memorisation'. From Carlini et al. (2021), section 5 (stated from memory of the paper, not re-fetched in this audit): the improved schemes, decaying temperature and Internet conditioning, raise the number of memorised samples found compared with top-n sampling.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The research literature supports a narrower point, that the decoding choice changes how much memorised text a model emits: Carlini and colleagues found more memorised GPT-2 text with some sampling schemes than others, and a later study defines text as extractable when greedy decoding reproduces it from a prefix. Neither tests decoding settings as a deployer's mitigation."
findings.note: Article :80 says r7/r8 'support the general point' right after Raschka's aim of reducing memorisation via decoding. Carlini 2021 compared sampling schemes as an attacker, and its temperature-decay and conditioning schemes found more memorised text, not less. Carlini 2023 uses greedy decoding only as a definition of extractability. Neither supports decoding as a mitigation, so 'the general point' overreaches. The paper's section 5 detail was checked from my own knowledge, not re-fetched.

findings.location: texts/second-brain.html:46-54, details.tldr, "One worked example compares NIST's risk profile with the memorisation literature."
findings.problem: The short version says there is an example but not what it found: that NIST's memorisation actions never name decoding settings. It also does not say what the finding rests on (one text search of the NIST document plus a textbook example) or what would overturn it. The most practical sentence in the piece, that the stronger 'greedy decoding is riskiest' claim is untested, appears only in the body. The box also says 'memorisation literature' where the heading says 'extraction literature'.
findings.evidence: TL;DR bullets at lines 49-52. The finding is at line 79 ('finds no mention of temperature, top-k, top-p or decoding'). The untested caveat is at line 80.
findings.fix: Replace bullet 2 with: "Worked example: NIST AI 600-1 treats training-data memorisation through red-teaming, deduplication and data review, but none of its actions names decoding settings, although it cites the extraction papers that vary them. This rests on a text search of the NIST document and one textbook example. A NIST action or companion document that addresses decoding would overturn it, and the stronger claim that greedy decoding leaks most is untested."
findings.note: TL;DR line 50 reads 'compares NIST's risk profile with the memorisation literature' and does not state the finding. The heading and meta description say 'extraction literature', so the terms are inconsistent. The fix is editorial, and its suggested wording should be adjusted to findings 4 and 5.

findings.location: texts/second-brain.html:79-80, "no mention of temperature, top-k, top-p or decoding" and "under greedy decoding"
findings.problem: The worked example depends on these terms, but none of them is explained at first use: decoding, greedy decoding, temperature, top-k and top-p. A reader who does not know that decoding is how a model picks each next token cannot see why its absence from NIST matters.
findings.evidence: Line 79 is the first use of temperature, top-k, top-p and decoding. Line 80 is the first use of greedy decoding. Neither line has an inline gloss.
findings.fix: At first use in line 79, add: "decoding (how the model picks each next word from its probabilities: greedy decoding always takes the most likely one, while temperature, top-k and top-p add controlled randomness)".
findings.note: Lines 79-80 use temperature, top-k, top-p, decoding and greedy decoding with no gloss anywhere in the article.
